abstract: The paper presents an artificial neural network concept (the Synchronizable Oscillator Networks) where the instants of individual firings in the form of point processes constitute the only form of information transmitted between joining neurons. This type of communication contrasts with that which is assumed in most other models which typically are continuous or discrete value-passing networks. Limiting the messages received by each processing unit to time markers that signal the firing of other units presents significant implemen tation advantages. In our model, neurons fire spontaneously and regularly in the absence of perturbation. When interaction is present, the scheduled firings are advanced or delayed by the firing of neighboring neurons. Networks of such neurons become global oscillators which exhibit multiple synchronizing attractors. From arbitrary initial states, energy minimization learning procedures can make the network converge to oscillatory modes that satisfy multi-dimensional constraints Such networks can directly represent routing and scheduling problems that conSist of ordering sequences of events.

paragraphs: The paper proposes networks in which neurons communicate only through the timing of individual firing events. A received message says that another neuron fired, rather than carrying a numerical activation value. The authors identify implementation advantages in restricting communication to these time markers.

Each neuron fires regularly on its own. Interaction changes the schedule: a neighboring neuron's firing can advance or delay the next event. Together, the neurons form a global oscillator with several possible synchronizing attractors, meaning that the network can settle into different coordinated patterns of repeated activity.

Energy-minimization learning procedures can guide the network from arbitrary initial states toward oscillatory modes satisfying multidimensional constraints. This gives the timing dynamics a computational role: the relationships among firing events can encode a solution. Routing and scheduling are direct applications because they involve arranging events in sequences. The contribution is an architecture in which event timing serves simultaneously as the communication medium and the representation of an ordered computational result.
summary.tldr: Networks that communicate through firing times can synchronize into oscillatory patterns representing routing and scheduling solutions.

title: Synchronization in Neural Nets

abstract: Local variable selection has proven to be a powerful technique for ap(cid:173) proximating functions in high-dimensional spaces. It is used in several statistical methods, including CART, ID3, C4, MARS, and others (see the bibliography for references to these algorithms). In this paper I present a tree-structured network which is a generalization of these techniques. The network provides a framework for understanding the behavior of such algorithms and for modifying them to suit particular applications.

paragraphs: This paper concerns function approximation in spaces with many input variables. Its starting point is local variable selection: choosing which variables matter in particular parts of the approximation problem. The abstract identifies this as a useful principle already shared by several statistical methods, including CART, ID3, C4, and MARS.

The proposed contribution is a tree-structured network that generalizes these approaches. It offers a common framework for viewing methods that otherwise appear as separate algorithms. The emphasis is on their shared organization around local choices of variables and how those choices contribute to approximating a function over a high-dimensional space.

That framework serves two stated purposes. It helps explain the behavior of existing algorithms, and it provides a basis for changing them to fit particular applications. The significance is therefore conceptual and methodological: a broader network representation can make relationships among established methods easier to understand and give modifications a common structure. The abstract presents this unifying framework as the central result.
summary.tldr: A tree-structured network unifies local variable selection methods and provides a framework for understanding and adapting them.

title: Basis-Function Trees as a Generalization of Local Variable Selection Methods for Function Approximation

abstract: Recently, Ott, Grebogi and Yorke (OGY) [6] found an effective method to control chaotic systems to unstable fixed points by us(cid:173) ing only small control forces; however, OGY's method is based on and limited to a linear theory and requires considerable knowledge of the dynamics of the system to be controlled. In this paper we use two radial basis function networks: one as a model of an unknown plant and the other as the controller. The controller is trained with a recurrent learning algorithm to minimize a novel objective function such that the controller can locate an unstable fixed point and drive the system into the fixed point with no a priori knowl(cid:173) edge of the system dynamics. Our results indicate that the neural controller offers many advantages over OGY's technique.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to control a chaotic system by bringing it to an unstable fixed point. Such a point is a state that remains unchanged in principle but is not naturally stable against deviations. The authors contrast their approach with an existing method that uses small control forces but depends on linear theory and considerable knowledge of system dynamics.

Their design uses two radial basis function networks with separate roles. One models the unknown system, while the other supplies control actions. A recurrent learning algorithm trains the controller against a newly proposed objective, connecting the learning procedure to the behavior of the controlled system over time.

The objective enables the controller to locate an unstable fixed point and drive the system into it without prior knowledge of the dynamics. The authors report advantages over the earlier technique. The central contribution is the combination of a learned dynamics model and a learned controller, allowing the target state and the actions needed to reach it to be addressed together.
summary.tldr: Two radial basis function networks learn system dynamics and control actions to locate and reach an unstable fixed point in a chaotic system.

title: Exploiting Chaos to Control the Future

abstract: "Topographic" mappings occur frequently in the brain. A pop(cid:173) ular approach to understanding the structure of such mappings is to map points representing input features in a space of a few dimensions to points in a 2 dimensional space using some self(cid:173) organizing algorithm. We argue that a more general approach may be useful, where similarities between features are not con(cid:173) strained to be geometric distances, and the objective function for topographic matching is chosen explicitly rather than being spec(cid:173) ified implicitly by the self-organizing algorithm. We investigate analytically an example of this more general approach applied to the structure of interdigitated mappings, such as the pattern of ocular dominance columns in primary visual cortex.

A pop(cid:173) ular approach to understanding the structure of such mappings is to map points representing input features in a space of a few dimensions to points in a 2 dimensional space using some self(cid:173) organizing algorithm. We argue that a more general approach may be useful, where similarities between features are not con(cid:173) strained to be geometric distances, and the objective function for topographic matching is chosen explicitly rather than being spec(cid:173) ified implicitly by the self-organizing algorithm. We investigate analytically an example of this more general approach applied to the structure of interdigitated mappings, such as the pattern of ocular dominance columns in primary visual cortex.

paragraphs: Topographic brain mappings organize features across a neural surface. A common modeling approach places those features in a low-dimensional geometric space and uses a self-organizing algorithm to map them onto two dimensions. This paper questions two choices embedded in that approach: how similarity is represented and how the mapping's objective is defined.

The authors propose allowing similarities that need not be geometric distances. They also advocate explicitly choosing the objective for topographic matching, making clear what the mapping is intended to optimize. This separates the desired organization from the particular self-organizing procedure used to generate it.

They analyze an example involving interdigitated mappings, where different representations form interleaving spatial patterns. Ocular dominance columns in primary visual cortex provide the motivating example. The contribution is a more general way to formulate and study cortical organization: specify the relevant feature similarities and the matching objective directly, then examine the resulting structure. This makes the assumptions governing a map available for explicit mathematical analysis.
summary.tldr: Explicit objectives and non-geometric feature similarities provide a more general framework for analyzing cortical maps.

title: Optimizing Cortical Mappings

abstract: Many neural systems extend their dynamic range by adaptation. We ex(cid:173) amine the timescales of adaptation in the context of dynamically mod(cid:173) ulated rapidly-varying stimuli, and demonstrate in the fly visual system that adaptation to the statistical ensemble of the stimulus dynamically maximizes information transmission about the time-dependent stimulus. Further, while the rate response has long transients, the adaptation takes place on timescales consistent with optimal variance estimation.
authors: Robert R. de Ruyter van Steveninck
originalAbstract: Many neural systems extend their dynamic range by adaptation. We ex(cid:173) amine the timescales of adaptation in the context of dynamically mod(cid:173) ulated rapidly-varying stimuli, and demonstrate in the fly visual system that adaptation to the statistical ensemble of the stimulus dynamically maximizes information transmission about the time-dependent stimulus. Further, while the rate response has long transients, the adaptation takes place on timescales consistent with optimal variance estimation.

paragraphs: The paper examines how quickly neural coding adapts when the statistical properties of a rapidly varying stimulus change. Adaptation allows many neural systems to operate across a wider dynamic range. The authors study its timing in the fly visual system using rapidly varying stimuli whose statistical ensemble is dynamically modulated.

They demonstrate that adaptation to this ensemble dynamically maximizes information transmission about the time-dependent stimulus. This relates adaptation to the information carried by neural responses, giving it a functional interpretation. The relevant question is how the coding of a changing stimulus adjusts as the stimulus statistics themselves change.

The authors also distinguish the timing of adaptation from the timing visible in the firing-rate response. Although that rate response has long transients, adaptation occurs on timescales consistent with optimal estimation of stimulus variance. Thus, a slowly settling rate response does not by itself describe how rapidly the code adjusts. The findings connect multiple response timescales to information transmission and statistical estimation in the examined visual system.
summary.tldr: Fly visual adaptation dynamically maximizes transmitted information on timescales consistent with optimal variance estimation, despite long firing-rate transients.

title: Multiple Timescales of Adaptation in a Neural Code

abstract: Successful application of reinforcement learning algorithms often involves considerable hand-crafting of the necessary non-linear features to reduce the complexity of the value functions and hence to promote convergence of the algorithm. In contrast, the human brain readily and autonomously finds the complex features when provided with sufficient training. Recent work in machine learning and neurophysiology has demonstrated the role of the basal ganglia and the frontal cortex in mammalian reinforcement learning. This paper develops and explores new learning algorithms that provides potential new approaches to the feature construction problem. The algorithms are compared and evaluated on the Acrobot task. inspired by neurological evidence

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often depends on choosing useful features before learning can proceed effectively. The paper focuses on nonlinear features that simplify the value function, making it easier for an algorithm to learn and potentially helping convergence. Constructing these features by hand can require substantial effort and knowledge of the task.

The authors draw motivation from the brain's ability to acquire complex features through training. They connect this motivation to work on the roles of the basal ganglia and frontal cortex in mammalian reinforcement learning. Neurological evidence serves as a basis for developing learning algorithms that offer possible approaches to the feature-construction problem.

The proposed algorithms are explored and compared on the Acrobot task. This evaluation grounds the feature-learning ideas in a concrete reinforcement-learning setting. The abstract presents the methods as potential new approaches, so the contribution is the development and examination of brain-inspired alternatives for constructing useful representations. Its stated motivation is to address the feature-design burden that can accompany practical reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops brain-inspired reinforcement-learning algorithms that explore automatic feature construction and evaluates them on Acrobot.

title: Brain Inspired Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Survey propagation is a powerful technique from statistical physics that has been applied to solve the 3-SAT problem both in principle and in practice. We give, using only probability arguments, a common deriva- tion of survey propagation, belief propagation and several interesting hy- brid methods. We then present numerical experiments which use WSAT (a widely used random-walk based SAT solver) to quantify the complex- ity of the 3-SAT formulae as a function of their parameters, both as ran- domly generated and after simplication, guided by survey propagation. Some properties of WSAT which have not previously been reported make it an ideal tool for this purpose its mean cost is proportional to the num- ber of variables in the formula (at a xed ratio of clauses to variables) in the easy-SAT regime and slightly beyond, and its behavior in the hard- SAT regime appears to reect the underlying structure of the solution space that has been predicted by replica symmetry-breaking arguments. An analysis of the tradeoffs between the various methods of search for satisfying assignments shows WSAT to be far more powerful than has been appreciated, and suggests some interesting new directions for prac- tical algorithm development.

paragraphs: This paper compares methods for solving 3-SAT, the problem of finding truth assignments that satisfy a collection of three-variable clauses. It first develops a shared derivation of survey propagation, belief propagation, and hybrid methods using probability arguments. This places several approaches within a common framework for examining their relationships.

The authors then use the random-walk solver WSAT to assess formula difficulty, both before and after simplification guided by survey propagation. Their numerical experiments examine how difficulty varies with formula parameters. At a fixed ratio of clauses to variables, WSAT’s mean cost grows proportionally with the number of variables in the easy satisfiable regime and somewhat beyond it.

In the hard satisfiable regime, WSAT’s behavior appears to reflect solution-space structure predicted by replica symmetry-breaking arguments. This is presented as an observed correspondence. The comparison of search tradeoffs indicates that WSAT is more powerful than previously appreciated and motivates further practical algorithm development alongside the unified probabilistic treatment of propagation methods.
summary.tldr: A unified probabilistic treatment of propagation methods and numerical comparisons reveal underappreciated strengths of the random-walk SAT solver WSAT.

title: Comparing Beliefs, Surveys, and Random Walks

abstract: We consider a framework for semi-supervised learning using spectral decomposition based un-supervised kernel design. This approach sub- sumes a class of previously proposed semi-supervised learning methods on data graphs. We examine various theoretical properties of such meth- ods. In particular, we derive a generalization performance bound, and obtain the optimal kernel design by minimizing the bound. Based on the theoretical analysis, we are able to demonstrate why spectral kernel design based methods can often improve the predictive performance. Ex- periments are used to illustrate the main consequences of our analysis.

This approach sub- sumes a class of previously proposed semi-supervised learning methods on data graphs. We examine various theoretical properties of such meth- ods. In particular, we derive a generalization performance bound, and obtain the optimal kernel design by minimizing the bound. Based on the theoretical analysis, we are able to demonstrate why spectral kernel design based methods can often improve the predictive performance. Ex- periments are used to illustrate the main consequences of our analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies semi-supervised learning methods that construct a kernel through an unsupervised spectral decomposition. The kernel provides the representation used for learning, while the spectral construction draws on structure in the data. The framework encompasses a class of earlier methods based on data graphs, allowing the authors to analyze them together.

The central theoretical result is a bound on generalization performance. The authors then choose the kernel design by minimizing that bound. This links the construction of the representation to a stated learning criterion: the selected design is optimal for the bound being minimized, rather than being presented as universally best for every prediction task.

The analysis explains why spectral kernel design can often improve predictive performance. Experiments illustrate the main consequences of the theory, connecting the mathematical treatment to observed behavior. The value of the work is both explanatory and prescriptive: it helps account for the success of existing graph methods and gives a principled objective for designing their kernels.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a generalization bound for spectral kernel methods and uses it to guide kernel design for semi-supervised learning.

title: Analysis of Spectral Kernel Design based Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: Fast and frugal heuristics are well studied models of bounded rationality. Psychological research has proposed the take-the-best heuristic as a successful strategy in decision making with limited resources. Take-thebest searches for a sufficiently good ordering of cues (features) in a task where objects are to be compared lexicographically. We investigate the complexity of the problem of approximating optimal cue permutations for lexicographic strategies. We show that no efficient algorithm can approximate the optimum to within any constant factor, if P = NP. We further consider a greedy approach for building lexicographic strategies and derive tight bounds for the performance ratio of a new and simple algorithm. This algorithm is proven to perform better than take-the-best.

Psychological research has proposed the take-the-best heuristic as a successful strategy in decision making with limited resources. Take-thebest searches for a sufficiently good ordering of cues (features) in a task where objects are to be compared lexicographically. We investigate the complexity of the problem of approximating optimal cue permutations for lexicographic strategies. We show that no efficient algorithm can approximate the optimum to within any constant factor, if P = NP. paragraphs: The paper studies decision rules that compare objects by checking cues in an ordered sequence. In these lexicographic strategies, cue ordering is central to the quality of the decisions. The motivating example is take-the-best, a fast and frugal heuristic intended to make effective decisions when computational resources are limited.

The authors investigate how difficult it is to approximate the best possible ordering of cues. The supplied abstract states that no efficient algorithm can approximate the optimum within any constant factor if P = NP. That is the condition as supplied; the computational claim must be read together with its stated condition rather than as an unconditional impossibility.

The paper also develops a simple greedy algorithm for constructing lexicographic strategies and derives tight bounds on its performance ratio. It proves that this algorithm performs better than take-the-best. The work therefore examines both the difficulty of obtaining good cue orderings and a concrete alternative with a stronger proven performance guarantee than the motivating heuristic.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes approximation of cue orderings and proves that a new greedy strategy performs better than take-the-best.

title: On the Accuracy of Bounded Rationality: How Far from Optimal Is Fast and Frugal?

abstract: Traditional analysis methods for single-trial classification of electro-encephalography (EEG) focus on two types of paradigms: phase locked methods, in which the amplitude of the signal is used as the feature for classification, i.e. event related potentials; and second order methods, in which the feature of interest is the power of the signal, i.e event related (de)synchronization. The process of deciding which paradigm to use is ad hoc and is driven by knowledge of neurological findings. Here we propose a unified method in which the algorithm learns the best first and second order spatial and temporal features for classification of EEG based on a bilinear model. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated in simulated and real EEG from a benchmark data set for Brain Computer Interface.

The process of deciding which paradigm to use is ad hoc and is driven by knowledge of neurological findings. Here we propose a unified method in which the algorithm learns the best first and second order spatial and temporal features for classification of EEG based on a bilinear model. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated in simulated and real EEG from a benchmark data set for Brain Computer Interface.

paragraphs: Single-trial EEG classification traditionally uses one of two kinds of signal information. Phase-locked methods use signal amplitude, as in event-related potentials. Second-order methods use signal power, as in event-related synchronization or desynchronization. Choosing between these approaches has often depended on neurological knowledge and an ad hoc decision about which signal properties should matter.

The paper proposes a unified bilinear model that learns first- and second-order features together. It searches for useful structure across both space and time, allowing classification to draw on amplitude-related and power-related information within one method. This moves the choice of discriminative features into the learning algorithm instead of requiring an initial commitment to one paradigm.

The authors demonstrate the method's efficiency using simulated EEG and real EEG from a brain-computer-interface benchmark dataset. The stated contribution is the unified learning formulation and its demonstration on both types of data. It offers a common route for learning which spatial and temporal signal characteristics are useful for classifying an individual EEG trial.
summary.tldr: A bilinear EEG classifier jointly learns amplitude- and power-related spatial and temporal features for individual trials.

title: Second Order Bilinear Discriminant Analysis for single trial EEG analysis

abstract: The inverse dynamics problem for a robotic manipulator is to compute the torques needed at the joints to drive it along a given trajectory; it is beneficial to be able to learn this function for adaptive control. A given robot manipulator will often need to be controlled while holding different loads in its end effector, giving rise to a multi-task learning problem. We show how the structure of the inverse dynamics problem gives rise to a multi-task Gaussian process prior over functions, where the inter-task similarity depends on the underlying dynamic parameters. Experiments demonstrate that this multi-task formulation generally improves performance over either learning only on single tasks or pooling the data over all tasks.
originalAbstract: The inverse dynamics problem for a robotic manipulator is to compute the torques needed at the joints to drive it along a given trajectory; it is beneficial to be able to learn this function for adaptive control. A given robot manipulator will often need to be controlled while holding different loads in its end effector, giving rise to a multi-task learning problem. We show how the structure of the inverse dynamics problem gives rise to a multi-task Gaussian process prior over functions, where the inter-task similarity depends on the underlying dynamic parameters. Experiments demonstrate that this multi-task formulation generally improves performance over either learning only on single tasks or pooling the data over all tasks.

paragraphs: Robot inverse dynamics determines the joint torques needed to follow a desired trajectory. Learning this relationship can support adaptive control, but the relationship changes when the robot carries different loads. The paper treats these load conditions as related learning tasks, each describing the same manipulator operating with different dynamics.

The authors use the structure of inverse dynamics to construct a multi-task Gaussian process prior over the relevant functions. Similarity between tasks depends on the underlying dynamic parameters. This gives the model a structured basis for sharing information: the relationship between load conditions is connected to the physical quantities that govern the robot's motion.

Experiments show that this multi-task formulation generally performs better than learning each task separately or pooling all task data together. Separate learning misses opportunities to share information, while pooling does not represent the tasks' differences in the same way. The reported result supports using the mechanics of the problem to determine how knowledge transfers across load conditions, while retaining a distinct prediction function for each task.
summary.tldr: A dynamics-informed multi-task Gaussian process generally improves learned robot inverse dynamics across different carried loads.

title: Multi-task Gaussian Process Learning of Robot Inverse Dynamics

abstract: We introduce a new interpretation of multiscale random fields (MSRFs) that admits efficient optimization in the framework of regular (single level) random fields (RFs). It is based on a new operator, called append, that combines sets of random variables (RVs) to single RVs. We assume that a MSRF can be decomposed into disjoint trees that link RVs at different pyramid levels. The append operator is then applied to map RVs in each tree structure to a single RV. We demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed approach on a challenging task involving grouping contours of target shapes in images. MSRFs provide a natural representation of multiscale contour models, which are needed in order to cope with unstable contour decompositions. The append operator allows us to find optimal image labels using the classical framework of relaxation labeling, Alternative methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) could also be used.

paragraphs: Multiscale random fields represent related variables at several levels of detail. This is useful for contour grouping in images, where decompositions into contour pieces can be unstable and a shape may need representation at multiple scales. The paper develops a new interpretation that makes such models accessible to efficient single-level random-field optimization.

The construction assumes that the multiscale field can be separated into disjoint trees connecting variables at different pyramid levels. An operator called append combines the variables within each tree into a single variable. This transformation turns the multilevel representation into a form that ordinary random-field methods can process.

The authors demonstrate the approach by grouping contours belonging to target shapes in images. Using the transformed representation, they obtain optimal image labels through classical relaxation labeling; they also identify MCMC as a possible alternative. The contribution is a bridge between multiscale shape modeling and established optimization machinery, with the disjoint-tree decomposition providing the stated structural condition for that bridge.
summary.tldr: An append operator converts suitably structured multiscale random fields into single-level models for efficient contour-grouping optimization.

title: Multiscale Random Fields with Application to Contour Grouping

abstract: We introduce a new family of positive-definite kernel functions that mimic the computation in large, multilayer neural nets. These kernel functions can be used in shallow architectures, such as support vector machines (SVMs), or in deep kernel-based architectures that we call multilayer kernel machines (MKMs). We evaluate SVMs and MKMs with these kernel functions on problems designed to illustrate the advantages of deep architectures. On several problems, we obtain better results than previous, leading benchmarks from both SVMs with Gaussian kernels as well as deep belief nets.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new family of positive-definite kernel functions that mimic the computation in large, multilayer neural nets. These kernel functions can be used in shallow architectures, such as support vector machines (SVMs), or in deep kernel-based architectures that we call multilayer kernel machines (MKMs). We evaluate SVMs and MKMs with these kernel functions on problems designed to illustrate the advantages of deep architectures. On several problems, we obtain better results than previous, leading benchmarks from both SVMs with Gaussian kernels as well as deep belief nets.

paragraphs: This paper connects kernel methods with the computations performed by large multilayer neural networks. It introduces a family of positive-definite kernels designed to mimic those computations. The aim is to make this kind of representation available within kernel-based learning, linking a neural-network-inspired similarity function with established kernel modeling approaches.

The kernels can be used in two ways. One places them inside a shallow model, such as a support vector machine. The other builds a deep architecture called a multilayer kernel machine. These alternatives distinguish the computation encoded by a kernel from the architecture that uses it: the proposed kernels support both shallow and multilayer models.

The authors evaluate both approaches on problems chosen to illustrate advantages of deep architectures. On several problems, they report better results than leading benchmarks from Gaussian-kernel support vector machines and deep belief networks. Those findings support the usefulness of this kernel family on the evaluated tasks and show that neural-network-like computations can be productive within kernel methods.
summary.tldr: Kernels that mimic multilayer neural computations improve results on several evaluated problems in both support vector machines and multilayer kernel machines.

title: Kernel Methods for Deep Learning

abstract: The sample complexity of active learning under the realizability assumption has been well-studied. The realizability assumption, however, rarely holds in practice. In this paper, we theoretically characterize the sample complexity of active learning in the non-realizable case under multi-view setting. We prove that, with unbounded Tsybakov noise, the sample complexity of multi-view active learning can be $\widetilde{O}(\log \frac{1}{\epsilon})$, contrasting to single-view setting where the polynomial improvement is the best possible achievement. We also prove that in general multi-view setting the sample complexity of active learning with unbounded Tsybakov noise is $\widetilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$, where the order of $1/\epsilon$ is independent of the parameter in Tsybakov noise, contrasting to previous polynomial bounds where the order of $1/\epsilon$ is related to the parameter in Tsybakov noise.
originalAbstract: The sample complexity of active learning under the realizability assumption has been well-studied. The realizability assumption, however, rarely holds in practice. In this paper, we theoretically characterize the sample complexity of active learning in the non-realizable case under multi-view setting. We prove that, with unbounded Tsybakov noise, the sample complexity of multi-view active learning can be $\widetilde{O}(\log \frac{1}{\epsilon})$, contrasting to single-view setting where the polynomial improvement is the best possible achievement. We also prove that in general multi-view setting the sample complexity of active learning with unbounded Tsybakov noise is $\widetilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$, where the order of $1/\epsilon$ is independent of the parameter in Tsybakov noise, contrasting to previous polynomial bounds where the order of $1/\epsilon$ is related to the parameter in Tsybakov noise.

paragraphs: Active learning concerns how many labeled examples a learner needs when it can choose which examples to query. Much theory assumes realizability, meaning that the available model class can perfectly represent the labeling rule. This paper studies the non-realizable case with multiple views of the data, addressing a setting where that ideal assumption does not hold.

Under unbounded Tsybakov noise, the authors prove that multi-view active learning can achieve a label requirement that grows logarithmically with inverse target error, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. They contrast this possibility with the single-view setting, where the best possible improvement is polynomial. The logarithmic result is a possible multi-view rate, rather than a guarantee for every such setting.

For the general multi-view setting, they establish a bound proportional to inverse target error, again up to logarithmic factors. Its exponent is independent of the Tsybakov noise parameter, unlike earlier polynomial bounds. Together, the results characterize how multiple views can change label requirements even when perfect realizability is unavailable.
summary.tldr: The paper proves improved multi-view active-learning label bounds under unbounded Tsybakov noise without assuming realizability.

title: Multi-View Active Learning in the Non-Realizable Case

abstract: We consider linear models for stochastic dynamics. Any such model can be associated a network (namely a directed graph) describing which degrees of freedom interact under the dynamics. We tackle the problem of learning such a network from observation of the system trajectory over a time interval T. We analyse the l1-regularized least squares algorithm and, in the setting in which the underlying network is sparse, we prove performance guarantees that are uniform in the sampling rate as long as this is sufficiently high. This result substantiates the notion of a well defined ‘time complexity’ for the network inference problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover interactions in a system with linear stochastic dynamics. Such a system can be represented by a directed graph whose connections describe which variables influence others during its evolution. The available evidence is an observed system trajectory spanning a time interval of length T.

The authors analyze an l1-regularized least-squares method for inferring this network. Their guarantees apply when the underlying network is sparse, meaning that relatively few interactions need to be recovered. A central feature of the analysis is that the performance guarantees remain uniform across sampling rates once the rate is sufficiently high.

This result supports describing the difficulty of network inference in terms of observation duration, or time complexity. Taking more closely spaced measurements and observing a system for longer are distinct aspects of data collection. By obtaining guarantees that do not deteriorate with changes among sufficiently high sampling rates, the paper gives theoretical substance to the idea that elapsed observation time is a meaningful resource for this inference problem.
summary.tldr: For sparse linear stochastic systems, l1-regularized network inference has guarantees uniform over sufficiently high sampling rates.

title: Learning Networks of Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: Inexpensive RGB-D cameras that give an RGB image together with depth data have become widely available. In this paper, we use this data to build 3D point clouds of full indoor scenes such as an office and address the task of semantic labeling of these 3D point clouds. We propose a graphical model that captures various features and contextual relations, including the local visual appearance and shape cues, object co-occurence relationships and geometric relationships. With a large number of object classes and relations, the model’s parsimony becomes important and we address that by using multiple types of edge potentials. The model admits efficient approximate inference, and we train it using a maximum-margin learning approach. In our experiments over a total of 52 3D scenes of homes and offices (composed from about 550 views, having 2495 segments labeled with 27 object classes), we get a performance of 84.06% in labeling 17 object classes for offices, and 73.38% in labeling 17 object classes for home scenes. Finally, we applied these algorithms successfully on a mobile robot for the task of finding objects in large cluttered rooms.

title: Semantic Labeling of 3D Point Clouds for Indoor Scenes

abstract: Hermitian positive definite matrices (HPD) recur throughout statistics and machine learning. In this paper we develop \emph{geometric optimisation} for globally optimising certain nonconvex loss functions arising in the modelling of data via elliptically contoured distributions (ECDs). We exploit the remarkable structure of the convex cone of positive definite matrices which allows one to uncover hidden geodesic convexity of objective functions that are nonconvex in the ordinary Euclidean sense. Going even beyond manifold convexity we show how further metric properties of HPD matrices can be exploited to globally optimise several ECD log-likelihoods that are not even geodesic convex. We present key results that help recognise this geometric structure, as well as obtain efficient fixed-point algorithms to optimise the corresponding objective functions. To our knowledge, ours are the most general results on geometric optimisation of HPD matrices known so far. Experiments reveal the benefits of our approach---it avoids any eigenvalue computations which makes it very competitive.

paragraphs: Some statistical estimation problems optimize over Hermitian positive definite matrices and produce losses that are nonconvex in ordinary Euclidean coordinates. This paper studies such problems for elliptically contoured distributions. Its central idea is to use the geometry of the positive definite matrix space to reveal optimization structure that ordinary convexity does not capture.

For certain objectives, the authors uncover geodesic convexity: convex behavior along paths defined by the matrix space's geometry. They also go beyond that case, exploiting additional metric properties to globally optimize several distribution log-likelihoods that are not geodesically convex. The global optimization conclusions concern the objective classes covered by these structural results.

The paper supplies results for recognizing the relevant geometry and derives efficient fixed-point algorithms for the corresponding objectives. These algorithms avoid eigenvalue computations, a computational feature the authors connect to competitive experimental performance. The contribution combines a way to establish global optimization properties with procedures that use those properties to carry out statistical estimation.
summary.tldr: The geometry of positive definite matrices enables global optimization of certain nonconvex statistical losses through efficient fixed-point algorithms.

title: Geometric optimisation on positive definite matrices for elliptically contoured distributions

abstract: Shannon's entropy is a basic quantity in information theory, and a fundamental building block for the analysis of neural codes. Estimating the entropy of a discrete distribution from samples is an important and difficult problem that has received considerable attention in statistics and theoretical neuroscience. However, neural responses have characteristic statistical structure that generic entropy estimators fail to exploit. For example, existing Bayesian entropy estimators make the naive assumption that all spike words are equally likely a priori, which makes for an inefficient allocation of prior probability mass in cases where spikes are sparse. Here we develop Bayesian estimators for the entropy of binary spike trains using priors designed to flexibly exploit the statistical structure of simultaneously-recorded spike responses. We define two prior distributions over spike words using mixtures of Dirichlet distributions centered on simple parametric models. The parametric model captures high-level statistical features of the data, such as the average spike count in a spike word, which allows the posterior over entropy to concentrate more rapidly than with standard estimators (e.g., in cases where the probability of spiking differs strongly from 0.5). Conversely, the Dirichlet distributions assign prior mass to distributions far from the parametric model, ensuring consistent estimates for arbitrary distributions. We devise a compact representation of the data and prior that allow for computationally efficient implementations of Bayesian least squares and empirical Bayes entropy estimators with large numbers of neurons. We apply these estimators to simulated and real neural data and show that they substantially outperform traditional methods.

paragraphs: Entropy measures uncertainty in neural response patterns, but estimating it from limited observations is difficult. Generic Bayesian estimators can waste prior probability on implausible patterns by treating all binary spike words symmetrically. This matters when spikes are sparse, because patterns with many spikes should not necessarily receive the same initial treatment as mostly silent patterns.

The paper constructs two priors from mixtures of Dirichlet distributions centered on simple parametric models. Those models encode broad features such as average spike count. This guidance can make the posterior over entropy concentrate faster, including when spiking probability is far from one half. The Dirichlet components also permit substantial departures from the parametric center, preserving consistency for arbitrary underlying distributions.

A compact representation of observations and priors supports efficient Bayesian least-squares and empirical Bayes implementations with many neurons. Tests on simulated and real neural data show substantial improvements over traditional methods. The approach therefore combines useful structural expectations with enough flexibility to learn response distributions that do not follow the initial parametric model.
summary.tldr: Structured yet flexible Bayesian priors improve entropy estimation for binary neural responses while retaining consistency beyond the guiding parametric model.

title: Bayesian entropy estimation for binary spike train data using parametric prior knowledge

abstract: Lazy local learning methods train a classifier on the fly" at test time, using only a subset of the training instances that are most relevant to the novel test example. The goal is to tailor the classifier to the properties of the data surrounding the test example. Existing methods assume that the instances most useful for building the local model are strictly those closest to the test example. However, this fails to account for the fact that the success of the resulting classifier depends on the full distribution of selected training instances. Rather than simply gather the test example's nearest neighbors, we propose to predict the subset of training data that is jointly relevant to training its local model. We develop an approach to discover patterns between queries and their "good" neighborhoods using large-scale multi-label classification with compressed sensing. Given a novel test point, we estimate both the composition and size of the training subset likely to yield an accurate local model. We demonstrate the approach on image classification tasks on SUN and aPascal and show it outperforms traditional global and local approaches."

The goal is to tailor the classifier to the properties of the data surrounding the test example. However, this fails to account for the fact that the success of the resulting classifier depends on the full distribution of selected training instances. Rather than simply gather the test example's nearest neighbors, we propose to predict the subset of training data that is jointly relevant to training its local model. paragraphs: Lazy local learning builds a classifier at prediction time using training examples selected for the new query. Standard approaches choose nearby examples, assuming proximity identifies useful training data. This paper argues that a local model's success depends on the entire selected collection, so closeness alone can overlook useful neighborhood structure.

The authors propose learning which subsets are jointly useful for training local classifiers. Their method discovers relationships between queries and good neighborhoods through large-scale multi-label classification with compressed sensing. For a new test point, it predicts both which training instances to include and how large the selected subset should be.

This changes neighborhood selection from a fixed distance-based rule into a learned component of prediction. The target is a collection likely to produce an accurate local model, which allows the composition and size of that collection to vary with the query. Experiments on SUN and aPascal image-classification tasks show improvements over traditional global and local methods. The results support selecting examples for their combined usefulness in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Predicting the composition and size of useful training neighborhoods improves local image classifiers in the reported experiments.

title: Predicting Useful Neighborhoods for Lazy Local Learning

abstract: Bayesian nonparametric models, such as Gaussian processes, provide a compelling framework for automatic statistical modelling: these models have a high degree of flexibility, and automatically calibrated complexity. However, automating human expertise remains elusive; for example, Gaussian processes with standard kernels struggle on function extrapolation problems that are trivial for human learners. In this paper, we create function extrapolation problems and acquire human responses, and then design a kernel learning framework to reverse engineer the inductive biases of human learners across a set of behavioral experiments. We use the learned kernels to gain psychological insights and to extrapolate in human-like ways that go beyond traditional stationary and polynomial kernels. Finally, we investigate Occam's razor in human and Gaussian process based function learning.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible statistical models with automatically calibrated complexity, yet standard kernels can struggle to extend patterns that people extrapolate easily. This paper investigates what human responses to function-extrapolation problems reveal about the assumptions guiding that behavior. The goal is to capture some of those assumptions in learned kernels.

The authors create extrapolation tasks, collect human responses, and develop a kernel-learning framework across behavioral experiments. They use it to reverse engineer inductive biases: the preferences that guide predictions beyond the observed portion of a function. Learning from responses connects a mathematical modeling component to measured human behavior.

The resulting kernels are used both to gain psychological insight and to extrapolate in human-like ways beyond traditional stationary and polynomial kernels. The paper also investigates Occam’s razor in human and Gaussian-process function learning. Its contribution links model construction with behavioral analysis, using the same learned representation to explore how people generalize and to reproduce aspects of their predictions.
summary.tldr: Kernels learned from human extrapolation responses capture inductive biases and enable more human-like function predictions.

title: The Human Kernel

abstract: In this paper, we extend the geometric descent method recently proposed by Bubeck, Lee and Singh to tackle nonsmooth and strongly convex composite problems. We prove that our proposed algorithm, dubbed geometric proximal gradient method (GeoPG), converges with a linear rate $(1-1/\sqrt{\kappa})$ and thus achieves the optimal rate among first-order methods, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of the problem. Numerical results on linear regression and logistic regression with elastic net regularization show that GeoPG compares favorably with Nesterov's accelerated proximal gradient method, especially when the problem is ill-conditioned.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we extend the geometric descent method recently proposed by Bubeck, Lee and Singh to tackle nonsmooth and strongly convex composite problems. We prove that our proposed algorithm, dubbed geometric proximal gradient method (GeoPG), converges with a linear rate $(1-1/\sqrt{\kappa})$ and thus achieves the optimal rate among first-order methods, where $\kappa$ is the condition number of the problem. Numerical results on linear regression and logistic regression with elastic net regularization show that GeoPG compares favorably with Nesterov's accelerated proximal gradient method, especially when the problem is ill-conditioned.

paragraphs: The paper extends geometric descent to optimization problems that are both strongly convex and composite, while allowing nonsmooth terms. This broadens the method's scope to objectives in which an otherwise smooth fitting problem is combined with a term that need not be differentiable. The resulting algorithm is called geometric proximal gradient, or GeoPG.

The main theoretical result is a linear convergence rate with factor 1 - 1/sqrt(kappa), where kappa is the problem's condition number. Here, linear convergence describes geometric reduction of optimization error across iterations. The authors show that this rate is optimal among first-order methods for the problem setting, placing the extension on a strong theoretical footing.

Numerical experiments consider linear and logistic regression with elastic net regularization. GeoPG compares favorably with Nesterov's accelerated proximal gradient method, particularly on ill-conditioned problems. These findings connect the convergence guarantee to concrete regularized learning objectives. The paper therefore offers both an extension of geometric descent and evidence that it can be useful in demanding optimization conditions.
summary.tldr: GeoPG extends geometric descent to nonsmooth strongly convex composite problems with an optimal first-order convergence rate.

title: Geometric Descent Method for Convex Composite Minimization

abstract: Responses generated by neural conversational models tend to lack informativeness and diversity. We present Adversarial Information Maximization (AIM), an adversarial learning framework that addresses these two related but distinct problems. To foster response diversity, we leverage adversarial training that allows distributional matching of synthetic and real responses. To improve informativeness, our framework explicitly optimizes a variational lower bound on pairwise mutual information between query and response. Empirical results from automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our methods significantly boost informativeness and diversity.
originalAbstract: Responses generated by neural conversational models tend to lack informativeness and diversity. We present Adversarial Information Maximization (AIM), an adversarial learning framework that addresses these two related but distinct problems. To foster response diversity, we leverage adversarial training that allows distributional matching of synthetic and real responses. To improve informativeness, our framework explicitly optimizes a variational lower bound on pairwise mutual information between query and response. Empirical results from automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our methods significantly boost informativeness and diversity.

paragraphs: Neural conversation models can produce responses that offer little information or vary too little across conversations. The paper treats informativeness and diversity as related but distinct goals. A method aimed at improving one therefore needs an explicit account of how it addresses the other, rather than relying on a single undifferentiated notion of response quality.

Adversarial Information Maximization, or AIM, combines two training components. Adversarial training encourages the distribution of generated responses to match the distribution of real responses, addressing diversity. A separate objective increases a variational lower bound on mutual information between a query and its response. This connects informativeness to how much information the paired utterances share.

The contribution is the combination of these objectives in one adversarial learning framework. It addresses variation among generated responses while also encouraging responses to carry information about their particular queries. Automatic evaluations and human assessments both show significant improvements in informativeness and diversity. These are empirical findings for the evaluated methods, supporting the proposed separation and joint treatment of the two goals.
summary.tldr: AIM combines adversarial response matching with a mutual-information objective to improve conversational diversity and informativeness in evaluations.

title: Generating Informative and Diverse Conversational Responses via Adversarial Information Maximization

abstract: Few-shot learning has become essential for producing models that generalize from few examples. In this work, we identify that metric scaling and metric task conditioning are important to improve the performance of few-shot algorithms. Our analysis reveals that simple metric scaling completely changes the nature of few-shot algorithm parameter updates. Metric scaling provides improvements up to 14% in accuracy for certain metrics on the mini-Imagenet 5-way 5-shot classification task. We further propose a simple and effective way of conditioning a learner on the task sample set, resulting in learning a task-dependent metric space. Moreover, we propose and empirically test a practical end-to-end optimization procedure based on auxiliary task co-training to learn a task-dependent metric space. The resulting few-shot learning model based on the task-dependent scaled metric achieves state of the art on mini-Imagenet. We confirm these results on another few-shot dataset that we introduce in this paper based on CIFAR100.

We confirm these results on another few-shot dataset that we introduce in this paper based on CIFAR100.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to generalize from only a small number of examples. TADAM studies how the metric used to compare examples affects this process. The paper identifies two influential choices: the scale of the metric and whether the comparison space adapts to the current task's sample set.

The analysis shows that simple metric scaling can fundamentally change parameter updates. For certain metrics on mini-ImageNet's five-way, five-shot classification task, scaling improves accuracy by up to 14%. The authors then condition the learner on the task examples so that it learns a task-dependent metric space, and introduce an end-to-end training procedure using auxiliary task co-training.

The resulting model combines metric scaling with task adaptation and achieves the reported state of the art on mini-ImageNet. The authors also confirm their findings on a few-shot dataset they introduce using CIFAR100. The significance is that both numerical scaling and task context affect how comparisons are learned; a distance function's role extends beyond simply ranking examples after training.
summary.tldr: TADAM improves few-shot learning by scaling comparison metrics and adapting the metric space to each task's examples.

title: TADAM: Task dependent adaptive metric for improved few-shot learning

abstract: We reduce the computational cost of Neural AutoML with transfer learning. AutoML relieves human effort by automating the design of ML algorithms. Neural AutoML has become popular for the design of deep learning architectures, however, this method has a high computation cost. To address this we propose Transfer Neural AutoML that uses knowledge from prior tasks to speed up network design. We extend RL-based architecture search methods to support parallel training on multiple tasks and then transfer the search strategy to new tasks. On language and image classification data, Transfer Neural AutoML reduces convergence time over single-task training by over an order of magnitude on many tasks.

We extend RL-based architecture search methods to support parallel training on multiple tasks and then transfer the search strategy to new tasks. On language and image classification data, Transfer Neural AutoML reduces convergence time over single-task training by over an order of magnitude on many tasks.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the computational expense of automatically designing neural network architectures. Neural AutoML reduces the human effort involved in architecture design, but searching for a suitable network can itself be costly. The proposed approach uses knowledge from earlier tasks to make subsequent architecture searches converge more quickly.

The authors extend reinforcement-learning-based architecture search so that it can train in parallel across multiple tasks. They then transfer the learned search strategy to new tasks. The transferable component is the strategy for searching for architectures, allowing experience with earlier design problems to inform how later design problems are explored.

On language and image classification data, Transfer Neural AutoML reduces convergence time by more than an order of magnitude relative to single-task training on many tasks. The qualification matters: the reported reduction applies to many evaluated tasks, rather than being stated as universal. The finding supports reusing search experience as a way to reduce the computational burden of automated network design.
summary.tldr: Transferring architecture search strategies across tasks cuts convergence time by more than an order of magnitude on many evaluated tasks.

title: Transfer Learning with Neural AutoML

abstract: We propose meta-curvature (MC), a framework to learn curvature information for better generalization and fast model adaptation. MC expands on the model-agnostic meta-learner (MAML) by learning to transform the gradients in the inner optimization such that the transformed gradients achieve better generalization performance to a new task. For training large scale neural networks, we decompose the curvature matrix into smaller matrices in a novel scheme where we capture the dependencies of the model's parameters with a series of tensor products. We demonstrate the effects of our proposed method on several few-shot learning tasks and datasets. Without any task specific techniques and architectures, the proposed method achieves substantial improvement upon previous MAML variants and outperforms the recent state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we observe faster convergence rates of the meta-training process. Finally, we present an analysis that explains better generalization performance with the meta-trained curvature.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to prepare a model to learn new tasks quickly. Meta-curvature extends model-agnostic meta-learning by learning how to transform the gradients used during adaptation. The transformation is trained so that the resulting updates generalize better to a new task, making the update rule itself part of what is learned across tasks.

Representing interactions among many model parameters can require a large curvature matrix. To make the approach suitable for large neural networks, the authors decompose that matrix into smaller matrices. A sequence of tensor products captures parameter dependencies through this more manageable representation, allowing the learned transformation to account for relationships among parameters.

Across several few-shot learning tasks and datasets, the paper reports substantial improvements over earlier MAML variants and performance exceeding recent leading methods, without task-specific techniques or architectures. It also observes faster convergence during meta-training and provides an analysis explaining improved generalization from the learned curvature. Together, these findings support learning the geometry of adaptation as a useful addition to learning a model's initial parameters.
summary.tldr: Meta-curvature learns structured gradient transformations that improve few-shot adaptation and generalization in the reported evaluations.

title: Meta-Curvature

abstract: We consider differentially private algorithms for reinforcement learning in continuous spaces, such that neighboring reward functions are indistinguishable. This protects the reward information from being exploited by methods such as inverse reinforcement learning. Existing studies that guarantee differential privacy are not extendable to infinite state spaces, as the noise level to ensure privacy will scale accordingly to infinity. Our aim is to protect the value function approximator, without regard to the number of states queried to the function. It is achieved by adding functional noise to the value function iteratively in the training. We show rigorous privacy guarantees by a series of analyses on the kernel of the noise space, the probabilistic bound of such noise samples, and the composition over the iterations. We gain insight into the utility analysis by proving the algorithm's approximate optimality when the state space is discrete. Experiments corroborate our theoretical findings and show improvement over existing approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning that protects information about its reward function. The privacy objective makes neighboring reward functions indistinguishable under differential privacy, helping prevent reward information from being recovered through methods such as inverse reinforcement learning. Continuous state spaces create a difficulty for existing approaches because their required noise can grow without bound as the state space becomes infinite.

The proposed method adds functional noise to the value-function approximator repeatedly during training. Its aim is to protect the function without making privacy depend on the number of states at which it is queried. The privacy proof analyzes the noise-space kernel, probabilistic bounds on noise samples, and how privacy guarantees compose across training iterations.

The paper also examines usefulness alongside privacy. It proves approximate optimality when the state space is discrete, providing a utility result under that specific condition. Experiments support the theoretical findings and show improvements over existing approaches. Thus, the continuous-space privacy contribution and the discrete-space optimality result have distinct scopes within the overall method.
summary.tldr: Functional noise enables differentially private Q-learning in continuous spaces, with a separate approximate-optimality result for discrete states.

title: Privacy-Preserving Q-Learning with Functional Noise in Continuous Spaces

abstract: We introduce a new tool for interpreting neural nets, namely full-gradients, which decomposes the neural net response into input sensitivity and per-neuron sensitivity components. This is the first proposed representation which satisfies two key properties: completeness and weak dependence, which provably cannot be satisfied by any saliency map-based interpretability method. Using full-gradients, we also propose an approximate saliency map representation for convolutional nets dubbed FullGrad, obtained by aggregating the full-gradient components. We experimentally evaluate the usefulness of FullGrad in explaining model behaviour with two quantitative tests: pixel perturbation and remove-and-retrain. Our experiments reveal that our method explains model behavior correctly, and more comprehensively than other methods in the literature. Visual inspection also reveals that our saliency maps are sharper and more tightly confined to object regions than other methods.

Visual inspection also reveals that our saliency maps are sharper and more tightly confined to object regions than other methods.

paragraphs: This paper introduces full-gradients as a representation for interpreting neural network responses. It separates the response into components associated with sensitivity to the input and sensitivity at individual neurons. The aim is to capture explanatory information beyond what can be expressed by a single input-focused saliency map.

The authors prove that the full-gradient representation satisfies two properties, completeness and weak dependence, that no saliency-map-based method can satisfy together. For convolutional networks, they then aggregate the full-gradient components into an approximate saliency representation called FullGrad. The distinction matters: the theoretical properties belong to the fuller representation, while the visual map is an approximation constructed from it.

The paper evaluates FullGrad using pixel perturbation and remove-and-retrain tests. The reported experiments indicate that it explains model behavior correctly and more comprehensively than comparison methods. Visual inspection also finds sharper maps concentrated more closely on object regions. The work thus pairs a theoretical argument for a richer representation with empirical evidence that its approximate visualization is useful.
summary.tldr: Full-gradients provide a richer theoretical representation of network responses, and their FullGrad visualization performs well in quantitative and visual evaluations.

title: Full-Gradient Representation for Neural Network Visualization

abstract: Algorithms that fuse multiple input sources benefit from both complementary and shared information. Shared information may provide robustness against faulty or noisy inputs, which is indispensable for safety-critical applications like self-driving cars. We investigate learning fusion algorithms that are robust against noise added to a single source. We first demonstrate that robustness against single source noise is not guaranteed in a linear fusion model. Motivated by this discovery, two possible approaches are proposed to increase robustness: a carefully designed loss with corresponding training algorithms for deep fusion models, and a simple convolutional fusion layer that has a structural advantage in dealing with noise. Experimental results show that both training algorithms and our fusion layer make a deep fusion-based 3D object detector robust against noise applied to a single source, while preserving the original performance on clean data.

Experimental results show that both training algorithms and our fusion layer make a deep fusion-based 3D object detector robust against noise applied to a single source, while preserving the original performance on clean data.

paragraphs: Combining multiple input sources can improve predictions because the sources contain both complementary and shared information. Shared information might also help when one input becomes noisy. This paper investigates that possibility directly, focusing on robustness when noise affects a single source in a fusion model.

The authors first show that a linear fusion model does not automatically guarantee such robustness. They then propose two approaches for deep fusion: a deliberately designed loss with corresponding training algorithms, and a simple convolutional fusion layer whose structure offers an advantage in handling noise. These interventions address the training procedure and the fusion architecture, respectively.

Experiments on a deep fusion-based 3D object detector show that the training algorithms and the proposed layer provide robustness to noise applied to one source while preserving performance on clean data. The findings support explicitly designing fusion for this failure condition. They also establish why the mere availability of several inputs is insufficient to guarantee that shared information will protect predictions.
summary.tldr: Specialized training and a convolutional fusion layer improve a 3D detector's robustness to single-source noise while preserving clean-data performance.

title: On Single Source Robustness in Deep Fusion Models

abstract: Robust MDPs (RMDPs) can be used to compute policies with provable worst-case guarantees in reinforcement learning. The quality and robustness of an RMDP solution are determined by the ambiguity set---the set of plausible transition probabilities---which is usually constructed as a multi-dimensional confidence region. Existing methods construct ambiguity sets as confidence regions using concentration inequalities which leads to overly conservative solutions. This paper proposes a new paradigm that can achieve better solutions with the same robustness guarantees without using confidence regions as ambiguity sets. To incorporate prior knowledge, our algorithms optimize the size and position of ambiguity sets using Bayesian inference. Our theoretical analysis shows the safety of the proposed method, and the empirical results demonstrate its practical promise.

paragraphs: Robust Markov decision processes choose policies while accounting for uncertainty about how actions change the environment. They represent this uncertainty with an ambiguity set: a collection of plausible transition probabilities. A policy is assessed against adverse possibilities within that set, so its construction affects both the resulting performance and the strength of its worst-case guarantee.

The paper argues that a common construction is unnecessarily conservative. Existing approaches use concentration inequalities to build multidimensional confidence regions and then take those regions as ambiguity sets. The authors propose constructing ambiguity sets without requiring them to be confidence regions. Their algorithms use Bayesian inference to incorporate prior knowledge and optimize both the size and position of the sets.

The proposed approach can produce better solutions while maintaining the same robustness guarantees. Theoretical analysis establishes the method's safety, and empirical results support its practical promise. The contribution is a way to make uncertainty sets more useful for robust decision-making while retaining the guarantees that motivate this approach to reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Bayesian construction of ambiguity sets can improve robust reinforcement-learning policies while preserving their worst-case guarantees.

title: Beyond Confidence Regions: Tight Bayesian Ambiguity Sets for Robust MDPs

abstract: Learning set functions is a key challenge arising in many domains, ranging from sketching graphs to black-box optimization with discrete parameters. In this paper we consider the problem of efficiently learning set functions that are defined over a ground set of size $n$ and that are sparse (say $k$-sparse) in the Fourier domain. This is a wide class, that includes graph and hypergraph cut functions, decision trees and more. Our central contribution is the first algorithm that allows learning functions whose Fourier support only contains low degree (say degree $d=o(n)$) polynomials using $O(k d \log n)$ sample complexity and runtime $O( kn \log^2 k \log n \log d)$. This implies that sparse graphs with $k$ edges can, for the first time, be learned from $O(k \log n)$ observations of cut values and in linear time in the number of vertices. Our algorithm can also efficiently learn (sums of) decision trees of small depth. The algorithm exploits techniques from the sparse Fourier transform literature and is easily implementable. Lastly, we also develop an efficient robust version of our algorithm and prove $\ell_2/\ell_2$ approximation guarantees without any statistical assumptions on the noise.

paragraphs: A set function assigns a value to a subset of a larger collection. Learning such functions appears in problems ranging from graph reconstruction to optimization over discrete choices. This paper studies functions that have only a small number of nonzero Fourier components, a class that includes graph and hypergraph cuts as well as decision trees.

The main algorithm uses techniques from sparse Fourier transforms. For a ground set of size n, Fourier sparsity k, and supported polynomial degrees at most d=o(n), it needs O(k d log n) samples. Its runtime is O(k n log² k log n log d). The low-degree condition is central to this stated efficiency result.

One consequence is that a graph with k edges can be learned from O(k log n) cut-value observations, with runtime linear in the number of vertices. The method also efficiently learns small-depth decision trees and sums of them. A robust version provides an ℓ₂/ℓ₂ approximation guarantee without statistical assumptions on noise, extending the approach beyond exact, noiseless recovery.
summary.tldr: A sparse Fourier algorithm efficiently learns low-degree set functions, with applications to graph recovery and a noise-robust approximation variant.

title: Efficiently Learning Fourier Sparse Set Functions

abstract: Data-augmentation is key to the training of neural networks for image classification. This paper first shows that existing augmentations induce a significant discrepancy between the size of the objects seen by the classifier at train and test time: in fact, a lower train resolution improves the classification at test time! We then propose a simple strategy to optimize the classifier performance, that employs different train and test resolutions. It relies on a computationally cheap fine-tuning of the network at the test resolution. This enables training strong classifiers using small training images, and therefore significantly reduce the training time. For instance, we obtain 77.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with a ResNet-50 trained on 128x128 images, and 79.8% with one trained at 224x224. A ResNeXt-101 32x48d pre-trained with weak supervision on 940 million 224x224 images and further optimized with our technique for test resolution 320x320 achieves 86.4% top-1 accuracy (top-5: 98.0%). To the best of our knowledge this is the highest ImageNet single-crop accuracy to date.

paragraphs: Image augmentation changes the training examples seen by a classifier, but it can also create a mismatch in apparent object size between training and testing. This paper identifies a substantial discrepancy of that kind. In the settings studied, lowering the training resolution can improve classification at test time.

The proposed strategy deliberately uses different resolutions for training and testing, then performs computationally inexpensive fine-tuning at the intended test resolution. This makes it possible to conduct training with smaller images while adapting the classifier to the resolution at which it will be evaluated. The authors report that this substantially reduces training time while retaining strong classification performance.

For ResNet-50, the reported ImageNet top-1 accuracies are 77.1% with training images of 128 by 128 pixels and 79.8% with training at 224 by 224. The method also improves a weakly supervised, pretrained ResNeXt model. These results highlight resolution choice and subsequent adaptation as consequential parts of the training procedure, beyond simply selecting a network architecture.
summary.tldr: Training with smaller images and cheaply fine-tuning at test resolution addresses object-size mismatch and yields strong classification results.

title: Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy

abstract: Current methods for training robust networks lead to a drop in test accuracy, which has led prior works to posit that a robustness-accuracy tradeoff may be inevitable in deep learning. We take a closer look at this phenomenon and first show that real image datasets are actually separated. With this property in mind, we then prove that robustness and accuracy should both be achievable for benchmark datasets through locally Lipschitz functions, and hence, there should be no inherent tradeoff between robustness and accuracy. Through extensive experiments with robustness methods, we argue that the gap between theory and practice arises from two limitations of current methods: either they fail to impose local Lipschitzness or they are insufficiently generalized. We explore combining dropout with robust training methods and obtain better generalization. We conclude that achieving robustness and accuracy in practice may require using methods that impose local Lipschitzness and augmenting them with deep learning generalization techniques.
