We conclude that achieving robustness and accuracy in practice may require using methods that impose local Lipschitzness and augmenting them with deep learning generalization techniques.

paragraphs: Methods that train neural networks to resist input perturbations often reduce accuracy on ordinary test examples. This paper asks whether that tension reflects a fundamental incompatibility or a limitation of current training methods. The authors first establish that real image datasets have a separation property, which supplies the basis for their theoretical argument.

Using that property, they prove that functions with suitable local Lipschitz behavior can achieve both robustness and accuracy on benchmark datasets. Local Lipschitz behavior constrains how sharply a function can change around nearby inputs. The result concerns what an appropriate function can achieve; it does not establish that existing training procedures will reliably find such a function.

Experiments point to two explanations for the practical gap: methods may fail to enforce the required local behavior, or they may generalize inadequately. Combining dropout with robust training improves generalization in the reported experiments. The authors therefore suggest that practical progress may require both local smoothness constraints and techniques that help learned behavior carry over to unseen data.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that robustness and accuracy can coexist on benchmark datasets, while current training methods struggle to realize both.

title: A Closer Look at Accuracy vs. Robustness

abstract: Although there is a vast body of literature related to methods for detecting change-points (CPs), less attention has been paid to assessing the statistical reliability of the detected CPs. In this paper, we introduce a novel method to perform statistical inference on the significance of the CPs, estimated by a Dynamic Programming (DP)-based optimal CP detection algorithm. Our main idea is to employ a Selective Inference (SI) approach---a new statistical inference framework that has recently received a lot of attention---to compute exact (non-asymptotic) valid p-values for the detected optimal CPs. Although it is well-known that SI has low statistical power because of over-conditioning, we address this drawback by introducing a novel method called parametric DP, which enables SI to be conducted with the minimum amount of conditioning, leading to high statistical power. We conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, through which we offer evidence that our proposed method is more powerful than existing methods, has decent performance in terms of computational efficiency, and provides good results in many practical applications.

paragraphs: Detecting a change in a sequence and establishing that the detected change is statistically reliable are separate problems. A detection algorithm deliberately selects locations that look unusual, so evaluating those locations must account for that selection. This paper develops significance testing for changepoints chosen by an optimal detection algorithm based on dynamic programming.

The method uses selective inference to compute valid p-values for the selected changepoints. These guarantees are exact rather than dependent on a large-sample approximation. A central challenge is that selective inference can lose statistical power when it conditions on too much information about how the result was selected. The authors introduce parametric dynamic programming to conduct the inference with minimal conditioning.

Reducing unnecessary conditioning allows the procedure to retain greater ability to identify significant changes while accounting for selection. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets provide evidence of higher statistical power than existing methods, along with reasonable computational efficiency and useful practical results. The contribution therefore links optimal changepoint detection to a more informative assessment of whether its discoveries are statistically meaningful.
summary.tldr: Parametric dynamic programming enables exact selective p-values for detected changepoints while reducing the conditioning that can weaken statistical power.

title: Computing Valid p-value for Optimal Changepoint by Selective Inference using Dynamic Programming

abstract: A recent breakthrough in deep learning theory shows that the training of over-parameterized deep neural networks can be characterized by a kernel function called \textit{neural tangent kernel} (NTK). However, it is known that this type of results does not perfectly match the practice, as NTK-based analysis requires the network weights to stay very close to their initialization throughout training, and cannot handle regularizers or gradient noises. In this paper, we provide a generalized neural tangent kernel analysis and show that noisy gradient descent with weight decay can still exhibit a ``kernel-like'' behavior. This implies that the training loss converges linearly up to a certain accuracy. We also establish a novel generalization error bound for two-layer neural networks trained by noisy gradient descent with weight decay.
originalAbstract: A recent breakthrough in deep learning theory shows that the training of over-parameterized deep neural networks can be characterized by a kernel function called \textit{neural tangent kernel} (NTK). However, it is known that this type of results does not perfectly match the practice, as NTK-based analysis requires the network weights to stay very close to their initialization throughout training, and cannot handle regularizers or gradient noises. In this paper, we provide a generalized neural tangent kernel analysis and show that noisy gradient descent with weight decay can still exhibit a ``kernel-like'' behavior. This implies that the training loss converges linearly up to a certain accuracy. We also establish a novel generalization error bound for two-layer neural networks trained by noisy gradient descent with weight decay.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel analysis explains some neural-network training through a kernel function that describes how the network responds to parameter updates. Existing analyses rely on weights remaining very close to their starting values. They also cannot accommodate regularization or gradient noise, creating a gap between the theoretical picture and training procedures that include these ingredients.

This paper extends that analysis to noisy gradient descent with weight decay. Its central result is that training can still behave like a kernel method even with these modifications. The contribution is therefore an expanded theoretical account of optimization: adding noise and a penalty on weights need not eliminate the kernel-like behavior that makes training mathematically tractable.

The analysis implies linear convergence of training loss up to a specified accuracy level, rather than unrestricted convergence to zero. It also establishes a generalization-error bound for two-layer networks trained this way. Together, these results address both progress on the training objective and performance beyond the training data within the paper's analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: A generalized neural tangent kernel analysis explains convergence and generalization for two-layer networks trained with gradient noise and weight decay.

title: A Generalized Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis for Two-layer Neural Networks

abstract: This paper relates parameter distance to gradient breakdown for a broad class of nonlinear compositional functions. The analysis leads to a new distance function called deep relative trust and a descent lemma for neural networks. Since the resulting learning rule seems to require little to no learning rate tuning, it may unlock a simpler workflow for training deeper and more complex neural networks. The Python code used in this paper is here: https://github.com/jxbz/fromage.
originalAbstract: This paper relates parameter distance to gradient breakdown for a broad class of nonlinear compositional functions. The analysis leads to a new distance function called deep relative trust and a descent lemma for neural networks. Since the resulting learning rule seems to require little to no learning rate tuning, it may unlock a simpler workflow for training deeper and more complex neural networks. The Python code used in this paper is here: https://github.com/jxbz/fromage.

paragraphs: A gradient describes how a function changes locally, but training moves the parameters away from the point where that gradient was computed. This paper studies the relationship between parameter distance and the breakdown of gradient information. Its analysis covers a broad class of nonlinear functions built by composing successive transformations.

From that analysis, the authors derive a distance function called deep relative trust and a descent lemma for neural networks. Together, these connect the size of a parameter change to reasoning about progress during optimization. The distance is therefore part of the theoretical basis for a learning rule, rather than only a way to compare two trained models.

The resulting rule appears to require little or no learning-rate tuning. The authors suggest that this could simplify training workflows for deeper and more complex networks. That practical implication is presented as a possibility, while the concrete mathematical contributions are the distance function and descent lemma. The paper thus connects a question about network proximity to the stability and usability of training.
summary.tldr: Deep relative trust links parameter changes to gradient reliability and yields a learning rule that may need little learning-rate tuning.

title: On the distance between two neural networks and the stability of learning

abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing a rank-one matrix from a revealed subset of its entries when some of the revealed entries are corrupted with perturbations that are unknown and can be arbitrarily large. It is not known which revealed entries are corrupted. We propose a new algorithm combining alternating minimization with extreme-value filtering and provide sufficient and necessary conditions to recover the original rank-one matrix. In particular, we show that our proposed algorithm is optimal when the set of revealed entries is given by an Erd\H os-R\'enyi random graph. These results are then applied to the problem of classification from crowdsourced data under the assumption that while the majority of the workers are governed by the standard single-coin David-Skene model (i.e., they output the correct answer with a certain probability), some of the workers can deviate arbitrarily from this model. In particular, the ``adversarial'' workers could even make decisions designed to make the algorithm output an incorrect answer. Extensive experimental results show our algorithm for this problem, based on rank-one matrix completion with perturbations, outperforms all other state-of-the-art methods in such an adversarial scenario.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover a rank-one matrix when only some entries are visible and an unknown subset of those entries has been corrupted. The corruptions can be arbitrarily large, so recovery cannot rely on every observed value being approximately correct. This mathematical problem becomes the foundation for a method that combines labels from potentially adversarial crowd workers.

The proposed algorithm combines alternating minimization with extreme-value filtering. The authors establish sufficient and necessary conditions for recovering the original matrix, and show that their algorithm is optimal when the pattern of revealed entries follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph. That optimality claim is tied to this stated observation model.

For crowdsourced classification, the majority of workers are assumed to answer correctly with worker-specific probabilities under a single-coin model. Other workers may behave arbitrarily, including deliberately trying to mislead the algorithm. Experiments show that the resulting matrix-completion approach outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in this adversarial setting, supporting its usefulness when ordinary worker-noise assumptions fail for part of the crowd.
summary.tldr: Robust rank-one matrix completion provides a way to combine crowd labels even when some workers deliberately supply misleading answers.

title: Adversarial Crowdsourcing Through Robust Rank-One Matrix Completion

abstract: A growing trend for value-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms is to capture more information than scalar value functions in the value network. One of the most well-known methods in this branch is distributional RL, which models return distribution instead of scalar value. In another line of work, hybrid reward architectures (HRA) in RL have studied to model source-specific value functions for each source of reward, which is also shown to be beneficial in performance. To fully inherit the benefits of distributional RL and hybrid reward architectures, we introduce Multi-Dimensional Distributional DQN (MD3QN), which extends distributional RL to model the joint return distribution from multiple reward sources. As a by-product of joint distribution modeling, MD3QN can capture not only the randomness in returns for each source of reward, but also the rich reward correlation between the randomness of different sources. We prove the convergence for the joint distributional Bellman operator and build our empirical algorithm by minimizing the Maximum Mean Discrepancy between joint return distribution and its Bellman target. In experiments, our method accurately models the joint return distribution in environments with richly correlated reward functions, and outperforms previous RL methods utilizing multi-dimensional reward functions in the control setting.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn more than a single expected return. Distributional methods model uncertainty in returns, while hybrid reward architectures maintain separate values for different reward sources. This paper combines these ideas through Multi-Dimensional Distributional DQN, or MD3QN, which learns the joint distribution of returns across multiple reward sources.

Modeling the joint distribution preserves information about how reward uncertainties relate to one another. Separate return distributions describe variability within each source, but the joint model can also capture correlations across sources. The authors prove convergence of the joint distributional Bellman operator. Their practical algorithm learns by minimizing Maximum Mean Discrepancy between its predicted joint distribution and the corresponding Bellman target.

Experiments show that MD3QN accurately models joint returns in environments with strongly correlated reward functions. In control experiments, it also outperforms previous reinforcement learning methods using multidimensional rewards. The findings support treating relationships among reward sources as useful learning information, while the operator result supplies a theoretical foundation for extending distributional reinforcement learning beyond a single reward dimension.
summary.tldr: MD3QN learns joint return distributions across reward sources, capturing their correlations and improving control in the reported experiments.

title: Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Dimensional Reward Functions

abstract: Vanilla models for object detection and instance segmentation suffer from the heavy bias toward detecting frequent objects in the long-tailed setting. Existing methods address this issue mostly during training, e.g., by re-sampling or re-weighting. In this paper, we investigate a largely overlooked approach --- post-processing calibration of confidence scores. We propose NorCal, Normalized Calibration for long-tailed object detection and instance segmentation, a simple and straightforward recipe that reweighs the predicted scores of each class by its training sample size. We show that separately handling the background class and normalizing the scores over classes for each proposal are keys to achieving superior performance. On the LVIS dataset, NorCal can effectively improve nearly all the baseline models not only on rare classes but also on common and frequent classes. Finally, we conduct extensive analysis and ablation studies to offer insights into various modeling choices and mechanisms of our approach. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tydpan/NorCal.

paragraphs: Object detection and instance segmentation models can favor classes that appear frequently in training data. This is especially problematic in long-tailed datasets, where many categories have relatively few examples. While existing solutions mostly change training through sampling or weighting, this paper investigates adjusting confidence scores after the model has made its predictions.

The proposed method, Normalized Calibration or NorCal, reweights each class's predicted scores using its training sample count. Two design choices are central: treating the background class separately and normalizing scores across classes for each proposed object region. Together, these choices address how class-frequency information enters the final competition among predicted categories.

On LVIS, NorCal improves nearly all evaluated baseline models. The gains extend beyond rare categories to common and frequent ones, showing that the reported benefits are not restricted to the least represented classes. Extensive analyses and ablations examine the method's mechanisms and design choices. The results establish post-processing calibration as an effective additional approach to long-tailed detection and segmentation.
summary.tldr: NorCal adjusts detection and segmentation confidence scores using class frequency, improving nearly all tested LVIS baselines across frequency groups.

title: On Model Calibration for Long-Tailed Object Detection and Instance Segmentation

abstract: A fundamental assumption of reinforcement learning in Markov decision processes (MDPs) is that the relevant decision process is, in fact, Markov. However, when MDPs have rich observations, agents typically learn by way of an abstract state representation, and such representations are not guaranteed to preserve the Markov property. We introduce a novel set of conditions and prove that they are sufficient for learning a Markov abstract state representation. We then describe a practical training procedure that combines inverse model estimation and temporal contrastive learning to learn an abstraction that approximately satisfies these conditions. Our novel training objective is compatible with both online and offline training: it does not require a reward signal, but agents can capitalize on reward information when available. We empirically evaluate our approach on a visual gridworld domain and a set of continuous control benchmarks. Our approach learns representations that capture the underlying structure of the domain and lead to improved sample efficiency over state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning with visual features---often matching or exceeding the performance achieved with hand-designed compact state information.

We then describe a practical training procedure that combines inverse model estimation and temporal contrastive learning to learn an abstraction that approximately satisfies these conditions. Our novel training objective is compatible with both online and offline training: it does not require a reward signal, but agents can capitalize on reward information when available. We empirically evaluate our approach on a visual gridworld domain and a set of continuous control benchmarks. Our approach learns representations that capture the underlying structure of the domain and lead to improved sample efficiency over state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning with visual features---often matching or exceeding the performance achieved with hand-designed compact state information.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly assumes that the current state contains the information needed to describe what happens next. When an agent compresses rich observations into a learned representation, that Markov property can be lost. This paper asks how to learn an abstract state that retains the relevant decision-process structure.

The authors introduce conditions that are sufficient for a Markov abstract representation and prove the corresponding result. They then design a practical objective combining inverse-model estimation with temporal contrastive learning to approximately satisfy those conditions. The procedure works with online or offline training and does not require rewards, although it can use reward information when available.

Experiments on a visual gridworld and continuous-control benchmarks show representations that capture underlying domain structure. The authors report improved sample efficiency over state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning using visual features, often matching or exceeding performance with hand-designed compact states. The theoretical result establishes sufficient conditions, while the practical method targets them approximately. Together, these contributions connect a structural requirement for reinforcement learning to an empirically useful representation-learning objective.
summary.tldr: A representation-learning objective approximately enforces sufficient conditions for Markov state abstractions and improves reinforcement-learning sample efficiency.

title: Learning Markov State Abstractions for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Vision Transformer has shown great visual representation power in substantial vision tasks such as recognition and detection, and thus been attracting fast-growing efforts on manually designing more effective architectures. In this paper, we propose to use neural architecture search to automate this process, by searching not only the architecture but also the search space. The central idea is to gradually evolve different search dimensions guided by their E-T Error computed using a weight-sharing supernet. Moreover, we provide design guidelines of general vision transformers with extensive analysis according to the space searching process, which could promote the understanding of vision transformer. Remarkably, the searched models, named S3 (short for Searching the Search Space), from the searched space achieve superior performance to recently proposed models, such as Swin, DeiT and ViT, when evaluated on ImageNet. The effectiveness of S3 is also illustrated on object detection, semantic segmentation and visual question answering, demonstrating its generality to downstream vision and vision-language tasks. Code and models will be available at https://github.com/microsoft/Cream.

paragraphs: Designing a vision transformer involves choosing an architecture, but automated architecture search also depends on which designs are allowed into the search. This paper tackles both choices together. It proposes searching the search space itself as part of the process of finding effective vision-transformer architectures.

The method gradually evolves different search dimensions using a measure called E-T Error computed with a weight-sharing supernet. The resulting models are named S3, for Searching the Search Space. The authors also analyze the space-searching process to derive design guidelines, aiming to make the search informative about transformer design as well as productive of particular models.

On ImageNet, the searched S3 models outperform the recently proposed Swin, DeiT, and ViT models considered in the evaluation. The paper also demonstrates effectiveness on object detection, semantic segmentation, and visual question answering. These results support the usefulness of the discovered designs across downstream vision and vision-language tasks, extending the evidence beyond the image-recognition setting.
summary.tldr: S3 jointly searches vision-transformer architectures and their search space, yielding strong evaluated models and broader architectural design guidance.

title: Searching the Search Space of Vision Transformer

abstract: Adversarial examples for neural network image classifiers are known to be transferable: examples optimized to be misclassified by a source classifier are often misclassified as well by classifiers with different architectures. However, targeted adversarial examples—optimized to be classified as a chosen target class—tend to be less transferable between architectures. While prior research on constructing transferable targeted attacks has focused on improving the optimization procedure, in this work we examine the role of the source classifier. Here, we show that training the source classifier to be "slightly robust"—that is, robust to small-magnitude adversarial examples—substantially improves the transferability of class-targeted and representation-targeted adversarial attacks, even between architectures as different as convolutional neural networks and transformers. The results we present provide insight into the nature of adversarial examples as well as the mechanisms underlying so-called "robust" classifiers.

paragraphs: An adversarial image designed to fool one classifier can also fool a different classifier. Getting both models to predict a particular chosen class is harder than merely causing an error. This paper studies that targeted transfer problem by examining the classifier used to construct the adversarial example.

The central intervention is to train the source classifier to resist small-magnitude adversarial perturbations. The authors call this being slightly robust. Earlier work emphasized improving the procedure that optimizes the attack; here, the source model's properties become the main object of investigation. The question is whether changing those properties makes the resulting targeted examples more transferable.

The reported results show substantial transfer improvements for attacks aimed at both class outputs and internal representations. These improvements extend across architectures as different as convolutional networks and transformers. The findings establish an empirical connection between limited source-model robustness and targeted attack transferability. They also provide evidence relevant to understanding robust classifiers and adversarial examples, without establishing that stronger robustness always produces better transfer.
summary.tldr: Training an attack's source classifier to resist small perturbations substantially improves the reported transfer of targeted adversarial examples across architectures.

title: A Little Robustness Goes a Long Way: Leveraging Robust Features for Targeted Transfer Attacks

abstract: Constrained clustering has gained significant attention in the field of machine learning as it can leverage prior information on a growing amount of only partially labeled data. Following recent advances in deep generative models, we propose a novel framework for constrained clustering that is intuitive, interpretable, and can be trained efficiently in the framework of stochastic gradient variational inference. By explicitly integrating domain knowledge in the form of probabilistic relations, our proposed model (DC-GMM) uncovers the underlying distribution of data conditioned on prior clustering preferences, expressed as \textit{pairwise constraints}. These constraints guide the clustering process towards a desirable partition of the data by indicating which samples should or should not belong to the same cluster. We provide extensive experiments to demonstrate that DC-GMM shows superior clustering performances and robustness compared to state-of-the-art deep constrained clustering methods on a wide range of data sets. We further demonstrate the usefulness of our approach on two challenging real-world applications.

paragraphs: Clustering groups observations, but available domain knowledge may already indicate that certain pairs belong together or should remain separate. This paper develops DC-GMM, a deep conditional Gaussian mixture model that incorporates those preferences. It targets settings with partially labeled data, where such relationships can guide grouping without requiring a complete label for every observation.

The model expresses domain knowledge as probabilistic relations and learns the data distribution conditioned on the supplied clustering preferences. Pairwise constraints identify samples that should or should not share a cluster, steering the partition toward the intended structure. The framework is designed to be interpretable and to support efficient training through stochastic gradient variational inference.

Across a broad range of datasets, the reported experiments show better clustering performance and robustness than leading deep constrained clustering methods. Two challenging real-world applications further demonstrate usefulness. The contribution is a probabilistic way to integrate prior relationships directly into a deep clustering model, with empirical evidence that this integration improves the resulting groups.
summary.tldr: DC-GMM incorporates probabilistic pairwise preferences into deep clustering and reports improved clustering quality and robustness.

title: Deep Conditional Gaussian Mixture Model for Constrained Clustering

abstract: We study the problem of online multiclass classification in a setting where the learner's feedback is determined by an arbitrary directed graph. While including bandit feedback as a special case, feedback graphs allow a much richer set of applications, including filtering and label efficient classification.We introduce \textproc{Gappletron}, the first online multiclass algorithm that works with arbitrary feedback graphs. For this new algorithm,we prove surrogate regret bounds that hold, both in expectation and with high probability, for a large class of surrogate losses. Our bounds are of order $B\sqrt{\rho KT}$, where $B$ is the diameter of the prediction space, $K$ is the number of classes, $T$ is the time horizon, and $\rho$ is the domination number (a graph-theoretic parameter affecting the amount of exploration). In the full information case, we show that \textproc{Gappletron} achieves a constant surrogate regret of order $B^2K$. We also prove a general lower bound of order $\max\big\{B^2K,\sqrt{T}\big\}$ showing that our upper bounds are not significantly improvable. Experiments on synthetic data show that for various feedback graphs our algorithm is competitive against known baselines.

paragraphs: In online multiclass classification, a learner repeatedly predicts a label and receives feedback. This paper allows the available feedback to be specified by an arbitrary directed graph. That setting includes bandit feedback but can also describe richer information patterns relevant to filtering and label-efficient classification.

The proposed algorithm, Gappletron, handles arbitrary feedback graphs. For a broad class of surrogate losses, the authors prove regret bounds both in expectation and with high probability. The bounds scale as B times the square root of rho K T, where B measures prediction-space diameter, K counts classes, T counts rounds, and rho is the graph's domination number. This graph parameter captures an aspect of the exploration requirement.

With full information, the surrogate-regret bound becomes constant in the number of rounds, scaling as B squared times K. A general lower bound shows that the upper bounds have limited room for improvement. Synthetic experiments also find competitive performance across several feedback graphs, complementing the theoretical account of how feedback structure affects learning.
summary.tldr: Gappletron learns under arbitrary graph-defined feedback and comes with regret guarantees that reflect the available information.

title: Beyond Bandit Feedback in Online Multiclass Classification

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental unsupervised learning problem where a dataset is partitioned into clusters that consist of nearby points in a metric space. A recent variant, fair clustering, associates a color with each point representing its group membership and requires that each color has (approximately) equal representation in each cluster to satisfy group fairness. In this model, the cost of the clustering objective increases due to enforcing fairness in the algorithm. The relative increase in the cost, the ```````''price of fairness,'' can indeed be unbounded. Therefore, in this paper we propose to treat an upper bound on the clustering objective as a constraint on the clustering problem, and to maximize equality of representation subject to it. We consider two fairness objectives: the group utilitarian objective and the group egalitarian objective, as well as the group leximin objective which generalizes the group egalitarian objective. We derive fundamental lower bounds on the approximation of the utilitarian and egalitarian objectives and introduce algorithms with provable guarantees for them. For the leximin objective we introduce an effective heuristic algorithm. We further derive impossibility results for other natural fairness objectives. We conclude with experimental results on real-world datasets that demonstrate the validity of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Fair clustering seeks clusters that represent demographic or other membership groups equitably while keeping nearby points together. Enforcing representation requirements can increase the ordinary clustering cost, and that relative increase can be unbounded. This paper reformulates the tradeoff by fixing an upper limit on cost and pursuing fairness within that budget.

The authors study several ways to evaluate group representation: utilitarian, egalitarian, and leximin objectives. For the first two, they derive lower bounds on approximation and provide algorithms with provable guarantees. These results address both what algorithms can achieve and the fundamental limits on approximating the chosen fairness objectives.

For leximin, which generalizes the egalitarian objective, the paper introduces an effective heuristic rather than the same type of guaranteed algorithm. It also establishes impossibility results for other natural fairness formulations. Experiments on real-world datasets support the proposed methods. The overall contribution is a framework for making representation more equal while explicitly respecting a chosen clustering-cost constraint.
summary.tldr: The paper optimizes group fairness subject to a clustering-cost budget, providing approximation guarantees, lower bounds, and a leximin heuristic.

title: Fair Clustering Under a Bounded Cost

abstract: Wasserstein gradient flows provide a powerful means of understanding and solving many diffusion equations. Specifically, Fokker-Planck equations, which model the diffusion of probability measures, can be understood as gradient descent over entropy functionals in Wasserstein space. This equivalence, introduced by Jordan, Kinderlehrer and Otto, inspired the so-called JKO scheme to approximate these diffusion processes via an implicit discretization of the gradient flow in Wasserstein space. Solving the optimization problem associated with each JKO step, however, presents serious computational challenges. We introduce a scalable method to approximate Wasserstein gradient flows, targeted to machine learning applications. Our approach relies on input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) to discretize the JKO steps, which can be optimized by stochastic gradient descent. Contrarily to previous work, our method does not require domain discretization or particle simulation. As a result, we can sample from the measure at each time step of the diffusion and compute its probability density. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm by computing diffusions following the Fokker-Planck equation and apply it to unnormalized density sampling as well as nonlinear filtering.

paragraphs: This paper develops a scalable way to approximate the evolution of probability distributions through Wasserstein gradient flows. In this perspective, certain diffusion equations become gradient descent over functionals of distributions. The JKO scheme turns that evolution into a sequence of implicit optimization steps, but solving each step can be computationally difficult.

The proposed method represents the JKO steps using input-convex neural networks and optimizes them through stochastic gradient descent. This brings a neural-network-based approximation to the core computational problem. Unlike the previous approaches discussed in the abstract, it does not require dividing the domain into a grid or simulating a collection of particles.

The representation allows the authors to sample from the evolving distribution and evaluate its probability density at each time step. They demonstrate the method on Fokker–Planck diffusions and apply it to sampling from unnormalized densities and nonlinear filtering. These applications connect the mathematical flow formulation to machine learning tasks that require practical access to changing probability distributions.
summary.tldr: Input-convex neural networks make Wasserstein diffusion steps scalable while supporting sampling and density evaluation over time.

title: Large-Scale Wasserstein Gradient Flows

abstract: We are interested in learning generative models for complex geometries described via manifolds, such as spheres, tori, and other implicit surfaces. Current extensions of existing (Euclidean) generative models are restricted to specific geometries and typically suffer from high computational costs. We introduce Moser Flow (MF), a new class of generative models within the family of continuous normalizing flows (CNF). MF also produces a CNF via a solution to the change-of-variable formula, however differently from other CNF methods, its model (learned) density is parameterized as the source (prior) density minus the divergence of a neural network (NN). The divergence is a local, linear differential operator, easy to approximate and calculate on manifolds. Therefore, unlike other CNFs, MF does not require invoking or backpropagating through an ODE solver during training. Furthermore, representing the model density explicitly as the divergence of a NN rather than as a solution of an ODE facilitates learning high fidelity densities. Theoretically, we prove that MF constitutes a universal density approximator under suitable assumptions. Empirically, we demonstrate for the first time the use of flow models for sampling from general curved surfaces and achieve significant improvements in density estimation, sample quality, and training complexity over existing CNFs on challenging synthetic geometries and real-world benchmarks from the earth and climate sciences.

Existing adaptations of generative models can be limited to particular geometries and computationally expensive. Moser Flow introduces a class of continuous normalizing flows designed to learn distributions on these kinds of spaces.

The approach links a geometry-compatible density representation with a simpler training computation and improved empirical modeling results.
summary.tldr: Moser Flow models densities on curved spaces through neural-network divergence, avoiding ODE solvers during training and improving reported modeling results.

title: Moser Flow: Divergence-based Generative Modeling on Manifolds

abstract: We provide a setting and a general approach to fair online learning with stochastic sensitive and non-sensitive contexts.The setting is a repeated game between the Player and Nature, where at each stage both pick actions based on the contexts. Inspired by the notion of unawareness, we assume that the Player can only access the non-sensitive context before making a decision, while we discuss both cases of Nature accessing the sensitive contexts and Nature unaware of the sensitive contexts. Adapting Blackwell's approachability theory to handle the case of an unknown contexts' distribution, we provide a general necessary and sufficient condition for learning objectives to be compatible with some fairness constraints. This condition is instantiated on (group-wise) no-regret and (group-wise) calibration objectives, and on demographic parity as an additional constraint. When the objective is not compatible with the constraint, the provided framework permits to characterise the optimal trade-off between the two.

paragraphs: Online learning involves making decisions repeatedly while information arrives over time. This paper asks when a learner can achieve its predictive or decision-making goals while also satisfying fairness requirements. It models the interaction as a repeated game between a decision-maker and Nature, with both sensitive and non-sensitive contextual information.

A central assumption is that the decision-maker sees only the non-sensitive context before acting. The authors consider both possibilities for Nature: access to sensitive information or lack of that access. They adapt Blackwell’s approachability theory to this setting, including the complication that the distribution generating contexts is unknown.

The resulting framework supplies a necessary and sufficient condition for compatibility between learning objectives and certain fairness constraints. The authors apply it to regret and calibration objectives, including group-specific versions, together with demographic parity. When an objective and a constraint cannot both be met, the framework characterizes their optimal trade-off. Its contribution is therefore a way to determine both what fair online learning can achieve and where competing requirements force compromises.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic framework characterizes when online learning objectives and fairness constraints are compatible and identifies optimal trade-offs when they conflict.

title: A Unified Approach to Fair Online Learning via Blackwell Approachability

abstract: We propose a deep reinforcement learning (RL) method to learn large neighborhood search (LNS) policy for integer programming (IP). The RL policy is trained as the destroy operator to select a subset of variables at each step, which is reoptimized by an IP solver as the repair operator. However, the combinatorial number of variable subsets prevents direct application of typical RL algorithms. To tackle this challenge, we represent all subsets by factorizing them into binary decisions on each variable. We then design a neural network to learn policies for each variable in parallel, trained by a customized actor-critic algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method on four representative IP problems. Results show that it can find better solutions than SCIP in much less time, and significantly outperform other LNS baselines with the same runtime. Moreover, these advantages notably persist when the policies generalize to larger problems. Further experiments with Gurobi also reveal that our method can outperform this state-of-the-art commercial solver within the same time limit.

paragraphs: Large neighborhood search improves an integer-programming solution by selecting some variables for reconsideration and letting a solver optimize that part of the problem. This paper learns the variable-selection step through deep reinforcement learning. The learned policy acts as the destroy operator, while an integer-programming solver supplies the repair step.

Selecting among all possible variable subsets creates a combinatorially large action space. The authors address this by expressing a subset as separate binary decisions about whether to select each variable. A neural network learns these decisions in parallel, using a customized actor-critic training algorithm. This representation makes learning a search policy manageable without assigning a separate action to every possible subset.

Across four representative integer-programming problems, the method finds better solutions than SCIP in substantially less time and outperforms other large neighborhood search baselines at equal runtime. The advantages persist when policies are applied to larger problems. Further experiments show that the approach can also outperform Gurobi within the same time limit, demonstrating the potential benefit of learned search guidance.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy chooses which integer-programming variables to reoptimize, improving solution quality within limited runtime.

title: Learning Large Neighborhood Search Policy for Integer Programming

abstract: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly being employed within a variety of creative domains. For example, ML tools are being used to analyze the authenticity of artworks, to simulate artistic styles, and to augment human creative processes. While this progress has opened up new creative avenues, it has also paved the way for adverse downstream effects such as cultural appropriation (e.g., cultural misrepresentation, offense, and undervaluing) and representational harm. Many such concerning issues stem from the training data in ways that diligent evaluation can uncover, prevent, and mitigate. We posit that, when developing an arts-based dataset, it is essential to consider the social factors that influenced the process of conception and design, and the resulting gaps must be examined in order to maximize understanding of the dataset's meaning and future impact. Each dataset creator's decision produces opportunities, but also omissions. Each choice, moreover, builds on preexisting histories of the data's formation and handling across time by prior actors including, but not limited to, art collectors, galleries, libraries, archives, museums, and digital repositories. To illuminate the aforementioned aspects, we provide a checklist of questions customized for use with art datasets in order to help guide assessment of the ways that dataset design may either perpetuate or shift exclusions found in repositories of art data. The checklist is organized to address the dataset creator's motivation together with dataset provenance, composition, collection, pre-processing, cleaning, labeling, use (including data generation), distribution, and maintenance. Two case studies exemplify the value and application of our questionnaire.

title: Artsheets for Art Datasets

abstract: When deploying person re-identification (ReID) model in safety-critical applications, it is pivotal to understanding the robustness of the model against a diverse array of image corruptions. However, current evaluations of person ReID only consider the performance on clean datasets and ignore images in various corrupted scenarios. In this work, we comprehensively establish five ReID benchmarks for learning corruption invariant representation. In the field of ReID, we are the first to conduct an exhaustive study on corruption invariant learning in single- and cross-modality datasets, including Market-1501, CUHK03, MSMT17, RegDB, SYSU-MM01. After reproducing and examining the robustness performance of 21 recent ReID methods, we have some observations: 1) transformer-based models are more robust towards corrupted images, compared with CNN-based models, 2) increasing the probability of random erasing (a commonly used augmentation method) hurts model corruption robustness, 3) cross-dataset generalization improves with corruption robustness increases.By analyzing the above observations, we propose a strong baseline on both single- and cross-modality ReID datasets which achieves improved robustness against diverse corruptions.Our codes are available on https://github.com/MinghuiChen43/CIL-ReID.

paragraphs: Person re-identification models need to remain useful when their input images are corrupted, particularly in safety-critical applications. Evaluations on clean images alone do not establish that robustness. This paper introduces five benchmarks that make corrupted-image performance an explicit evaluation target, covering both single-modality and cross-modality person re-identification.

The authors reproduce and assess 21 recent methods. In their study, transformer-based models handle corruptions better than convolutional models. They also find that raising the probability of random erasing, a commonly used training augmentation, hurts corruption robustness. That observation matters because increasing an augmentation does not necessarily improve the particular kind of robustness being tested.

The experiments additionally associate greater corruption robustness with better generalization across datasets. Drawing on these observations, the authors propose a baseline that improves robustness against diverse corruptions in both modality settings. The contribution combines a shared evaluation resource with empirical guidance about model and training choices; the reported comparisons concern the methods and conditions examined in the study.
summary.tldr: Five benchmarks reveal how person re-identification methods respond to image corruption and support a baseline with improved robustness.

title: Benchmarks for Corruption Invariant Person Re-identification

abstract: Due to the outstanding competence in capturing long-range relationships, self-attention mechanism has achieved remarkable progress in point cloud tasks. Nevertheless, point cloud object often has complex non-Euclidean spatial structures, with the behavior changing dynamically and unpredictably. Most current self-attention modules highly rely on the dot product multiplication in Euclidean space, which cannot capture internal non-Euclidean structures of point cloud objects, especially the long-range relationships along the curve of the implicit manifold surface represented by point cloud objects. To address this problem, in this paper, we introduce a novel metric on the Riemannian manifold to capture the long-range geometrical dependencies of point cloud objects to replace traditional self-attention modules, namely, the Geodesic Self-Attention (GSA) module. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to point cloud Transformers on object classification, few-shot classification and part segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: A point cloud represents a three-dimensional object through a collection of points, while the object's underlying surface can have complicated geometry. Self-attention helps connect distant parts of that collection. The paper argues that conventional attention based on Euclidean dot products does not adequately capture long-range relationships that follow the curved surface represented by the points.

The authors introduce Geodesic Self-Attention, or GSA, as a replacement attention module. It uses a metric on a Riemannian manifold to represent long-range geometric dependencies. The central change concerns how relationships are measured: the module is designed around the object's non-Euclidean structure, including connections along its implicit surface.

The approach reports state-of-the-art performance relative to point-cloud Transformers on object classification, few-shot classification, and part segmentation benchmarks. These tasks cover recognizing complete objects, recognizing them from limited examples, and labeling their parts. Together, the findings support incorporating surface-aware geometry into attention across several point-cloud tasks, rather than treating long-range interaction solely through conventional Euclidean similarity.
summary.tldr: Geodesic Self-Attention uses manifold geometry to model point-cloud relationships and improves results across classification and segmentation benchmarks.

title: Geodesic Self-Attention for 3D Point Clouds

abstract: Recent research has proposed a series of specialized optimization algorithms for deep multi-task models. It is often claimed that these multi-task optimization (MTO) methods yield solutions that are superior to the ones found by simply optimizing a weighted average of the task losses. In this paper, we perform large-scale experiments on a variety of language and vision tasks to examine the empirical validity of these claims. We show that, despite the added design and computational complexity of these algorithms, MTO methods do not yield any performance improvements beyond what is achievable via traditional optimization approaches. We highlight alternative strategies that consistently yield improvements to the performance profile and point out common training pitfalls that might cause suboptimal results. Finally, we outline challenges in reliably evaluating the performance of MTO algorithms and discuss potential solutions.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains one model to handle several tasks, requiring a choice about how their training losses interact. Specialized multi-task optimization methods are often presented as better than ordinary optimization of a weighted average of those losses. This paper tests that claim through large-scale experiments on language and vision tasks.

Across the investigated settings, the specialized methods do not improve performance beyond what traditional optimization approaches can achieve. This finding matters because the specialized algorithms also introduce design and computational complexity. The evidence challenges whether that additional complexity produces a useful performance advantage in the evaluated tasks.

The authors also identify alternative strategies that consistently improve the performance profile and discuss training pitfalls that can lead to poor results. They examine difficulties in evaluating multi-task optimizers reliably and outline potential solutions. The contribution therefore concerns both empirical outcomes and how comparisons should be conducted. Its conclusion is grounded in the tested methods and settings, rather than a proof about every possible multi-task optimization algorithm.
summary.tldr: Large-scale experiments find no advantage for the tested specialized multi-task optimizers over achievable traditional optimization results.

title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?

abstract: Most complex machine learning and modelling techniques are prone to over-fitting and may subsequently generalise poorly to future data. Artificial neural networks are no different in this regard and, despite having a level of implicit regularisation when trained with gradient descent, often require the aid of explicit regularisers. We introduce a new framework, Model Gradient Similarity (MGS), that (1) serves as a metric of regularisation, which can be used to monitor neural network training, (2) adds insight into how explicit regularisers, while derived from widely different principles, operate via the same mechanism underneath by increasing MGS, and (3) provides the basis for a new regularisation scheme which exhibits excellent performance, especially in challenging settings such as high levels of label noise or limited sample sizes.

paragraphs: Neural networks can fit their training data closely while performing poorly on future examples. Regularization aims to control this tendency, but different regularizers are often motivated by different principles. This paper introduces Model Gradient Similarity, or MGS, as a framework for examining their behavior through a shared measure.

MGS serves three connected purposes. It provides a metric of regularization that can be monitored during training, offers an interpretation of how explicit regularizers work, and forms the basis of a new regularization method. The authors describe an underlying common mechanism in which regularizers increase MGS. This connects methods with different starting motivations through their effect on model gradient similarity.

The proposed MGS-based regularization scheme is reported to perform especially well with noisy labels or limited training samples. Those findings make the framework relevant both for understanding training and for changing it. Its contribution is therefore broader than a new penalty alone: it links a monitoring quantity, an explanation of regularization behavior, and a method built from that explanation.
summary.tldr: Model Gradient Similarity provides a shared interpretation of regularization and motivates a method effective with noisy labels or limited data.

title: On the Interpretability of Regularisation for Neural Networks Through Model Gradient Similarity

abstract: Joint visual and language modeling on large-scale datasets has recently shown good progress in multi-modal tasks when compared to single modal learning. However, robustness of these approaches against real-world perturbations has not been studied. In this work, we perform the first extensive robustness study of video-language models against various real-world perturbations. We focus on text-to-video retrieval and propose two large-scale benchmark datasets, MSRVTT-P and YouCook2-P, which utilize 90 different visual and 35 different text perturbations. The study reveals some interesting initial findings from the studied models: 1) models are more robust when text is perturbed versus when video is perturbed, 2) models that are pre-trained are more robust than those trained from scratch, 3) models attend more to scene and objects rather than motion and action. We hope this study will serve as a benchmark and guide future research in robust video-language learning. The benchmark introduced in this study along with the code and datasets is available at https://bit.ly/3CNOly4.

paragraphs: Video-language models combine visual and textual information, but success on ordinary evaluation data does not establish how well they handle altered inputs. This paper studies robustness in text-to-video retrieval, where a textual query is used to find relevant video. It creates two large benchmark datasets, MSRVTT-P and YouCook2-P, to make such evaluation systematic.

The benchmarks include 90 visual perturbations and 35 text perturbations. Testing both sides of the retrieval task helps distinguish sensitivity to changes in video from sensitivity to changes in language. The study also compares pretrained models with models trained from scratch and examines the kinds of visual information the evaluated systems attend to.

Three initial findings emerge for the studied models: text changes are handled more robustly than video changes, pretraining is associated with greater robustness, and attention favors scenes and objects over motion and actions. These are observations about the evaluated systems. The benchmarks provide a basis for investigating those patterns and for assessing future progress in video-language robustness.
summary.tldr: New perturbation benchmarks reveal that studied video-language models are more sensitive to video changes and emphasize scenes and objects over motion.

title: Robustness Analysis of Video-Language Models Against Visual and Language Perturbations

abstract: We present GLIPv2, a grounded VL understanding model, that serves both localization tasks (e.g., object detection, instance segmentation) and Vision-Language (VL) understanding tasks (e.g., VQA, image captioning). GLIPv2 elegantly unifies localization pre-training and Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) with three pre-training tasks: phrase grounding as a VL reformulation of the detection task, region-word contrastive learning as a novel region-word level contrastive learning task, and the masked language modeling. This unification not only simplifies the previous multi-stage VLP procedure but also achieves mutual benefits between localization and understanding tasks. Experimental results show that a single GLIPv2 model (all model weights are shared) achieves near SoTA performance on various localization and understanding tasks. The model also shows (1) strong zero-shot and few-shot adaption performance on open-vocabulary object detection tasks and (2) superior grounding capability on VL understanding tasks.

paragraphs: GLIPv2 brings object localization and image-language understanding into one model. Localization includes finding objects or identifying their individual image regions; understanding includes answering questions about images and generating captions. The paper's goal is to make training for these activities support a common set of model weights.

The approach combines three pretraining tasks. Phrase grounding expresses object detection through links between language phrases and image regions. Region-word contrastive learning trains relationships between visual regions and words. Masked language modeling adds a task of recovering hidden language content. Together, these objectives unify localization pretraining with vision-language pretraining and simplify an earlier multistage procedure.

Experiments show that the shared model reaches near-state-of-the-art performance across several localization and understanding tasks. The authors also report strong zero-shot and few-shot adaptation for open-vocabulary object detection, alongside superior grounding on vision-language understanding tasks. These findings support the claim that the two task families can benefit each other, with one model learning both where described content appears and how visual content relates to language.
summary.tldr: GLIPv2 unifies localization and vision-language pretraining in one shared model, achieving near-state-of-the-art results across both task families.

title: GLIPv2: Unifying Localization and Vision-Language Understanding

abstract: We present Imagen, a text-to-image diffusion model with an unprecedented degree of photorealism and a deep level of language understanding. Imagen builds on the power of large transformer language models in understanding text and hinges on the strength of diffusion models in high-fidelity image generation. Our key discovery is that generic large language models (e.g., T5), pretrained on text-only corpora, are surprisingly effective at encoding text for image synthesis: increasing the size of the language model in Imagen boosts both sample fidelity and image-text alignment much more than increasing the size of the image diffusion model. Imagen achieves a new state-of-the-art FID score of 7.27 on the COCO dataset, without ever training on COCO, and human raters find Imagen samples to be on par with the COCO data itself in image-text alignment. To assess text-to-image models in greater depth, we introduce DrawBench, a comprehensive and challenging benchmark for text-to-image models. With DrawBench, we compare Imagen with recent methods including VQ-GAN+CLIP, Latent Diffusion Models, and DALL-E 2, and find that human raters prefer Imagen over other models in side-by-side comparisons, both in terms of sample quality and image-text alignment.

paragraphs: Imagen combines a large transformer language model with a diffusion image generator to turn text into realistic images. The paper's central finding concerns the text component: language models pretrained only on text, such as T5, can encode descriptions effectively for image synthesis.

In the reported scaling comparisons, increasing the language model's size improves both image fidelity and agreement with the description more than increasing the diffusion model's size. This points to text understanding as an important contributor to generation quality. Imagen achieves a COCO FID score of 7.27 without training on COCO, and human raters judge its image-text alignment to be on par with the dataset's own images.

Together, these results support the architecture and its emphasis on language representation, while the human preferences describe the comparisons performed in the study.
summary.tldr: Imagen shows that scaling a text-pretrained language encoder can substantially improve diffusion image quality and text alignment.

title: Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Deep Language Understanding

abstract: Identifying latent variables and causal structures from observational data is essential to many real-world applications involving biological data, medical data, and unstructured data such as images and languages. However, this task can be highly challenging, especially when observed variables are generated by causally related latent variables and the relationships are nonlinear. In this work, we investigate the identification problem for nonlinear latent hierarchical causal models in which observed variables are generated by a set of causally related latent variables, and some latent variables may not have observed children. We show that the identifiability of causal structures and latent variables (up to invertible transformations) can be achieved under mild assumptions: on causal structures, we allow for multiple paths between any pair of variables in the graph, which relaxes latent tree assumptions in prior work; on structural functions, we permit general nonlinearity and multi-dimensional continuous variables, alleviating existing work's parametric assumptions. Specifically, we first develop an identification criterion in the form of novel identifiability guarantees for an elementary latent variable model. Leveraging this criterion, we show that both causal structures and latent variables of the hierarchical model can be identified asymptotically by explicitly constructing an estimation procedure. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to establish identifiability guarantees for both causal structures and latent variables in nonlinear latent hierarchical models.

paragraphs: The paper asks when observational data can reveal hidden variables and the causal hierarchy connecting them. The setting is challenging because observed measurements arise from causally related latent variables through nonlinear relationships. Some hidden variables may have no directly observed children, so their influence must be understood through the wider hierarchy.

The authors establish identification guarantees under assumptions they describe as mild. Their permitted structures can contain multiple paths between variables, relaxing earlier latent-tree restrictions. The functions can be generally nonlinear, and variables can be multidimensional and continuous, reducing reliance on restrictive parametric descriptions.

The analysis begins with an identification criterion for an elementary latent-variable model and builds an explicit estimation procedure for the hierarchy. The resulting guarantee is asymptotic, and latent variables are identifiable up to invertible transformations. Thus, recovery allows changes of representation that preserve information rather than requiring one unique numerical coordinate system. The contribution establishes conditions under which both hidden structure and hidden variables can be recovered within this broader nonlinear setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional, asymptotic identification of nonlinear latent causal hierarchies, recovering hidden variables up to invertible transformations.

title: Identification of Nonlinear Latent Hierarchical Models

abstract: Modern reinforcement learning (RL) has shown empirical success in various real world settings with complex models and large state-action spaces. The existing analytical results, however, typically focus on settings with a small number of state-actions or simple models such as linearly modeled state-action value functions. To derive RL policies that efficiently handle large state-action spaces with more general value functions, some recent works have considered nonlinear function approximation using kernel ridge regression. We propose $\pi$-KRVI, an optimistic modification of least-squares value iteration, when the action-value function is represented by an RKHS. We prove the first order-optimal regret guarantees under a general setting. Our results show a significant polynomial in the number of episodes improvement over the state of the art. In particular, with highly non-smooth kernels (such as Neural Tangent kernel or some Matérn kernels) the existing results lead to trivial (superlinear in the number of episodes) regret bounds. We show a sublinear regret bound that is order optimal in the cases where a lower bound on regret is known (which includes the kernels mentioned above).

The existing analytical results, however, typically focus on settings with a small number of state-actions or simple models such as linearly modeled state-action value functions. To derive RL policies that efficiently handle large state-action spaces with more general value functions, some recent works have considered nonlinear function approximation using kernel ridge regression. We propose $\pi$-KRVI, an optimistic modification of least-squares value iteration, when the action-value function is represented by an RKHS. In particular, with highly non-smooth kernels (such as Neural Tangent kernel or some Matérn kernels) the existing results lead to trivial (superlinear in the number of episodes) regret bounds. paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning theory often studies small state-action spaces or relatively simple value functions, even though practical applications can be much more complex. Kernel methods offer a way to represent nonlinear value functions in larger spaces. This paper develops π-KRVI, an optimistic version of least-squares value iteration whose action-value function belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

The main contribution is a regret analysis that improves on earlier guarantees by a polynomial factor in the number of episodes. Regret tracks the accumulated performance shortfall during learning. A sublinear bound means this accumulated shortfall grows more slowly than the number of episodes, providing a meaningful guarantee of improving average performance.

The improvement is particularly consequential for highly nonsmooth kernels, including the Neural Tangent kernel and some Matérn kernels. Earlier results gave superlinear bounds for these cases, whereas the new analysis gives sublinear regret. Where matching lower bounds are known, including the mentioned kernel cases, the upper bounds are order optimal. That qualification ties the optimality claim to established limits.
summary.tldr: π-KRVI provides sharper kernelized reinforcement-learning regret bounds, achieving order-optimal rates in cases with known lower bounds.

title: Kernelized Reinforcement Learning with Order Optimal Regret Bounds

abstract: Diffusion-based image generation models, such as Stable Diffusion or DALL·E 2, are able to learn from given images and generate high-quality samples following the guidance from prompts. For instance, they can be used to create artistic images that mimic the style of an artist based on his/her original artworks or to maliciously edit the original images for fake content. However, such ability also brings serious ethical issues without proper authorization from the owner of the original images. In response, several attempts have been made to protect the original images from such unauthorized data usage by adding imperceptible perturbations, which are designed to mislead the diffusion model and make it unable to properly generate new samples. In this work, we introduce a perturbation purification platform, named IMPRESS, to evaluate the effectiveness of imperceptible perturbations as a protective measure.IMPRESS is based on the key observation that imperceptible perturbations could lead to a perceptible inconsistency between the original image and the diffusion-reconstructed image, which can be used to devise a new optimization strategy for purifying the image, which may weaken the protection of the original image from unauthorized data usage (e.g., style mimicking, malicious editing).The proposed IMPRESS platform offers a comprehensive evaluation of several contemporary protection methods, and can be used as an evaluation platform for future protection methods.

paragraphs: Some image-protection methods add changes that people cannot readily see but that interfere with diffusion-based generation. The aim is to discourage unauthorized uses such as imitating an artist's style or maliciously editing an image. IMPRESS evaluates how resilient these protections are when someone attempts to purify the protected image.

The method starts from an observation about reconstruction: visually imperceptible perturbations can produce perceptible disagreement between an image and its diffusion-reconstructed version. IMPRESS uses this inconsistency to formulate an optimization strategy for purification. The resulting processing may weaken the perturbations' protective effect and allow forms of usage that the original protection was designed to obstruct.

The authors use the platform to evaluate several contemporary protection methods and propose it as a testing resource for future methods. The contribution is therefore an evaluation approach tied to a specific potential weakness in protective perturbations. It provides a way to examine whether protection remains effective after purification, without establishing that every perturbation-based defense will necessarily fail.
summary.tldr: IMPRESS tests image-protection perturbations using reconstruction-based purification that may weaken their resistance to unauthorized diffusion-model usage.

title: IMPRESS: Evaluating the Resilience of Imperceptible Perturbations Against Unauthorized Data Usage in Diffusion-Based Generative AI

abstract: Algorithmic reproducibility measures the deviation in outputs of machine learning algorithms upon minor changes in the training process. Previous work suggests that first-order methods would need to trade-off convergence rate (gradient complexity) for better reproducibility. In this work, we challenge this perception and demonstrate that both optimal reproducibility and near-optimal convergence guarantees can be achieved for smooth convex minimization and smooth convex-concave minimax problems under various error-prone oracle settings. Particularly, given the inexact initialization oracle, our regularization-based algorithms achieve the best of both worlds -- optimal reproducibility and near-optimal gradient complexity -- for minimization and minimax optimization. With the inexact gradient oracle, the near-optimal guarantees also hold for minimax optimization. Additionally, with the stochastic gradient oracle, we show that stochastic gradient descent ascent is optimal in terms of both reproducibility and gradient complexity. We believe our results contribute to an enhanced understanding of the reproducibility-convergence trade-off in the context of convex optimization.
originalAbstract: Algorithmic reproducibility measures the deviation in outputs of machine learning algorithms upon minor changes in the training process. Previous work suggests that first-order methods would need to trade-off convergence rate (gradient complexity) for better reproducibility. In this work, we challenge this perception and demonstrate that both optimal reproducibility and near-optimal convergence guarantees can be achieved for smooth convex minimization and smooth convex-concave minimax problems under various error-prone oracle settings. Particularly, given the inexact initialization oracle, our regularization-based algorithms achieve the best of both worlds -- optimal reproducibility and near-optimal gradient complexity -- for minimization and minimax optimization. With the inexact gradient oracle, the near-optimal guarantees also hold for minimax optimization. Additionally, with the stochastic gradient oracle, we show that stochastic gradient descent ascent is optimal in terms of both reproducibility and gradient complexity. We believe our results contribute to an enhanced understanding of the reproducibility-convergence trade-off in the context of convex optimization.

paragraphs: Algorithmic reproducibility concerns how much an algorithm's output changes after small changes to training. Earlier work suggested that improving reproducibility could require slower convergence, measured by more gradient evaluations. This paper shows that optimal reproducibility and near-optimal gradient complexity can coexist in specified smooth convex optimization settings.

The authors study both convex minimization and convex-concave minimax problems under several sources of imperfect information. When initialization is inexact, their regularization-based algorithms achieve optimal reproducibility with near-optimal gradient complexity for both problem types. With inexact gradients, they also establish near-optimal guarantees for minimax optimization.

For a stochastic gradient oracle, they show that stochastic gradient descent ascent is optimal in both reproducibility and gradient complexity. The contribution is therefore a collection of guarantees tied to particular optimization problems and error settings. It challenges the idea of an unavoidable reproducibility-speed tradeoff within those settings, showing that the right algorithm can control output variation while retaining strong convergence efficiency.
summary.tldr: In specified smooth convex settings, algorithms can achieve optimal reproducibility alongside optimal or near-optimal gradient complexity.

title: Optimal Guarantees for Algorithmic Reproducibility and Gradient Complexity in Convex Optimization

abstract: State-of-the-art machine learning models can be vulnerable to very small input perturbations that are adversarially constructed. Adversarial training is an effective approach to defend against it. Formulated as a min-max problem, it searches for the best solution when the training data were corrupted by the worst-case attacks. Linear models are among the simple models where vulnerabilities can be observed and are the focus of our study. In this case, adversarial training leads to a convex optimization problem which can be formulated as the minimization of a finite sum. We provide a comparative analysis between the solution of adversarial training in linear regression and other regularization methods. Our main findings are that: (A) Adversarial training yields the minimum-norm interpolating solution in the overparameterized regime (more parameters than data), as long as the maximum disturbance radius is smaller than a threshold. And, conversely, the minimum-norm interpolator is the solution to adversarial training with a given radius. (B) Adversarial training can be equivalent to parameter shrinking methods (ridge regression and Lasso). This happens in the underparametrized region, for an appropriate choice of adversarial radius and zero-mean symmetrically distributed covariates. (C) For $\ell_\infty$-adversarial training---as in square-root Lasso---the choice of adversarial radius for optimal bounds does not depend on the additive noise variance. We confirm our theoretical findings with numerical examples.
