paragraphs: Adversarial training fits a model against worst-case perturbations of its training inputs. This paper studies linear regression, where the resulting optimization problem is convex, to understand how that training relates to familiar regularization methods. The analysis identifies several equivalences, each tied to particular conditions.

When there are more parameters than data points, adversarial training yields a minimum-norm interpolating solution if the maximum disturbance radius is below a threshold. Conversely, a minimum-norm interpolator solves an adversarial training problem with a corresponding radius. In the underparameterized regime, equivalence with ridge regression or Lasso can occur for suitable radii when covariates have a zero-mean symmetric distribution.

A further result concerns attacks bounded in the infinity norm. As with square-root Lasso, the disturbance radius used to obtain optimal bounds need not depend on additive noise variance. Numerical examples confirm the theoretical findings. The results explain how robustness to input perturbations can impose recognizable preferences on fitted parameters, while making clear that the particular preference depends on the regime, perturbation choice, and distributional conditions.
summary.tldr: Under specified conditions, adversarial linear regression connects to minimum-norm interpolation, ridge regression, and Lasso.

title: Regularization properties of adversarially-trained linear regression

abstract: 3D object detection (3DOD) from multi-view images is an economically appealing alternative to expensive LiDAR-based detectors, but also an extremely challenging task due to the absence of precise spatial cues. Recent studies have leveraged the teacher-student paradigm for cross-modal distillation, where a strong LiDAR-modality teacher transfers useful knowledge to a multi-view-based image-modality student. However, prior approaches have only focused on minimizing global distances between cross-modal features, which may lead to suboptimal knowledge distillation results. Based on these insights, we propose a novel structural and temporal cross-modal knowledge distillation (STXD) framework for multi-view 3DOD. First, STXD reduces redundancy of the feature components of the student by regularizing the cross-correlation of cross-modal features, while maximizing their similarities. Second, to effectively transfer temporal knowledge, STXD encodes temporal relations of features across a sequence of frames via similarity maps. Lastly, STXD also adopts a response distillation method to further enhance the quality of knowledge distillation at the output-level. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that STXD significantly improves the NDS and mAP of the based student detectors by 2.8%~4.5% on the nuScenes testing dataset.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from multiple camera views is economically attractive compared with LiDAR, but images lack equally precise spatial cues. STXD improves image-based detectors through a teacher-student setup: a stronger LiDAR model supplies knowledge during training. The paper argues that simply minimizing global differences between their features can leave useful information poorly transferred.

Its structural component regularizes correlations between teacher and student features while increasing their similarity, reducing redundancy among student feature components. Its temporal component represents relationships across frames using similarity maps. This gives the student supervision about how features relate over time, alongside information about their structure within the representations.

STXD also transfers knowledge at the output level through response distillation. Together, these components address feature structure, temporal relationships, and final predictions. Experiments on the nuScenes test set report improvements of 2.8%–4.5% in NDS and mAP for the underlying student detectors. The findings support a richer transfer objective for improving multi-view image-based 3D detection.
summary.tldr: STXD improves camera-based 3D detection by transferring structural, temporal, and output-level knowledge from a LiDAR teacher.

title: STXD: Structural and Temporal Cross-Modal Distillation for Multi-View 3D Object Detection

abstract: Most of existing neural methods for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) problems solely rely on decomposition, which often leads to repetitive solutions for the respective subproblems, thus a limited Pareto set. Beyond decomposition, we propose a novel neural heuristic with diversity enhancement (NHDE) to produce more Pareto solutions from two perspectives. On the one hand, to hinder duplicated solutions for different subproblems, we propose an indicator-enhanced deep reinforcement learning method to guide the model, and design a heterogeneous graph attention mechanism to capture the relations between the instance graph and the Pareto front graph. On the other hand, to excavate more solutions in the neighborhood of each subproblem, we present a multiple Pareto optima strategy to sample and preserve desirable solutions. Experimental results on classic MOCO problems show that our NHDE is able to generate a Pareto front with higher diversity, thereby achieving superior overall performance. Moreover, our NHDE is generic and can be applied to different neural methods for MOCO.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to multiobjective combinatorial optimization often split a problem into subproblems representing different tradeoffs. However, multiple subproblems can return the same solution, leaving a limited collection of Pareto alternatives. This paper addresses that duplication directly, aiming to produce a more diverse set of useful tradeoffs rather than repeatedly discovering the same candidates.

The proposed neural heuristic with diversity enhancement, NHDE, works in two ways. An indicator-enhanced reinforcement learning method discourages duplicate solutions across subproblems. A heterogeneous graph attention mechanism connects information about the problem instance with information about the Pareto front. Separately, a multiple Pareto optima strategy samples and retains desirable solutions near each subproblem, expanding the search around individual tradeoffs.

Experiments on classic multiobjective combinatorial problems show more diverse Pareto fronts and better overall performance. The authors also describe NHDE as applicable to different neural optimization methods. Its contribution is to make diversity an explicit part of both coordination across subproblems and exploration within their neighborhoods, addressing two sources of missed solutions.
summary.tldr: NHDE reduces duplicate solutions and explores nearby alternatives to produce more diverse Pareto fronts in neural combinatorial optimization.

title: Neural Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization with Diversity Enhancement

abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models have transformed image generation with their impressive fidelity and diversity.We show that they also excel in estimating optical flow and monocular depth, surprisingly without task-specific architectures and loss functions that are predominant for these tasks. Compared to the point estimates of conventional regression-based methods, diffusion models also enable Monte Carlo inference, e.g., capturing uncertainty and ambiguity in flow and depth.With self-supervised pre-training, the combined use of synthetic and real data for supervised training, and technical innovations (infilling and step-unrolled denoising diffusion training) to handle noisy-incomplete training data, one can train state-of-the-art diffusion models for depth and optical flow estimation, with additional zero-shot coarse-to-fine refinement for high resolution estimates. Extensive experiments focus on quantitative performance against benchmarks, ablations, and the model's ability to capture uncertainty and multimodality, and impute missing values. Our model obtains a state-of-the-art relative depth error of 0.074 on the indoor NYU benchmark and an Fl-all score of 3.26\% on the KITTI optical flow benchmark, about 25\% better than the best published method.

paragraphs: This paper applies denoising diffusion models to optical flow and single-image depth estimation. These tasks usually rely on specialized architectures and loss functions, but the authors show strong results without those task-specific designs. Diffusion also supports sampling multiple estimates, allowing the model to represent uncertainty and alternative plausible interpretations of motion or depth.

The training approach combines self-supervised pretraining with supervised learning on synthetic and real data. Infilling and step-unrolled denoising diffusion training address noisy or incomplete training information. The method additionally supports zero-shot refinement from coarse estimates to higher-resolution outputs. Together, these components adapt diffusion modeling to the practical characteristics of flow and depth data.

Experiments examine benchmark accuracy, component contributions, uncertainty, multiple plausible outputs, and missing-value imputation. The model achieves a relative depth error of 0.074 on NYU and a KITTI optical-flow Fl-all score of 3.26%, the latter reported as about 25% better than the best published method. The results demonstrate both competitive point-estimation performance and richer probabilistic outputs.
summary.tldr: Diffusion models achieve leading reported flow and depth results while supporting uncertainty estimates, multiple plausible outputs, and missing-value completion.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Diffusion Models for Optical Flow and Monocular Depth Estimation

abstract: We study the asymptotic generalization of an overparameterized linear model for multiclass classification under the Gaussian covariates bi-level model introduced in Subramanian et al. (NeurIPS'22), where the number of data points, features, and classes all grow together. We fully resolve the conjecture posed in Subramanian et al. '22, matching the predicted regimes for which the model does and does not generalize. Furthermore, our new lower bounds are akin to an information-theoretic strong converse: they establish that the misclassification rate goes to 0 or 1 asymptotically. One surprising consequence of our tight results is that the min-norm interpolating classifier can be asymptotically suboptimal relative to noninterpolating classifiers in the regime where the min-norm interpolating regressor is known to be optimal. The key to our tight analysis is a new variant of the Hanson-Wright inequality which is broadly useful for multiclass problems with sparse labels. As an application, we show that the same type of analysis can be used to analyze the related multi-label classification problem under the same bi-level ensemble.

One surprising consequence of our tight results is that the min-norm interpolating classifier can be asymptotically suboptimal relative to noninterpolating classifiers in the regime where the min-norm interpolating regressor is known to be optimal. paragraphs: This paper analyses when an overparameterised linear classifier generalises as its numbers of examples, features, and classes all increase. The analysis uses a specified Gaussian bi-level data model. Within that setting, the authors resolve a conjecture about which growth regimes lead to successful generalisation and which lead to failure.

Their tight bounds establish a sharp asymptotic distinction: the misclassification rate approaches either zero or one in the identified regimes. One consequence separates classification from regression. A minimum-norm classifier that fits the training data can be asymptotically worse than classifiers that do not interpolate, even in a regime where the corresponding minimum-norm interpolating regressor is known to be optimal.

The proof develops a variant of the Hanson–Wright inequality suited to multiclass problems with sparse labels. The authors also apply the analysis to multi-label classification under the same bi-level ensemble. The findings give precise conclusions for this mathematical setting and show why conclusions about interpolation in regression need not carry directly into multiclass classification.
summary.tldr: Under a growing Gaussian bi-level model, tight bounds identify when multiclass linear classification succeeds or fails and expose limits of minimum-norm interpolation.

title: Precise asymptotic generalization for multiclass classification with overparameterized linear models

abstract: Pre-trained multi-modal models, such as CLIP, provide transferable embeddings and show promising results in diverse applications. However, the analysis of learned multi-modal embeddings is relatively unexplored, and the embedding transferability can be improved. In this work, we observe that CLIP holds separated embedding subspaces for two different modalities, and then we investigate it through the lens of \textit{uniformity-alignment} to measure the quality of learned representation. Both theoretically and empirically, we show that CLIP retains poor uniformity and alignment even after fine-tuning. Such a lack of alignment and uniformity might restrict the transferability and robustness of embeddings. To this end, we devise a new fine-tuning method for robust representation equipping better alignment and uniformity. First, we propose a \textit{Geodesic Multi-Modal Mixup} that mixes the embeddings of image and text to generate hard negative samples on the hypersphere. Then, we fine-tune the model on hard negatives as well as original negatives and positives with contrastive loss. Based on the theoretical analysis about hardness guarantee and limiting behavior, we justify the use of our method. Extensive experiments on retrieval, calibration, few- or zero-shot classification (under distribution shift), embedding arithmetic, and image captioning further show that our method provides transferable representations, enabling robust model adaptation on diverse tasks.

Experiments span retrieval, calibration, classification under distribution shift, embedding arithmetic, and image captioning. The reported findings show transferable representations that support robust adaptation across these tasks. The approach matters because it turns an observed geometric weakness into a concrete training intervention: changing which difficult examples the model encounters while refining its shared representation space.
summary.tldr: Geodesic image-text embedding mixup creates hard negatives that improve representation alignment, uniformity, and adaptation in the reported experiments.

title: Geodesic Multi-Modal Mixup for Robust Fine-Tuning

abstract: Vision transformers have gained significant attention and achieved state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision tasks, including image classification, instance segmentation, and object detection. However, challenges remain in addressing attention complexity and effectively capturing fine-grained information within images. Existing solutions often resort to down-sampling operations, such as pooling, to reduce computational cost. Unfortunately, such operations are non-invertible and can result in information loss. In this paper, we present a novel approach called Scattering Vision Transformer (SVT) to tackle these challenges. SVT incorporates a spectrally scattering network that enables the capture of intricate image details. SVT overcomes the invertibility issue associated with down-sampling operations by separating low-frequency and high-frequency components. Furthermore, SVT introduces a unique spectral gating network utilizing Einstein multiplication for token and channel mixing, effectively reducing complexity. We show that SVT achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ImageNet dataset with a significant reduction in a number of parameters and FLOPS. SVT shows 2\% improvement over LiTv2 and iFormer. SVT-H-S reaches 84.2\% top-1 accuracy, while SVT-H-B reaches 85.2\% (state-of-art for base versions) and SVT-H-L reaches 85.7\% (again state-of-art for large versions). SVT also shows comparable results in other vision tasks such as instance segmentation. SVT also outperforms other transformers in transfer learning on standard datasets such as CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Oxford Flower, and Stanford Car datasets. The project page is available on this webpage.\url{https://badripatro.github.io/svt/}.

paragraphs: Vision transformers must balance computational cost with preserving detailed image information. Downsampling operations such as pooling reduce computation but can discard information because they are not invertible. Scattering Vision Transformer addresses this tension by treating low-frequency and high-frequency image components separately rather than relying on that form of information reduction.

The architecture includes a spectral scattering network to capture fine image details. It also uses a spectral gating network with Einstein multiplication to mix information across tokens and channels while reducing complexity. These components combine a way to represent image detail with a less costly mechanism for exchanging information within the model.

The authors report state-of-the-art ImageNet performance alongside reductions in parameters and FLOPs. The small, base, and large variants reach 84.2%, 85.2%, and 85.7% top-1 accuracy, respectively. Results are comparable on other vision tasks such as instance segmentation, while transfer-learning evaluations outperform other transformers on the listed datasets. The findings support spectral processing as a useful architectural choice for both efficiency and visual recognition.
summary.tldr: Scattering Vision Transformer combines frequency-separated image representations and spectral mixing to improve recognition with fewer parameters and operations.

title: Scattering Vision Transformer: Spectral Mixing Matters

abstract: Detecting anomalies in real-world multivariate time series data is challenging due to complex temporal dependencies and inter-variable correlations. Recently, reconstruction-based deep models have been widely used to solve the problem. However, these methods still suffer from an over-generalization issue and fail to deliver consistently high performance. To address this issue, we propose the MEMTO, a memory-guided Transformer using a reconstruction-based approach. It is designed to incorporate a novel memory module that can learn the degree to which each memory item should be updated in response to the input data. To stabilize the training procedure, we use a two-phase training paradigm which involves using K-means clustering for initializing memory items. Additionally, we introduce a bi-dimensional deviation-based detection criterion that calculates anomaly scores considering both input space and latent space. We evaluate our proposed method on five real-world datasets from diverse domains, and it achieves an average anomaly detection F1-score of 95.74%, significantly outperforming the previous state-of-the-art methods. We also conduct extensive experiments to empirically validate the effectiveness of our proposed model's key components.

paragraphs: MEMTO detects unusual behavior in time series containing multiple interacting variables. These data are difficult because relationships occur both across time and between variables. Reconstruction-based models attempt to reproduce their inputs, but excessive generalization can weaken their ability to distinguish anomalies. The paper addresses this issue with a Transformer guided by a learned memory.

The memory module learns how strongly each stored item should be updated in response to incoming data. A two-phase training procedure uses K-means clustering to initialize those memory items and stabilize learning. For detection, MEMTO measures deviations in both the original input space and the model's internal representation space, combining two views of abnormality.

Across five real-world datasets from diverse domains, the method achieves an average anomaly-detection F1 score of 95.74%, significantly exceeding previous state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. Additional experiments support the effectiveness of its main components. These findings connect the memory mechanism and dual-space detection criterion to stronger performance on the evaluated multivariate time series.
summary.tldr: MEMTO combines adaptive memory with input-space and latent-space deviations to improve multivariate time-series anomaly detection.

title: MEMTO: Memory-guided Transformer for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

abstract: Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated the ability to learn and leverage Internet-scale knowledge through pre-training with autoregressive models. Unfortunately, applying such models to settings with embodied agents, such as robots, is challenging due to their lack of experience with the physical world, inability to parse non-language observations, and ignorance of rewards or safety constraints that robots may require. On the other hand, language-conditioned robotic policies that learn from interaction data can provide the necessary grounding that allows the agent to be correctly situated in the real world, but such policies are limited by the lack of high-level semantic understanding due to the limited breadth of the interaction data available for training them. Thus, if we want to make use of the semantic knowledge in a language model while still situating it in an embodied setting, we must construct an action sequence that is both likely according to the language model and also realizable according to grounded models of the environment. We frame this as a problem similar to probabilistic filtering: decode a sequence that both has high probability under the language model and high probability under a set of grounded model objectives. We demonstrate how such grounded models can be obtained across three simulation and real-world domains, and that the proposed decoding strategy is able to solve complex, long-horizon embodiment tasks in a robotic setting by leveraging the knowledge of both models.

paragraphs: Language models contain broad semantic knowledge, but that knowledge alone does not tell a robot what it can physically accomplish. Such models may lack access to non-language observations and the rewards or constraints relevant to action. Policies trained through interaction offer physical grounding, yet their more limited training data can leave them short of high-level semantic understanding.

Grounded Decoding combines these complementary sources of knowledge while constructing an action sequence. It seeks sequences that receive high probability from the language model and also satisfy probabilistic objectives supplied by grounded models. The authors frame this process as similar to probabilistic filtering: generation is guided jointly by linguistic plausibility and models of what the environment supports.

The paper demonstrates how to obtain grounded models across three simulation and real-world domains. Its decoding strategy solves complex, long-horizon embodied tasks in the reported robotic settings. The result supports using environmental knowledge during sequence generation, so the language model’s semantic knowledge contributes to plans that grounded models also judge realizable.
summary.tldr: Grounded Decoding combines language-model probabilities with environment-grounded objectives to generate realizable action sequences for embodied tasks.

title: Grounded Decoding: Guiding Text Generation with Grounded Models for Embodied Agents

abstract: Learners sharing similar implicit cognitive states often display comparable observable problem-solving performances. Leveraging collaborative connections among such similar learners proves valuable in comprehending human learning. Motivated by the success of collaborative modeling in various domains, such as recommender systems, we aim to investigate how collaborative signals among learners contribute to the diagnosis of human cognitive states (i.e., knowledge proficiency) in the context of intelligent education.The primary challenges lie in identifying implicit collaborative connections and disentangling the entangled cognitive factors of learners for improved explainability and controllability in learner Cognitive Diagnosis (CD). However, there has been no work on CD capable of simultaneously modeling collaborative and disentangled cognitive states. To address this gap, we present Coral, a $\underline{Co}$llabo$\underline{ra}$tive cognitive diagnosis model with disentang$\underline{l}$ed representation learning. Specifically, Coral first introduces a disentangled state encoder to achieve the initial disentanglement of learners' states.Subsequently, a meticulously designed collaborative representation learning procedure captures collaborative signals. It dynamically constructs a collaborative graph of learners by iteratively searching for optimal neighbors in a context-aware manner. Using the constructed graph, collaborative information is extracted through node representation learning. Finally, a decoding process aligns the initial cognitive states and collaborative states, achieving co-disentanglement with practice performance reconstructions.Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of Coral, showcasing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several real-world datasets.Our code is available at https://github.com/bigdata-ustc/Coral.

Leveraging collaborative connections among such similar learners proves valuable in comprehending human learning. However, there has been no work on CD capable of simultaneously modeling collaborative and disentangled cognitive states. To address this gap, we present Coral, a $\underline{Co}$llabo$\underline{ra}$tive cognitive diagnosis model with disentang$\underline{l}$ed representation learning. Specifically, Coral first introduces a disentangled state encoder to achieve the initial disentanglement of learners' states.Subsequently, a meticulously designed collaborative representation learning procedure captures collaborative signals. It dynamically constructs a collaborative graph of learners by iteratively searching for optimal neighbors in a context-aware manner. Using the constructed graph, collaborative information is extracted through node representation learning. Finally, a decoding process aligns the initial cognitive states and collaborative states, achieving co-disentanglement with practice performance reconstructions.Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of Coral, showcasing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several real-world datasets.Our code is available at https://github.com/bigdata-ustc/Coral.

paragraphs: Cognitive diagnosis estimates learners’ knowledge proficiency from their observed problem-solving performance. Learners with similar underlying cognitive states often show similar performance, so information from related learners may help diagnose an individual. Coral combines this collaborative information with representations intended to separate different cognitive factors, addressing both sources of structure in one model.

The model first encodes learners into initially disentangled states. It then repeatedly searches for suitable neighbors in a context-aware way, constructing a graph that represents relationships among learners. Learning node representations on this graph extracts collaborative information. A final decoding stage aligns the initial states with the collaborative states while reconstructing practice performance, further coordinating the separation of cognitive factors.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The approach matters because the relationships used for collaboration are themselves learned, rather than assumed to be directly observable. At the same time, separating cognitive factors is part of the representation-learning process, supporting the paper’s aim of making learner models more explainable and controllable.
summary.tldr: Coral improves learner modeling by jointly learning relationships among learners and separating their underlying cognitive factors.

title: Collaborative Cognitive Diagnosis with Disentangled Representation Learning for Learner Modeling

abstract: Powered by remarkable advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities in manifold tasks.However, the practical application scenarios of MLLMs are intricate, exposing them to potential malicious instructions and thereby posing safety risks.While current benchmarks do incorporate certain safety considerations, they often lack comprehensive coverage and fail to exhibit the necessary rigor and robustness.For instance, the common practice of employing GPT-4V as both the evaluator and a model to be evaluated lacks credibility, as it tends to exhibit a bias toward its own responses.In this paper, we present MLLMGuard, a multi-dimensional safety evaluation suite for MLLMs, including a bilingual image-text evaluation dataset, inference utilities, and a lightweight evaluator.MLLMGuard's assessment comprehensively covers two languages (English and Chinese) and five important safety dimensions (Privacy, Bias, Toxicity, Truthfulness, and Legality), each with corresponding rich subtasks.Focusing on these dimensions, our evaluation dataset is primarily sourced from platforms such as social media, and it integrates text-based and image-based red teaming techniques with meticulous annotation by human experts.This can prevent inaccurate evaluation caused by data leakage when using open-source datasets and ensures the quality and challenging nature of our benchmark.Additionally, a fully automated lightweight evaluator termed GuardRank is developed, which achieves significantly higher evaluation accuracy than GPT-4.Our evaluation results across 13 advanced models indicate that MLLMs still have a substantial journey ahead before they can be considered safe and responsible.

paragraphs: Models that handle images and text face safety challenges that may be missed by narrowly focused tests. MLLMGuard provides a broader evaluation suite covering English and Chinese across privacy, bias, toxicity, truthfulness, and legality. It combines an image-text dataset, tools for running inference, and an automated evaluator.

The dataset draws primarily from sources such as social media and incorporates adversarial testing through both text and images. Human experts carefully annotate the examples. This construction aims to produce challenging, high-quality tests and reduce inaccurate evaluation associated with leakage from existing open datasets. The paper also questions evaluating a model with itself, citing GPT-4V's preference for its own responses.

The authors introduce GuardRank as a lightweight alternative evaluator and report significantly higher evaluation accuracy than GPT-4. Tests across 13 advanced models reveal substantial remaining safety shortcomings. The suite's contribution is to make several distinct safety dimensions assessable within one bilingual framework, while treating evaluator quality as part of the measurement problem.
summary.tldr: MLLMGuard evaluates image-text models across five safety dimensions in English and Chinese, revealing substantial shortcomings in 13 tested models.

title: MLLMGuard: A Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation Suite for Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Designing single-task image restoration models for specific degradation has seen great success in recent years. To achieve generalized image restoration, all-in-one methods have recently been proposed and shown potential for multiple restoration tasks using one single model. Despite the promising results, the existing all-in-one paradigm still suffers from high computational costs as well as limited generalization on unseen degradations. In this work, we introduce an alternative solution to improve the generalization of image restoration models. Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in Parameter Efficient Transfer Learning (PETL), we aim to tune only a small number of parameters to adapt pre-trained restoration models to various tasks. However, current PETL methods fail to generalize across varied restoration tasks due to their homogeneous representation nature. To this end, we propose AdaptIR, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with orthogonal multi-branch design to capture local spatial, global spatial, and channel representation bases, followed by adaptive base combination to obtain heterogeneous representation for different degradations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our AdaptIR achieves stable performance on single-degradation tasks, and excels in hybrid-degradation tasks, with training only 0.6% parameters for 8 hours.

paragraphs: AdaptIR addresses how a pre-trained image-restoration model can adapt to different kinds of degradation while updating few parameters. The authors identify high computational cost and limited generalization to unseen degradations as problems for existing all-in-one restoration models. They investigate parameter-efficient transfer as an alternative, while arguing that homogeneous representations restrict existing adaptation methods.

Their solution is a mixture of experts with an orthogonal multibranch design. Different branches capture local spatial, global spatial, and channel representations. An adaptive combination mechanism then brings these representation bases together for different degradations. The architecture is intended to supply varied types of features within a compact adaptation mechanism.

Experiments report stable performance on tasks involving a single degradation and strong results on tasks combining degradations. The reported setup trains only 0.6% of parameters for eight hours. These findings support the value of heterogeneous representations when adapting restoration models: a small trainable component can draw on several complementary forms of image information.
summary.tldr: AdaptIR adapts restoration models through complementary expert branches, reporting strong hybrid-degradation results while training only 0.6% of parameters.

title: Parameter Efficient Adaptation for Image Restoration with Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has recently been applied to the parameter-efficient fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs). While promising, it raises significant challenges due to the heterogeneous resources and data distributions of clients.This study introduces FlexLoRA, a simple yet effective aggregation scheme for LLM fine-tuning, which mitigates the "buckets effect" in traditional FL that restricts the potential of clients with ample resources by tying them to the capabilities of the least-resourced participants. FlexLoRA allows for dynamic adjustment of local LoRA ranks, fostering the development of a global model imbued with broader, less task-specific knowledge. By synthesizing a full-size LoRA weight from individual client contributions and employing Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for weight redistribution, FlexLoRA fully leverages heterogeneous client resources. Involving thousands of clients performing heterogeneous NLP tasks and client resources, our experiments validate the efficacy of FlexLoRA, with the federated global model achieving consistently better improvement over SOTA FL methods in downstream NLP task performance across various heterogeneous distributions. FlexLoRA's practicality is further underscored by our theoretical analysis and its seamless integration with existing LoRA-based FL methods, offering a path toward cross-device, privacy-preserving federated tuning for LLMs.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning brings together clients with different data, tasks, and computing resources. When every client must use an adaptation capacity suited to the least capable participant, better-resourced clients cannot fully contribute. FlexLoRA addresses this bottleneck for language-model fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation, or LoRA.

The method lets local LoRA ranks vary dynamically, so clients can use different adaptation capacities. During aggregation, it combines client contributions into a full-size LoRA weight. It then uses singular value decomposition to redistribute weights in forms appropriate for the clients. This provides a common aggregation process despite differences in their local ranks.

Experiments involve thousands of clients with heterogeneous NLP tasks and resource levels. Across the tested heterogeneous distributions, the global model achieves consistently better downstream task improvements than the compared state-of-the-art federated methods. The paper also provides theoretical analysis and describes compatibility with existing LoRA-based federated approaches. Together, these contributions offer a practical route toward federated tuning that makes better use of unequal client resources.
summary.tldr: FlexLoRA aggregates and redistributes variable-rank LoRA updates so federated language-model tuning can benefit from clients with unequal resources.

title: Federated Fine-tuning of Large Language Models under Heterogeneous Tasks and Client Resources

abstract: In image editing, Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) inversion has become a widely adopted method and is extensively used in various image editing approaches. The core concept of DDIM inversion stems from the deterministic sampling technique of DDIM, which allows the DDIM process to be viewed as an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) process that is reversible. This enables the prediction of corresponding noise from a reference image, ensuring that the restored image from this noise remains consistent with the reference image. Image editing exploits this property by modifying the cross-attention between text and images to edit specific objects while preserving the remaining regions. However, in the DDIM inversion, using the $t-1$ time step to approximate the noise prediction at time step $t$ introduces errors between the restored image and the reference image. Recent approaches have modeled each step of the DDIM inversion process as finding a fixed-point problem of an implicit function. This approach significantly mitigates the error in the restored image but lacks theoretical support regarding the existence of such fixed points. Therefore, this paper focuses on the study of fixed points in DDIM inversion and provides theoretical support. Based on the obtained theoretical insights, we further optimize the loss function for the convergence of fixed points in the original DDIM inversion, improving the visual quality of the edited image. Finally, we extend the fixed-point based image editing to the application of unsupervised image dehazing, introducing a novel text-based approach for unsupervised dehazing.

Recent methods reduce these errors by casting each inversion step as a fixed-point problem, but their theoretical basis was incomplete.

This paper studies the existence of those fixed points and uses the resulting theory to optimize a convergence-oriented loss for inversion. The objective is to reconstruct the reference image more faithfully and improve the visual quality of subsequent edits.

The authors also extend fixed-point-based editing to text-based unsupervised image dehazing. The abstract does not provide quantitative reconstruction, editing, or dehazing results, nor does it state the exact existence assumptions. The contribution connects a practical inversion technique to mathematical support and uses that connection to refine the editing procedure and explore a related restoration task.
summary.tldr: Fixed-point analysis improves DDIM inversion and supports an unsupervised dehazing application.

title: Exploring Fixed Point in Image Editing: Theoretical Support and Convergence Optimization

abstract: Generative models at times produce "invalid" outputs, such as images with generation artifacts and unnatural sounds. Validity-constrained distribution learning attempts to address this problem by requiring that the learned distribution have a provably small fraction of its mass in invalid parts of space -- something which standard loss minimization does not always ensure. To this end, a learner in this model can guide the learning via "validity queries", which allow it to ascertain the validity of individual examples. Prior work on this problem takes a worst-case stance, showing that proper learning requires an exponential number of validity queries, and demonstrating an improper algorithm which -- while generating guarantees in a wide-range of settings -- makes a relatively large polynomial number of validity queries. In this work, we take a first step towards characterizing regimes where guaranteeing validity is easier than in the worst-case. We show that when the data distribution lies in the model class and the log-loss is minimized, the number samples required to ensure validity has a weak dependence on the validity requirement. Additionally, we show that when the validity region belongs to a VC-class, a limited number of validity queries are often sufficient.

paragraphs: A generative model can fit its training objective yet still produce invalid outputs, such as images with artifacts or unnatural sounds. Validity-constrained distribution learning asks for a stronger guarantee: only a small fraction of the learned distribution's probability should fall on invalid examples. The learner can query whether individual examples are valid.

Earlier worst-case results make this goal look expensive. Learning within the designated model class can require exponentially many validity queries, while a method allowed to go outside that class uses a relatively large polynomial number. This paper investigates circumstances in which validity guarantees become easier to obtain than these worst-case results suggest.

The authors identify two favorable regimes. When the true data distribution belongs to the model class and learning minimizes log-loss, the required sample count depends only weakly on the validity requirement. When the valid region belongs to a VC-class, limited validity queries are often sufficient. These are conditional results: they connect more manageable validity guarantees to assumptions about the data distribution, learning objective, or structure of the valid region.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies structured settings where learning a distribution with few invalid outputs requires less effort than worst-case results suggest.

title: Distribution Learning with Valid Outputs Beyond the Worst-Case

abstract: Digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) are simulated 2D X-ray images generated from 3D CT volumes, widely used in preoperative settings but limited in intraoperative applications due to computational bottlenecks. Physics-based Monte Carlo simulations provide accurate representations but are extremely computationally intensity. Analytical DRR renderers are much more efficient, but at the price of ignoring anisotropic X-ray image formation phenomena such as Compton scattering. We propose a novel approach that balances realistic physics-inspired X-ray simulation with efficient, differentiable DRR generation using 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Our direction-disentangled 3DGS (DDGS) method decomposes the radiosity contribution into isotropic and direction-dependent components, able to approximate complex anisotropic interactions without complex runtime simulations. Additionally, we adapt the 3DGS initialization to account for tomography data properties, enhancing accuracy and efficiency. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in image accuracy and inference speed, demonstrating its potential for intraoperative applications and inverse problems like pose registration.

paragraphs: DDGS-CT generates simulated two-dimensional X-ray images from three-dimensional CT volumes. Accurate Monte Carlo simulation is computationally expensive, while faster analytical renderers can omit direction-dependent effects such as Compton scattering. The paper seeks a practical balance between representing those effects and generating images efficiently.

The method uses three-dimensional Gaussian splatting and separates the radiosity contribution into direction-independent and direction-dependent components. The authors also modify initialization to reflect the properties of tomography data, improving how the representation starts from the available volume information.

summary.tldr: DDGS-CT separates direction-dependent X-ray effects in Gaussian splatting to produce fast, differentiable simulated radiographs.

title: DDGS-CT: Direction-Disentangled Gaussian Splatting for Realistic Volume Rendering

abstract: Building a general-purpose agent is a long-standing vision in the field of artificial intelligence. Existing agents have made remarkable progress in many domains, yet they still struggle to complete long-horizon tasks in an open world. We attribute this to the lack of necessary world knowledge and multimodal experience that can guide agents through a variety of long-horizon tasks. In this paper, we propose a Hybrid Multimodal Memory module to address the above challenges. It 1) transforms knowledge into Hierarchical Directed Knowledge Graph that allows agents to explicitly represent and learn world knowledge, and 2) summarises historical information into Abstracted Multimodal Experience Pool that provide agents with rich references for in-context learning. On top of the Hybrid Multimodal Memory module, a multimodal agent, Optimus-1, is constructed with dedicated Knowledge-guided Planner and Experience-Driven Reflector, contributing to a better planning and reflection in the face of long-horizon tasks in Minecraft. Extensive experimental results show that Optimus-1 significantly outperforms all existing agents on challenging long-horizon task benchmarks, and exhibits near human-level performance on many tasks. In addition, we introduce various Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as the backbone of Optimus-1. Experimental results show that Optimus-1 exhibits strong generalization with the help of the Hybrid Multimodal Memory module, outperforming the GPT-4V baseline on many tasks.

paragraphs: Optimus-1 tackles tasks that require an agent to sustain useful behavior over many steps in an open world. The authors attribute existing agents’ difficulties partly to insufficient world knowledge and multimodal experience. Their solution gives an agent two complementary forms of memory: structured knowledge about the world and summarized experience from its previous activity.

The knowledge component organizes information into a hierarchical directed graph, supporting explicit representation and learning of world knowledge. The experience component stores abstracted multimodal histories that can serve as references for in-context learning. Optimus-1 combines these memories with a planner guided by knowledge and a reflector guided by experience, supporting planning and reflection during Minecraft tasks.

On challenging long-horizon benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over existing agents and near-human performance on many tasks. They also test different multimodal language-model backbones and report strong generalization with the memory module, including results above the GPT-4V baseline on many tasks. These findings support combining structured knowledge and past experience for extended agent behavior.
summary.tldr: Optimus-1 combines structured world knowledge and summarized multimodal experience to improve planning and reflection on long-horizon Minecraft tasks.

title: Optimus-1: Hybrid Multimodal Memory Empowered Agents Excel in Long-Horizon Tasks

abstract: In practical distributed systems, workers are typically not homogeneous, and due to differences in hardware configurations and network conditions, can have highly varying processing times. We consider smooth nonconvex finite-sum (empirical risk minimization) problems in this setup and introduce a new parallel method, Freya PAGE, designed to handle arbitrarily heterogeneous and asynchronous computations. By being robust to "stragglers" and adaptively ignoring slow computations, Freya PAGE offers significantly improved time complexity guarantees compared to all previous methods, including Asynchronous SGD, Rennala SGD, SPIDER, and PAGE, while requiring weaker assumptions. The algorithm relies on novel generic stochastic gradient collection strategies with theoretical guarantees that can be of interest on their own, and may be used in the design of future optimization methods. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems in the asynchronous setup, providing a fundamental time complexity limit. This lower bound is tight and demonstrates the optimality of Freya PAGE in the large-scale regime, i.e., when $\sqrt{m} \geq n,$ where $n$ is \# of workers, and $m$ is \# of data samples.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization often runs on workers with different processing speeds because hardware and network conditions vary. A method that handles calculations efficiently can still lose time waiting for slow workers. Freya PAGE addresses smooth, nonconvex finite-sum optimization in a setting where workers operate asynchronously and can have arbitrarily different speeds.

The method adaptively ignores slow computations and uses new strategies for collecting stochastic gradients. The authors give these collection strategies theoretical guarantees and suggest that they may also be useful in other optimization methods. Freya PAGE obtains stronger time-complexity guarantees than the compared methods, including asynchronous SGD and PAGE, while requiring weaker assumptions.

The paper also proves a lower bound on the time required for this class of problems in the asynchronous setting. Freya PAGE matches that limit in the large-scale regime where the square root of the number of samples is at least the number of workers. Its optimality claim is tied to that regime, making the relationship between dataset size and worker count central to the theoretical result.
summary.tldr: Freya PAGE handles unequal asynchronous workers and achieves optimal time complexity in a specified large-scale optimization regime.

title: Freya PAGE: First Optimal Time Complexity for Large-Scale Nonconvex Finite-Sum Optimization with Heterogeneous Asynchronous Computations

abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has expanded their capabilities across various data modalities, extending from well-established image data to increasingly popular graph data. Given the limitation of LLMs in hallucinations and inaccuracies in recalling factual knowledge, Knowledge Graph (KG) has emerged as a crucial data modality to support more accurate reasoning by LLMs. However, integrating structured knowledge from KGs into LLMs remains challenging, as most current KG-enhanced LLM methods directly convert the KG into linearized text triples, which is not as expressive as the original structured data. To address this, we introduce GraphVis, which conserves the intricate graph structure through the visual modality to enhance the comprehension of KGs with the aid of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs). Our approach incorporates a unique curriculum fine-tuning scheme which first instructs LVLMs to recognize basic graphical features from the images, and subsequently incorporates reasoning on QA tasks with the visual graphs. This cross-modal methodology not only markedly enhances performance on standard textual QA but also shows improved zero-shot VQA performance by utilizing synthetic graph images to augment the data for VQA tasks. We present comprehensive evaluations across commonsense reasoning QA benchmarks, where GraphVis provides an average improvement of 11.1% over its base model and outperforms existing KG-enhanced LLM approaches. Across VQA benchmarks such as ScienceQA that share similar scientific diagram images, GraphVis provides a notable gain of 4.32%.

This ordering connects graph-image comprehension with reasoning over the represented knowledge. Synthetic graph images also provide additional training material that can benefit visual question answering.

On commonsense question-answering benchmarks, GraphVis reports an average improvement of 11.1% over its base model and outperforms the compared knowledge-graph-enhanced language-model methods. It also improves zero-shot visual question answering, with a reported gain of 4.32% on benchmarks such as ScienceQA that contain related scientific diagrams. Together, these results suggest that learning to interpret visual graph structure can benefit both textual reasoning and some diagram-related visual tasks.
summary.tldr: GraphVis teaches vision-language models to interpret knowledge graphs as images, improving textual and visual question answering in the reported evaluations.

title: GraphVis: Boosting LLMs with Visual Knowledge Graph Integration

abstract: Models trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) are prone to be biased towards spurious correlations between target labels and bias attributes, which leads to poor performance on data groups lacking spurious correlations. It is particularly challenging to address this problem when access to bias labels is not permitted. To mitigate the effect of spurious correlations without bias labels, we first introduce a novel training objective designed to robustly enhance model performance across all data samples, irrespective of the presence of spurious correlations. From this objective, we then derive a debiasing method, Disagreement Probability based Resampling for debiasing (DPR), which does not require bias labels. DPR leverages the disagreement between the target label and the prediction of a biased model to identify bias-conflicting samples—those without spurious correlations—and upsamples them according to the disagreement probability. Empirical evaluations on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DPR achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baselines that do not use bias labels. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis that details how DPR reduces dependency on spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Models trained to minimize average training error can rely on incidental relationships between labels and bias attributes. That reliance hurts examples where those relationships do not hold. This paper tackles the setting in which bias labels are unavailable, so training cannot directly identify disadvantaged groups through annotations of the bias attribute.

The authors first formulate an objective intended to improve performance across examples regardless of whether they follow the spurious relationship. From it they derive Disagreement Probability based Resampling, or DPR. DPR compares the target label with a biased model’s prediction and uses the probability of disagreement to identify and upsample examples that conflict with the bias.

The mechanism gives greater training presence to examples that a biased model struggles to explain, using ordinary target labels without requiring bias labels. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report leading performance among compared methods operating without bias labels. They also provide theoretical analysis explaining how DPR reduces dependence on spurious correlations. The empirical and theoretical contributions support disagreement-guided resampling as a way to weaken shortcut reliance.
summary.tldr: DPR uses a biased model’s disagreement with target labels to upsample bias-conflicting examples without requiring bias annotations.

title: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Disagreement Probability

abstract: Selling a single item to $n$ self-interested bidders is a fundamental problem in economics, where the two objectives typically considered are welfare maximization and revenue maximization. Since the optimal auctions are often impractical and do not work for sequential bidders, posted pricing auctions, where fixed prices are set for the item for different bidders, have emerged as a practical and effective alternative. This paper investigates how many samples are needed from bidders' value distributions to find near-optimal posted prices, considering both independent and correlated bidder distributions, and welfare versus revenue maximization. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds (up to logarithmic terms) on the sample complexity for all these settings.

paragraphs: Selling one item to several self-interested bidders can involve two different goals: maximizing welfare or maximizing the seller's revenue. Optimal auction designs may be impractical, particularly when bidders arrive sequentially. Posted pricing offers a practical alternative by setting fixed prices for different bidders rather than relying on a more elaborate auction procedure.

This paper asks how much information is needed to learn good posted prices. The information comes as samples from the distributions of bidders' values, and the target is pricing that is close to optimal. The authors consider both independent bidder values and correlated values, separately addressing welfare and revenue objectives.

For every setting studied, the paper provides upper and lower bounds on the required number of samples that match up to logarithmic factors. Upper bounds establish that sufficiently good prices can be learned with a certain amount of data; lower bounds show why substantially less data cannot generally suffice. Together, they characterize the statistical demands of learning posted prices across these different economic settings.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching sample requirements for learning near-optimal posted prices under welfare and revenue objectives.

title: Sample Complexity of Posted Pricing for a Single Item

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become more capable of handling increasingly complex tasks, the evaluation set must keep pace with these advancements to ensure it remains sufficiently discriminative. Item Discrimination (ID) theory, which is widely used in educational assessment, measures the ability of individual test items to differentiate between high and low performers. Inspired by this theory, we propose an ID-induced prompt synthesis framework for evaluating LLMs so that the evaluation set continually updates and refines according to model abilities. Our data synthesis framework prioritizes both breadth and specificity. It can generate prompts that comprehensively evaluate the capabilities of LLMs while revealing meaningful performance differences between models, allowing for effective discrimination of their relative strengths and weaknesses across various tasks and domains.To produce high-quality data, we incorporate a self-correct mechanism into our generalization framework and develop two models to predict prompt discrimination and difficulty score to facilitate our data synthesis framework, contributing valuable tools to evaluation data synthesis research. We apply our generated data to evaluate five SOTA models. Our data achieves an average score of 51.92, accompanied by a variance of 10.06. By contrast, previous works (i.e., SELF-INSTRUCT and WizardLM) obtain an average score exceeding 67, with a variance below 3.2.The results demonstrate that the data generated by our framework is more challenging and discriminative compared to previous works.We will release a dataset of over 3,000 carefully crafted prompts to facilitate evaluation research of LLMs.

paragraphs: As language models improve, an evaluation can lose usefulness if its questions no longer separate stronger models from weaker ones. IDGen draws on item discrimination from educational assessment: the ability of an individual question to distinguish different levels of performance. It uses this idea to guide the generation and refinement of evaluation prompts.

The framework aims for broad coverage across tasks and domains while generating questions that expose meaningful differences between models. It incorporates a self-correction mechanism and two predictive models, one for prompt discrimination and another for difficulty. These components help direct synthesis toward questions that are both challenging and useful for comparing capabilities.

The authors evaluate five state-of-the-art models using the generated data. They report an average score of 51.92 and variance of 10.06, compared with averages above 67 and variances below 3.2 for SELF-INSTRUCT and WizardLM data. They interpret the lower scores and greater spread as evidence of increased challenge and discrimination. The abstract also announces a planned release of more than 3,000 prompts.
summary.tldr: IDGen generates evaluation prompts guided by difficulty and item discrimination to better distinguish language-model capabilities.

title: IDGen: Item Discrimination Induced Prompt Generation for LLM Evaluation

abstract: LLMs can now act as autonomous agents that interact with digital environments and complete specific objectives (e.g., arranging an online meeting). However, accuracy is still far from satisfactory, partly due to a lack of large-scale, direct demonstrations for digital tasks. Obtaining supervised data from humans is costly, and automatic data collection through exploration or reinforcement learning relies on complex environmental and content setup, resulting in datasets that lack comprehensive coverage of various scenarios. On the other hand, there is abundant knowledge that may indirectly assist task completion, such as online tutorials that were created for human consumption. In this work, we present Synatra, an approach that effectively transforms this indirect knowledge into direct supervision at scale. We define different types of indirect knowledge, and carefully study the available sources to obtain it, methods to encode the structure of direct demonstrations, and finally methods to transform indirect knowledge into direct demonstrations. We use 100k such synthetically-created demonstrations to finetune a 7B CodeLlama, and demonstrate that the resulting agent surpasses all comparably sized models on three web-based task benchmarks Mind2Web, MiniWoB++ and WebArena, as well as surpassing GPT-3.5 on WebArena and Mind2Web. In addition, while synthetic demonstrations prove to be only 3% the cost of human demonstrations (at $0.031 each), we show that the synthetic demonstrations can be more effective than an identical number of human demonstrations collected from limited domains.

paragraphs: Digital agents need demonstrations of how to complete tasks, but collecting them from people is expensive. Automatic exploration also requires substantial environment setup and may cover a limited range of scenarios. Synatra instead draws on indirect knowledge, such as tutorials written for people, and converts it into direct supervision for agents.

The paper studies types and sources of indirect knowledge, ways to represent the structure of demonstrations, and methods for performing the conversion. The authors generate 100,000 synthetic demonstrations and use them to fine-tune a 7-billion-parameter CodeLlama model. This turns existing instructional material into data that directly supports learning digital actions.

The resulting agent surpasses the comparably sized models evaluated on Mind2Web, MiniWoB++, and WebArena, and surpasses GPT-3.5 on Mind2Web and WebArena. The synthetic demonstrations cost $0.031 each, reported as 3% of human-demonstration cost. They can also outperform an equal number of human demonstrations collected from limited domains. That comparison highlights the potential value of coverage as well as collection cost.
summary.tldr: Synatra converts indirect instructional knowledge into inexpensive synthetic demonstrations that improve a digital agent on three web-task benchmarks.

title: Synatra: Turning Indirect Knowledge into Direct Demonstrations for Digital Agents at Scale

abstract: Efficient transfer learning has shown remarkable performance in tuning large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) toward downstream tasks with limited data resources. The key challenge of efficient transfer lies in adjusting image-text alignment to be task-specific while preserving pre-trained general knowledge. However, existing methods adjust image-text alignment merely on a set of observed samples, e.g., data set and external knowledge base, which cannot guarantee to keep the correspondence of general concepts between image and text latent manifolds without being disrupted and thereby a weak generalization of the adjusted alignment. In this work, we propose a Homology Consistency (HC) constraint for efficient transfer on VLMs, which explicitly constrains the correspondence of image and text latent manifolds through structural equivalence based on persistent homology in downstream tuning. Specifically, we build simplicial complex on the top of data to mimic the topology of latent manifolds, then track the persistence of the homology classes of topological features across multiple scales, and guide the directions of persistence tracks in image and text manifolds to coincide each other, with a deviating perturbation additionally. For practical application, we tailor the implementation of our proposed HC constraint for two main paradigms of adapter tuning. Extensive experiments on few-shot learning over 11 datasets and domain generalization demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method.

paragraphs: Adapting a vision-language model with limited data requires adjusting image-text alignment while preserving useful pretrained knowledge. The paper argues that matching only observed examples can disrupt broader relationships between visual and textual concepts. It proposes a Homology Consistency constraint to preserve correspondence between the structures of the two representation spaces during tuning.

The method builds mathematical structures called simplicial complexes from the data to approximate the shape of those spaces. Persistent homology then tracks topological features across multiple scales. The constraint guides the directions of these persistence tracks to agree between image and text representations, with an additional deviating perturbation included in the procedure.

This approach makes structural correspondence part of the adaptation objective, extending attention beyond individual observed image-text matches. The authors tailor the constraint to two main adapter-tuning paradigms. Experiments on few-shot learning across 11 datasets and on domain generalization demonstrate effectiveness and robustness, providing empirical support for using topological structure to guide efficient vision-language transfer.
summary.tldr: A persistent-homology constraint helps preserve structural correspondence between image and text representations during efficient vision-language model tuning.

title: Homology Consistency Constrained Efficient Tuning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Fitness functions map large combinatorial spaces of biological sequences to properties of interest. Inferring these multimodal functions from experimental data is a central task in modern protein engineering. Global epistasis models are an effective and physically-grounded class of models for estimating fitness functions from observed data. These models assume that a sparse latent function is transformed by a monotonic nonlinearity to emit measurable fitness. Here we demonstrate that minimizing supervised contrastive loss functions, such as the Bradley-Terry loss, is a simple and flexible technique for extracting the sparse latent function implied by global epistasis. We argue by way of a fitness-epistasis uncertainty principle that the nonlinearities in global epistasis models can produce observed fitness functions that do not admit sparse representations, and thus may be inefficient to learn from observations when using a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss (a common practice). We show that contrastive losses are able to accurately estimate a ranking function from limited data even in regimes where MSE is ineffective and validate the practical utility of this insight by demonstrating that contrastive loss functions result in consistently improved performance on empirical benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Protein engineering often requires learning how biological sequences map to a measured property, or fitness. Global epistasis models describe this relationship using a sparse hidden function followed by a monotonic nonlinear transformation. The paper investigates how to recover that simpler hidden structure when the measured fitness function itself may be difficult to learn.

The authors show that supervised contrastive objectives, including the Bradley-Terry loss, provide a flexible way to extract the latent function implied by this model. Their argument is that the nonlinear transformation can turn a sparse latent relationship into an observed function without a sparse representation. Directly fitting observed values with mean squared error can therefore be inefficient.

Contrastive losses instead support learning a ranking function from limited data, including regimes where mean squared error is ineffective. The authors report consistently improved performance on empirical benchmark tasks. The result connects the choice of training objective to the assumed biological structure: comparisons can recover useful ordering information even when the transformation to measured fitness makes direct value prediction difficult.
summary.tldr: Contrastive losses can recover useful fitness rankings from limited biological sequence data when nonlinear effects make direct value fitting ineffective.

title: Contrastive losses as generalized models of global epistasis

abstract: We present OxonFair, a new open source toolkit for enforcing fairness in binary classification. Compared to existing toolkits: (i) We support NLP and Computer Vision classification as well as standard tabular problems. (ii) We support enforcing fairness on validation data, making us robust to a wide range of overfitting challenges. (iii) Our approach can optimize any measure based on True Positives, False Positive, False Negatives, and True Negatives. This makes it easily extensible and much more expressive than existing toolkits. It supports all 9 and all 10 of the decision-based group metrics of two popular review articles. (iv) We jointly optimize a performance objective alongside fairness constraints. This minimizes degradation while enforcing fairness, and even improves the performance of inadequately tuned unfair baselines. OxonFair is compatible with standard ML toolkits, including sklearn, Autogluon, and PyTorch and is available at https://github.com/oxfordinternetinstitute/oxonfair.

paragraphs: OxonFair is an open-source toolkit for enforcing fairness constraints in binary classification. It supports tabular data, language tasks, and computer vision classification. The toolkit jointly optimizes a performance objective and fairness requirements, aiming to limit the performance loss that can accompany enforcing a chosen fairness constraint.

Its measures can be built from true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives. That flexibility makes the toolkit extensible and lets it express all the decision-based group metrics covered by two review articles discussed in the paper. Fairness can also be enforced using validation data, which the authors describe as providing robustness to a range of overfitting challenges.

The paper reports that joint optimization can even improve performance when the unfair baseline is inadequately tuned. This is a qualified finding about those baselines, alongside the broader aim of minimizing degradation. Compatibility with sklearn, Autogluon, and PyTorch makes the approach usable with established machine-learning workflows, bringing varied fairness objectives into a shared practical toolkit.
summary.tldr: OxonFair jointly optimizes classification performance and flexible fairness constraints across tabular, language, and vision tasks.

title: OxonFair: A Flexible Toolkit for Algorithmic Fairness

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an appealing paradigm that allows a group of machines(a.k.a. clients) to learn collectively while keeping their data local. However, dueto the heterogeneity between the clients’ data distributions, the model obtainedthrough the use of FL algorithms may perform poorly on some client’s data.Personalization addresses this issue by enabling each client to have a differentmodel tailored to their own data while simultaneously benefiting from the otherclients’ data. We consider an FL setting where some clients can be adversarial, andwe derive conditions under which full collaboration fails. Specifically, we analyzethe generalization performance of an interpolated personalized FL framework in thepresence of adversarial clients, and we precisely characterize situations when fullcollaboration performs strictly worse than fine-tuned personalization. Our analysisdetermines how much we should scale down the level of collaboration, accordingto data heterogeneity and the tolerable fraction of adversarial clients. We supportour findings with empirical results on mean estimation and binary classificationproblems, considering synthetic and benchmark image classification datasets

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients learn together while retaining their data locally, but a shared model can fit some clients poorly when their data differ. Personalization adjusts models to individual clients while retaining benefits from collaboration. This paper examines how to choose that balance when some participating clients may also behave adversarially.

The authors analyze the generalization performance of an interpolated personalized framework, in which the level of collaboration can be adjusted. They characterize conditions where full collaboration performs strictly worse than fine-tuned personalization. Their analysis connects the appropriate reduction in collaboration to both differences among clients' data distributions and the fraction of adversarial clients the system is intended to tolerate.

Experiments on mean estimation and binary classification support the theoretical findings, using synthetic data and benchmark image classification datasets. The conclusion is conditional: the paper identifies settings where reducing collaboration is beneficial. It provides a principled way to relate personalization to data heterogeneity and adversarial participation, rather than treating collaboration level as an isolated choice.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when personalized federated learning outperforms full collaboration in the presence of adversarial clients.

title: Fine-Tuning Personalization in Federated Learning to Mitigate Adversarial Clients

abstract: Preference learning algorithms (e.g., RLHF and DPO) are frequently used to steer LLMs to produce generations that are more preferred by humans, but our understanding of their inner workings is still limited. In this work, we study the conventional wisdom that preference learning trains models to assign higher likelihoods to more preferred outputs than less preferred outputs, measured via *ranking accuracy*.Surprisingly, we find that most state-of-the-art preference-tuned models achieve a ranking accuracy of less than 60% on common preference datasets. We furthermore derive the *idealized ranking accuracy* that a preference-tuned LLM would achieve if it optimized the DPO or RLHF objective perfectly. We demonstrate that existing models exhibit a significant *alignment gap* -- *i.e.*, a gap between the observed and idealized ranking accuracies. We attribute this discrepancy to the DPO objective, which is empirically and theoretically ill-suited to correct even mild ranking errors in the reference model, and derive a simple and efficient formula for quantifying the difficulty of learning a given preference datapoint.Finally, we demonstrate that ranking accuracy strongly correlates with the empirically popular win rate metric when the model is close to the reference model used in the objective, shedding further light on the differences between on-policy (e.g., RLHF) and off-policy (e.g., DPO) preference learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Preference learning is commonly used to make language-model responses more desirable to humans. This paper examines a specific expectation: whether preference-tuned models assign greater likelihood to preferred outputs than to less preferred ones. On common preference datasets, most state-of-the-art models studied achieve less than 60% accuracy on this ranking task.

The authors derive the ranking accuracy an idealized model would reach if it perfectly optimized the DPO or RLHF objective. Existing models fall substantially short of that idealized level, producing an alignment gap. The analysis attributes this discrepancy to the DPO objective's difficulty correcting even mild ranking mistakes inherited from its reference model, supported by theoretical and empirical evidence.

The paper also derives an efficient formula for measuring how difficult an individual preference example is to learn. Finally, ranking accuracy strongly correlates with win rate when the model remains close to its reference model. That condition is central to the finding and helps clarify differences between on-policy and off-policy preference learning.
summary.tldr: Preference-tuned models often rank preferred outputs poorly, and the paper identifies an objective-related gap between observed and idealized ranking accuracy.

title: Preference Learning Algorithms Do Not Learn Preference Rankings

abstract: The stable periodic patterns present in time series data serve as the foundation for conducting long-horizon forecasts. In this paper, we pioneer the exploration of explicitly modeling this periodicity to enhance the performance of models in long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) tasks. Specifically, we introduce the Residual Cycle Forecasting (RCF) technique, which utilizes learnable recurrent cycles to model the inherent periodic patterns within sequences, and then performs predictions on the residual components of the modeled cycles. Combining RCF with a Linear layer or a shallow MLP forms the simple yet powerful method proposed in this paper, called CycleNet. CycleNet achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy in multiple domains including electricity, weather, and energy, while offering significant efficiency advantages by reducing over 90% of the required parameter quantity. Furthermore, as a novel plug-and-play technique, the RCF can also significantly improve the prediction accuracy of existing models, including PatchTST and iTransformer. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ACAT-SCUT/CycleNet.
