paragraphs: Standard sparse coding and dictionary learning assume that observations are vectors in a Euclidean space. Their operations rely on that space's linear structure and distance measure. The paper addresses data originating on Riemannian manifolds, where a global linear structure is unavailable and the intrinsic geometry may matter to the application.

The authors propose a framework for learning dictionaries and sparse representations directly in this more general geometric setting. Existing Euclidean methods appear as special cases of the framework. This relationship explains how the proposal extends familiar methods while accommodating data whose geometry does not support the same global vector operations.

The paper shows that dictionaries and sparse codes can be computed effectively for several important classes of Riemannian manifolds. It validates the approach on two classification problems in computer vision and medical imaging analysis. The contribution is both conceptual and computational: it broadens the setting in which sparse coding is defined and demonstrates that the resulting formulation can be used on practical classification tasks.
summary.tldr: A manifold-based framework generalizes sparse coding and dictionary learning, with Euclidean methods as special cases.

title: On A Nonlinear Generalization of Sparse Coding and Dictionary Learning

abstract: We tackle the problem of inferring node labels in a partially labeled graph where each node in the graph has multiple label types and each label type has a large number of possible labels. Our primary example, and the focus of this paper, is the joint inference of label types such as hometown, current city, and employers, for users connected by a social network. Standard label propagation fails to consider the properties of the label types and the interactions between them. Our proposed method, called EdgeExplain, explicitly models these, while still enabling scalable inference under a distributed message-passing architecture. On a billion-node subset of the Facebook social network, EdgeExplain significantly outperforms label propagation for several label types, with lifts of up to 120% for recall@1 and 60% for recall@3.

paragraphs: The paper addresses missing labels in a partially labeled network where each node has several kinds of attributes, each with many possible values. Its main example is a social network with hometown, current city, and employer labels. Predicting these attributes jointly requires accounting for both their individual properties and their interactions.

The proposed method, EdgeExplain, explicitly models those properties and interactions. This addresses a weakness identified in standard label propagation, which does not account for them. EdgeExplain also supports distributed message passing, allowing its richer treatment of labels to be used for inference on a very large graph.

On a billion-node subset of Facebook's social network, EdgeExplain significantly outperforms label propagation for several label types. Reported improvements reach 120% for recall@1 and 60% for recall@3, measuring recovery among the first one or three predictions. These are the largest reported lifts, rather than gains stated for every label type. The experiment demonstrates joint inference at substantial network scale.
summary.tldr: EdgeExplain models interactions among node-label types and improves label inference over label propagation on a billion-node social network.

title: Joint Inference of Multiple Label Types in Large Networks

abstract: We describe a learning procedure enhancing L1-penalized regression by adding dynamically generated rules describing multidimensional “box” sets. Our rule-adding procedure is based on the classical column generation method for high-dimensional linear programming. The pricing problem for our column generation procedure reduces to the NP-hard rectangular maximum agreement (RMA) problem of finding a box that best discriminates between two weighted datasets. We solve this problem exactly using a parallel branch-and-bound procedure. The resulting rule-enhanced regression procedure is computation-intensive, but has promising prediction performance.

The rules are generated dynamically during learning, making rule discovery part of the fitting procedure.

The authors organize this process using column generation, a classical approach from high-dimensional linear programming. Its pricing problem determines which rule to introduce. Here that problem becomes rectangular maximum agreement: finding a box that best separates two weighted datasets. This links the statistical task of improving regression to a specific combinatorial optimization problem.

The resulting regression method is computationally intensive, but the authors report promising prediction performance. Its significance is the combination of dynamically discovered box rules with penalized regression, together with an exact rule-search procedure. The computational cost is an explicit part of the reported tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Column generation adds dynamically optimized box rules to L1-penalized regression, offering promising predictions at substantial computational cost.

title: Rule-Enhanced Penalized Regression by Column Generation using Rectangular Maximum Agreement

abstract: Coherent uncertainty quantification is a key strength of Bayesian methods. But modern algorithms for approximate Bayesian posterior inference often sacrifice accurate posterior uncertainty estimation in the pursuit of scalability. This work shows that previous Bayesian coreset construction algorithms—which build a small, weighted subset of the data that approximates the full dataset—are no exception. We demonstrate that these algorithms scale the coreset log-likelihood suboptimally, resulting in underestimated posterior uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, we develop greedy iterative geodesic ascent (GIGA), a novel algorithm for Bayesian coreset construction that scales the coreset log-likelihood optimally. GIGA provides geometric decay in posterior approximation error as a function of coreset size, and maintains the fast running time of its predecessors. The paper concludes with validation of GIGA on both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating that it reduces posterior approximation error by orders of magnitude compared with previous coreset constructions.

The paper examines whether this compression preserves uncertainty accurately. It finds that previous coreset construction methods scale the subset’s log-likelihood poorly, causing the resulting posterior to underestimate uncertainty.

The authors introduce Greedy Iterative Geodesic Ascent, or GIGA, to correct that scaling problem. Its construction optimally scales the coreset log-likelihood while maintaining the fast running time of earlier methods. The issue is therefore not simply how many examples a summary contains, but also how strongly their combined evidence influences the posterior.

The paper establishes geometric decay in posterior approximation error as coreset size increases. This describes a progressively shrinking error at a geometric rate as more data are included in the summary. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report orders-of-magnitude reductions in approximation error compared with earlier constructions. Together, these results show how improved coreset construction can support scalability while better preserving Bayesian uncertainty.
summary.tldr: GIGA improves Bayesian coresets by correcting log-likelihood scaling, reducing posterior approximation error while retaining fast construction.

title: Bayesian Coreset Construction via Greedy Iterative Geodesic Ascent

abstract: We present a new algorithm for identifying the transition and emission probabilities of a hidden Markov model (HMM) from the emitted data. Expectation-maximization becomes computationally prohibitive for long observation records, which are often required for identification. The new algorithm is particularly suitable for cases where the available sample size is large enough to accurately estimate second-order output probabilities, but not higher-order ones. We show that if one is only able to obtain a reliable estimate of the pairwise co-occurrence probabilities of the emissions, it is still possible to uniquely identify the HMM if the emission probability is sufficiently scattered . We apply our method to hidden topic Markov modeling, and demonstrate that we can learn topics with higher quality if documents are modeled as observations of HMMs sharing the same emission (topic) probability, compared to the simple but widely used bag-of-words model.

Learning these quantities can require long records, making expectation-maximization computationally prohibitive. This paper proposes an alternative suited to data that support reliable estimates of pairwise output probabilities but not higher-order statistics.

The authors show that pairwise co-occurrences can suffice to identify the model uniquely when the emission probabilities satisfy a sufficiently scattered condition. This is a conditional identifiability result: pairwise information is adequate for the stated class, rather than for every possible hidden Markov model. The algorithm uses that result to estimate transitions and emissions from observed data.

For topic modeling, the authors treat documents as observations from hidden Markov models that share the same topic emission probabilities. They report higher-quality topics than with a bag-of-words model. This application shows the potential value of modeling sequential structure while learning from pairwise statistics that can be estimated reliably.
summary.tldr: Pairwise emission statistics can uniquely identify an HMM under a sufficiently scattered emission condition, with benefits demonstrated in topic modeling.

title: Learning Hidden Markov Models from Pairwise Co-occurrences with Application to Topic Modeling

abstract: In this paper we advocate for a hyperparametric approach to learn diffusion in the independent cascade (IC) model. The sample complexity of this model is a function of the number of edges in the network and consequently learning becomes infeasible when the network is large. We study a natural restriction of the hypothesis class using additional information available in order to dramatically reduce the sample complexity of the learning process. In particular we assume that diffusion probabilities can be described as a function of a global hyperparameter and features of the individuals in the network. One of the main challenges with this approach is that training a model reduces to optimizing a non-convex objective. Despite this obstacle, we can shrink the best-known sample complexity bound for learning IC by a factor of |E|/d where |E| is the number of edges in the graph and d is the dimension of the hyperparameter. We show that under mild assumptions about the distribution generating the samples one can provably train a model with low generalization error. Finally, we use large-scale diffusion data from Facebook to show that a hyperparametric model using approximately 20 features per node achieves remarkably high accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning how diffusion spreads through a network can require too much data when the learning problem grows with the number of edges. This paper studies that problem in the independent cascade model. It restricts the model class by using additional information about individuals to describe diffusion probabilities more compactly.

The central assumption is that diffusion probabilities can be expressed through individual features and a shared global hyperparameter. This lets many network connections draw on the same parameterization. Although fitting the resulting model involves a non-convex objective, the authors improve the best-known sample-complexity bound by a factor of |E|/d, where |E| counts edges and d is the hyperparameter dimension.

Under mild assumptions about the distribution producing the samples, the authors show that a model with low generalization error can be trained. They also evaluate the approach on large-scale Facebook diffusion data, reporting high accuracy with approximately 20 features per node. The findings support a compact, feature-based description of diffusion when the shared-parameter assumption is appropriate.
summary.tldr: Modeling diffusion probabilities with shared parameters and individual features reduces sample complexity under stated assumptions and performs well on Facebook diffusion data.

title: Learning Diffusion using Hyperparameters

abstract: We introduce a conceptually simple and scalable framework for continual learning domains where tasks are learned sequentially. Our method is constant in the number of parameters and is designed to preserve performance on previously encountered tasks while accelerating learning progress on subsequent problems. This is achieved by training a network with two components: A knowledge base, capable of solving previously encountered problems, which is connected to an active column that is employed to efficiently learn the current task. After learning a new task, the active column is distilled into the knowledge base, taking care to protect any previously acquired skills. This cycle of active learning (progression) followed by consolidation (compression) requires no architecture growth, no access to or storing of previous data or tasks, and no task-specific parameters. We demonstrate the progress & compress approach on sequential classification of handwritten alphabets as well as two reinforcement learning domains: Atari games and 3D maze navigation.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a system to acquire tasks sequentially while retaining earlier skills. Progress & Compress addresses this with a fixed-size architecture designed to preserve previous performance and accelerate later learning. Its central idea is to alternate between learning the current task and consolidating what was learned.

The network has a knowledge base for previously encountered problems and a connected active column for the current task. During progression, the active column learns the new problem. During compression, its knowledge is distilled into the knowledge base with protection for existing skills. This separates immediate task learning from the subsequent integration of that knowledge.

The cycle requires no architectural growth, no stored or accessible previous task data, and no task-specific parameters. These properties directly address resource growth as the task sequence lengthens. The authors demonstrate the framework on sequential handwritten-alphabet classification, Atari games, and three-dimensional maze navigation, showing its application across both supervised learning and reinforcement learning domains.
summary.tldr: Progress & Compress alternates new-task learning with protected knowledge consolidation in a fixed-size network without storing previous task data.

title: Progress & Compress: A scalable framework for continual learning

abstract: We study an online and streaming unsupervised classification system. Our setting consists of a collection of classifiers (with unknown confusion matrices) each of which can classify one sample per unit time, and which are accessed by a stream of unlabeled samples. Each sample is dispatched to one or more classifiers, and depending on the labels collected from these classifiers, may be sent to other classifiers to collect additional labels. The labels are continually aggregated. Once the aggregated label has high enough accuracy (a pre-specified threshold for accuracy) or the sample is sent to all the classifiers, the now labeled sample is ejected from the system. For any given pre-specified threshold for accuracy, the objective is to sustain the maximum possible rate of arrival of new samples, such that the number of samples in memory does not grow unbounded. In this paper, we characterize the Pareto-optimal region of accuracy and arrival rate, and develop an algorithm that can operate at any point within this region. Our algorithm uses queueing-based routing and scheduling approaches combined with novel online tensor decomposition method to learn the hidden parameters, to Pareto-optimality guarantees. We finally verify our theoretical results through simulations on two ensembles formed using AlexNet, VGG, and ResNet deep image classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper studies a stream of unlabeled samples served by classifiers whose error patterns are initially unknown. Each classifier can process one sample per time unit. A sample may visit several classifiers as their labels are aggregated, leaving when its accuracy threshold is reached or every classifier has been used.

The objective is to admit samples as quickly as possible without an ever-growing backlog, for a specified accuracy requirement. The authors characterize the Pareto-optimal region relating accuracy to arrival rate. This describes the achievable tradeoff between label quality and sustained throughput, treating classification and the management of limited processing capacity as one problem.

Their algorithm combines queue-based routing and scheduling with an online tensor decomposition method for learning hidden parameters. It can operate at any point within the characterized region, with Pareto-optimality guarantees. Simulations using two ensembles built from AlexNet, VGG, and ResNet classifiers verify the theoretical results, connecting the analysis to ensembles of deep image classifiers.
summary.tldr: A routing and learning algorithm achieves the characterized accuracy-throughput tradeoff for streaming classification with initially unknown classifier error patterns.

title: Pareto Optimal Streaming Unsupervised Classification

abstract: We expose a structure in deep classifying neural networks in the derivative of the logits with respect to the parameters of the model, which is used to explain the existence of outliers in the spectrum of the Hessian. Previous works decomposed the Hessian into two components, attributing the outliers to one of them, the so-called Covariance of gradients. We show this term is not a Covariance but a second moment matrix, i.e., it is influenced by means of gradients. These means possess an additive two-way structure that is the source of the outliers in the spectrum. This structure can be used to approximate the principal subspace of the Hessian using certain "averaging" operations, avoiding the need for high-dimensional eigenanalysis. We corroborate this claim across different datasets, architectures and sample sizes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why some eigenvalues of a deep classifier's Hessian stand apart from the rest. The Hessian describes curvature with respect to model parameters. The authors connect these spectral outliers to structure in the derivatives of logits, the model's class scores, with respect to those parameters.

Earlier work attributed the outliers to a Hessian component described as a covariance of gradients. The authors show that this component is actually a second moment matrix, so gradient means contribute to it. Those means have an additive two-way structure, which the paper identifies as the source of the spectral outliers.

This explanation also suggests a computational shortcut. Certain averaging operations can approximate the Hessian's principal subspace, avoiding high-dimensional eigenanalysis. Measurements across different datasets, architectures, and sample sizes corroborate the claim. The contribution therefore combines a correction to the interpretation of a Hessian component with a way to recover important curvature directions from the mean structure of derivatives.
summary.tldr: Structured gradient means explain Hessian spectral outliers and enable approximation of its principal subspace through averaging operations.

title: Measurements of Three-Level Hierarchical Structure in the Outliers in the Spectrum of Deepnet Hessians

abstract: Adversarial examples are inputs to machine learning models designed by an adversary to cause an incorrect output. So far, adversarial examples have been studied most extensively in the image domain. In this domain, adversarial examples can be constructed by imperceptibly modifying images to cause misclassification, and are practical in the physical world. In contrast, current targeted adversarial examples on speech recognition systems have neither of these properties: humans can easily identify the adversarial perturbations, and they are not effective when played over-the-air. This paper makes progress on both of these fronts. First, we develop effectively imperceptible audio adversarial examples (verified through a human study) by leveraging the psychoacoustic principle of auditory masking, while retaining 100% targeted success rate on arbitrary full-sentence targets. Then, we make progress towards physical-world audio adversarial examples by constructing perturbations which remain effective even after applying highly-realistic simulated environmental distortions.

paragraphs: An adversarial audio example is modified speech intended to make a recognition system output an incorrect transcription chosen by an attacker. The paper addresses two obstacles identified in earlier targeted speech attacks: listeners could hear the modifications, and the attacks did not remain effective when audio was played through the physical environment.

For perceptual quality, the authors use auditory masking, a property of hearing in which some sounds obscure others. They construct audio modifications that are effectively imperceptible and verify that property through a human study. The reported attacks retain a 100% targeted success rate for arbitrary full-sentence targets in the evaluated setting.

The paper separately advances environmental robustness by constructing modifications that survive highly realistic simulated distortions. This supports progress toward physical-world audio attacks, while the stated evidence concerns simulation rather than demonstrated over-the-air effectiveness. Together, the results show that targeted transcription errors can coexist with low perceptibility and that environmental distortion need not always eliminate an attack. The two findings address complementary challenges in assessing speech recognition robustness.
summary.tldr: Auditory masking enables effectively imperceptible targeted speech attacks, while additional constructions remain effective under realistic simulated environmental distortions.

title: Imperceptible, Robust, and Targeted Adversarial Examples for Automatic Speech Recognition

abstract: Probabilistic programming has emerged as a powerful paradigm in statistics, applied science, and machine learning: by decoupling modelling from inference, it promises to allow modellers to directly reason about the processes generating data. However, the performance of inference algorithms can be dramatically affected by the parameterisation used to express a model, requiring users to transform their programs in non-intuitive ways. We argue for automating these transformations, and demonstrate that mechanisms available in recent modelling frameworks can implement non-centring and related reparameterisations. This enables new inference algorithms, and we propose two: a simple approach using interleaved sampling and a novel variational formulation that searches over a continuous space of parameterisations. We show that these approaches enable robust inference across a range of models, and can yield more efficient samplers than the best fixed parameterisation.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming aims to let users describe how data are generated while inference machinery handles the resulting calculations. In practice, the mathematical parameterization of a model can strongly affect inference performance. Users may therefore need to rewrite an otherwise suitable model in ways that are difficult to anticipate from the modeling problem itself.

This paper argues that those transformations should be automated. It demonstrates how mechanisms in recent modeling frameworks can implement non-centering and related reparameterizations. The contribution makes alternative expressions of a model available to inference algorithms without requiring users to perform each transformation manually.

The authors introduce two inference approaches built on this capability. One uses interleaved sampling; the other uses a variational formulation that searches continuously over parameterizations. Across a range of models, these approaches support robust inference and can produce samplers more efficient than the best fixed parameterization. The result suggests that selecting or combining parameterizations during inference can offer benefits beyond choosing one representation in advance.
summary.tldr: Automated model reparameterization enables inference methods that can outperform the best fixed parameterization across the studied models.

title: Automatic Reparameterisation of Probabilistic Programs

abstract: In the presence of noisy or incorrect labels, neural networks have the undesirable tendency to memorize information about the noise. Standard regularization techniques such as dropout, weight decay or data augmentation sometimes help, but do not prevent this behavior. If one considers neural network weights as random variables that depend on the data and stochasticity of training, the amount of memorized information can be quantified with the Shannon mutual information between weights and the vector of all training labels given inputs, $I(w; \mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})$. We show that for any training algorithm, low values of this term correspond to reduction in memorization of label-noise and better generalization bounds. To obtain these low values, we propose training algorithms that employ an auxiliary network that predicts gradients in the final layers of a classifier without accessing labels. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach on versions of MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 corrupted with various noise models, and on a large-scale dataset Clothing1M that has noisy labels.

This paper studies memorization through the information stored in network weights. It treats the weights as random variables influenced by both training data and training randomness, then measures their mutual information with the training labels while conditioning on the inputs.

The authors show that, for any training algorithm, lower values of this information quantity correspond to less memorization of label noise and better generalization bounds. This supplies a theoretical target for training. The quantity concerns how much label information the weights retain once the input examples are already accounted for.

To pursue that target, the proposed algorithms use an auxiliary network to predict gradients for the classifier’s final layers without accessing labels. The authors illustrate effectiveness on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with several label-noise models, and on the naturally noisy Clothing1M dataset. The contribution connects an information-based account of memorization to a concrete modification of how classifier updates are generated.
summary.tldr: The paper links reduced label information in network weights to less noise memorization and proposes label-free gradient prediction to pursue that objective.

title: Improving generalization by controlling label-noise information in neural network weights

abstract: Evidence-based decision-making entails collecting (costly) observations about an underlying phenomenon of interest, and subsequently committing to an (informed) decision on the basis of accumulated evidence. In this setting, *active sensing* is the goal-oriented problem of efficiently selecting which acquisitions to make, and when and what decision to settle on. As its complement, *inverse active sensing* seeks to uncover an agent’s preferences and strategy given their observable decision-making behavior. In this paper, we develop an expressive, unified framework for the general setting of evidence-based decision-making under endogenous, context-dependent time pressure—which requires negotiating (subjective) tradeoffs between accuracy, speediness, and cost of information. Using this language, we demonstrate how it enables *modeling* intuitive notions of surprise, suspense, and optimality in decision strategies (the forward problem). Finally, we illustrate how this formulation enables *understanding* decision-making behavior by quantifying preferences implicit in observed decision strategies (the inverse problem).

paragraphs: Making an informed decision involves choosing what evidence to collect, how much to spend collecting it, and when to stop. Active sensing studies those choices in pursuit of a goal. Inverse active sensing starts with observed behavior and asks what preferences and strategy could explain an agent’s sequence of information gathering and commitment.

The paper develops a unified framework for these problems when time pressure arises within the decision setting and depends on context. It represents subjective tradeoffs among accuracy, speed, and information cost. This makes the timing of a decision part of the strategy being modeled, alongside which observations to acquire and which final decision to make.

For the forward problem, the framework expresses intuitive concepts such as surprise, suspense, and optimality in decision strategies. For the inverse problem, the authors illustrate how it can quantify preferences implicit in observed strategies. The contribution is a shared mathematical language for constructing decision models and interpreting behavior through the tradeoffs those models represent.
summary.tldr: The paper models evidence gathering under time pressure and uses observed decisions to infer preferences about accuracy, speed, and information cost.

title: Inverse Active Sensing: Modeling and Understanding Timely Decision-Making

abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved great success in various areas, but recent works have found that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which leads to a hot topic nowadays. Although many approaches have been proposed to enhance the robustness of neural networks, few of them explored robust architectures for neural networks. On this account, we try to address such an issue from the perspective of dynamic system in this work. By viewing ResNet as an explicit Euler discretization of an ordinary differential equation (ODE), for the first time, we find that the adversarial robustness of ResNet is connected to the numerical stability of the corresponding dynamic system, i.e., more stable numerical schemes may correspond to more robust deep networks. Furthermore, inspired by the implicit Euler method for solving numerical ODE problems, we propose Implicit Euler skip connections (IE-Skips) by modifying the original skip connection in ResNet or its variants. Then we theoretically prove its advantages under the adversarial attack and the experimental results show that our ResNet with IE-Skips can largely improve the robustness and the generalization ability under adversarial attacks when compared with the vanilla ResNet of the same parameter size.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial robustness through network architecture and numerical methods. It views a residual network as an explicit Euler discretization of an ordinary differential equation. From this perspective, the authors connect the network's robustness to the numerical stability of the corresponding dynamical system, suggesting that more stable numerical schemes may produce more robust networks.

Inspired by the implicit Euler method, they introduce Implicit Euler skip connections, or IE-Skips. The change modifies the original skip connection in ResNet or related architectures. This makes the organization of the network itself part of the robustness approach, using the differential-equation interpretation to motivate the architectural choice.

The authors provide a theoretical proof of advantages under adversarial attack. Their experiments also show substantial improvements in robustness and generalization under attacks compared with a standard ResNet of the same parameter size. The empirical comparison supports IE-Skips specifically, while the broader relationship between numerical stability and robustness is presented as a possible correspondence rather than a universal rule.
summary.tldr: Skip connections inspired by implicit Euler integration improve adversarial robustness in evaluated ResNets and receive theoretical support.

title: Implicit Euler Skip Connections: Enhancing Adversarial Robustness via Numerical Stability

abstract: Phase I dose-finding trials are increasingly challenging as the relationship between efficacy and toxicity of new compounds (or combination of them) becomes more complex. Despite this, most commonly used methods in practice focus on identifying a Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD) by learning only from toxicity events. We present a novel adaptive clinical trial methodology, called Safe Efficacy Exploration Dose Allocation (SEEDA), that aims at maximizing the cumulative efficacies while satisfying the toxicity safety constraint with high probability. We evaluate performance objectives that have operational meanings in practical clinical trials, including cumulative efficacy, recommendation/allocation success probabilities, toxicity violation probability, and sample efficiency. An extended SEEDA-Plateau algorithm that is tailored for the increase-then-plateau efficacy behavior of molecularly targeted agents (MTA) is also presented. Through numerical experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets, we show that SEEDA outperforms state-of-the-art clinical trial designs by finding the optimal dose with higher success rate and fewer patients.

paragraphs: Dose-finding trials face a difficult tradeoff when a treatment’s efficacy and toxicity do not move together simply. Common approaches focus on identifying a maximum tolerated dose using toxicity events. This paper introduces Safe Efficacy Exploration Dose Allocation, or SEEDA, which instead aims to maximize cumulative efficacy while satisfying a toxicity safety constraint with high probability.

That objective makes outcomes during allocation part of the learning problem, alongside the eventual dose recommendation. The authors evaluate cumulative efficacy, recommendation and allocation success, toxicity-constraint violations, and sample efficiency. They also propose SEEDA-Plateau for molecularly targeted agents whose efficacy increases and then levels off, explicitly adapting the algorithm to that response pattern.

Numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets report that SEEDA finds the optimal dose more successfully and with fewer patients than state-of-the-art trial designs. These findings support the methodology in the evaluated settings. Its safety objective remains probabilistic: the framework seeks high-probability satisfaction of a toxicity constraint while learning which dose offers the best efficacy.
summary.tldr: SEEDA adaptively allocates doses to improve cumulative efficacy while targeting high-probability satisfaction of a toxicity constraint.

title: Learning for Dose Allocation in Adaptive Clinical Trials with Safety Constraints

abstract: In this article, we propose novel structural nested models to estimate causal effects of continuous treatments based on mobile health data. To find the treatment regime which optimizes the short-term outcomes for the patients, we define the weighted lag K advantage. The optimal treatment regime is then defined to be the one which maximizes this advantage. This method imposes minimal assumptions on the data generating process. Statistical inference can also be provided for the estimated parameters. Simulation studies and an application to the Ohio type 1 diabetes dataset show that our method could provide meaningful insights for dose suggestions with mobile health data.

paragraphs: Mobile health data can describe treatments whose amounts vary continuously, making dose selection a question of degree. This paper proposes structural nested models for estimating the causal effects of such treatments. The aim is to use those estimates to help identify treatment regimes that improve patients' short-term outcomes, linking effect estimation directly to a defined treatment-selection objective.

The authors introduce a quantity called the weighted lag K advantage. They define the optimal treatment regime as the one that maximizes this quantity. This gives the optimization target an explicit statistical meaning: a suggested regime is evaluated through the advantage measure the paper defines. The method also supports statistical inference for its estimated parameters.

The approach is described as imposing minimal assumptions on the data-generating process, rather than requiring no assumptions. Simulation studies and an application to the Ohio type 1 diabetes dataset suggest that it could provide meaningful insights for dose suggestions. The stated evidence supports its usefulness as a modeling and estimation approach for mobile health data, with the optimization specifically focused on short-term outcomes.
summary.tldr: Structural nested models connect continuous-treatment causal estimates to a defined objective for short-term dose suggestions.

title: Causal Effect Estimation and Optimal Dose Suggestions in Mobile Health

abstract: Temporal-Difference (TD) learning is a general and very useful tool for estimating the value function of a given policy, which in turn is required to find good policies. Generally speaking, TD learning updates states whenever they are visited. When the agent lands in a state, its value can be used to compute the TD-error, which is then propagated to other states. However, it may be interesting, when computing updates, to take into account other information than whether a state is visited or not. For example, some states might be more important than others (such as states which are frequently seen in a successful trajectory). Or, some states might have unreliable value estimates (for example, due to partial observability or lack of data), making their values less desirable as targets. We propose an approach to re-weighting states used in TD updates, both when they are the input and when they provide the target for the update. We prove that our approach converges with linear function approximation and illustrate its desirable empirical behaviour compared to other TD-style methods.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates how valuable states are under a given policy. A visited state can play two roles: its estimate can be updated, and its current value can help form a target for updating other states. This paper asks whether those roles should depend on information beyond visitation alone.

The proposed method reweights states both as inputs to updates and as sources of targets. This allows the learning procedure to reflect differences in importance or reliability. For example, a state frequently encountered on successful trajectories may deserve emphasis, while a state with little data or partial observability may supply an unreliable target.

The authors prove convergence with linear function approximation and demonstrate desirable empirical behavior compared with other temporal-difference methods. The convergence claim applies to that stated approximation setting. The broader contribution is a way to distinguish where learning effort is directed from which estimates are trusted to guide it, giving state preferences a role in both sides of a temporal-difference update.
summary.tldr: Preferential temporal-difference learning reweights states as both update inputs and targets, with convergence proved for linear function approximation.

title: Preferential Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Biclustering structures exist ubiquitously in data matrices and the biclustering problem was first formalized by John Hartigan (1972) to cluster rows and columns simultaneously. In this paper, we develop a theory for the estimation of general biclustering models, where the data is assumed to follow certain statistical distribution with underlying biclustering structure. Due to the existence of latent variables, directly computing the maximal likelihood estimator is prohibitively difficult in practice and we instead consider the variational inference (VI) approach to solve the parameter estimation problem. Although variational inference method generally has good empirical performance, there are very few theoretical results around VI. In this paper, we obtain the precise estimation bound of variational estimator and show that it matches the minimax rate in terms of estimation error under mild assumptions in biclustering setting. Furthermore, we study the convergence property of the coordinate ascent variational inference algorithm, where both local and global convergence results have been provided. Numerical results validate our new theories.

paragraphs: Biclustering groups both the rows and the columns of a data matrix, revealing structure that depends on the two groupings together. This paper studies parameter estimation for statistical models with such hidden structure. The latent variables make direct maximum-likelihood estimation prohibitively difficult in practice, motivating the use of variational inference as a more tractable approach.

The authors establish a precise estimation-error bound for the variational estimator. Under mild assumptions in the biclustering setting, the bound matches the minimax rate: its error scales at the best achievable worst-case rate for the modeled problem. This gives theoretical support to an approximation method whose practical usefulness has outpaced the available guarantees.

The paper also analyzes coordinate ascent variational inference, providing both local and global convergence results. These address algorithmic behavior, complementing the statistical result about estimator accuracy. Numerical experiments validate the theories. The combined contribution concerns both whether the variational estimator can be statistically accurate and how the procedure used to compute it converges.
summary.tldr: For biclustering models under mild assumptions, variational estimation attains the minimax error rate, with additional convergence results for coordinate ascent.

title: On Variational Inference in Biclustering Models

abstract: We study decision making problems in which an agent sequentially interacts with a stochastic environment defined by means of a tree structure. The agent repeatedly faces the environment over time, and, after each round, it perceives a utility and a cost, which are both stochastic. The goal of the agent is to learn an optimal strategy in an online fashion, while, at the same time, keeping costs below a given safety threshold. Our model naturally fits many real-world scenarios, such as, e.g., opponent exploitation in games and web link selection. We study the hard-threshold problem of achieving sublinear regret while guaranteeing that the threshold constraint is satisfied at every iteration with high probability. First, we show that, in general, any algorithm with such a guarantee incurs in a linear regret. This motivates the introduction of a relaxed problem, namely the soft-threshold problem, in which we only require that the cumulative violation of the threshold constraint grows sublinearly, and, thus, we can provide an algorithm with sublinear regret. Next, we show how, in the hard-threshold problem, a sublinear regret algorithm can be designed under the additional assumption that there exists a known strategy strictly satisfying the threshold constraint. We also show that our regret bounds are tight. Finally, we cast the opponent exploitation problem to our model, and we experimentally evaluate our algorithms on a standard testbed of games.

paragraphs: This paper studies an agent repeatedly making sequential decisions in a stochastic environment represented by a tree. Each round produces both utility and cost. The agent must learn a good strategy while keeping costs under a safety threshold, creating a tension between improving decisions and respecting constraints.

For a hard threshold, the constraint must hold at every iteration with high probability. The authors show that, in general, any algorithm providing this guarantee incurs linear regret. They therefore consider a softer requirement: cumulative threshold violations need only grow sublinearly. Under that relaxation, they provide an algorithm with sublinear regret, so average regret and average cumulative violation diminish over time.

A hard-threshold guarantee with sublinear regret becomes possible under an additional assumption: a known strategy strictly satisfies the safety constraint. The authors give an algorithm for this setting and show their regret bounds are tight. They also formulate opponent exploitation within the framework and evaluate the algorithms on a standard collection of games.
summary.tldr: Sublinear-regret safe learning requires either relaxed cumulative constraints or, for strict per-round safety, a known strictly safe strategy.

title: Safe Learning in Tree-Form Sequential Decision Making: Handling Hard and Soft Constraints

abstract: Many important questions (e.g. "How to eat healthier?") require conversation to establish context and explore in depth. However, conversational question answering (ConvQA) systems have long been stymied by scarce training data that is expensive to collect. To address this problem, we propose a new technique for synthetically generating diverse and high-quality dialog data: dialog inpainting. Our approach takes the text of any document and transforms it into a two-person dialog between the writer and an imagined reader: we treat sentences from the article as utterances spoken by the writer, and then use a dialog inpainter to predict what the imagined reader asked or said in between each of the writer’s utterances. By applying this approach to passages from Wikipedia and the web, we produce WikiDialog and WebDialog, two datasets totalling 19 million diverse information-seeking dialogs – 1,000x larger than the largest existing ConvQA dataset. Furthermore, human raters judge the answer adequacy and conversationality of WikiDialog to be as good or better than existing manually-collected datasets. Remarkably, our approach shows strong zero-shot capability, generating high quality synthetic data without using any in-domain ConvQA data. Using our inpainted data to pre-train ConvQA retrieval systems, we significantly advance state-of-the-art across three benchmarks (QReCC, OR-QuAC, TREC CAsT) yielding up to 40% relative gains on standard evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: Conversational question answering needs training examples in which questions develop through an exchange, but collecting such conversations is expensive. Dialog inpainting creates synthetic exchanges from existing documents. It treats document sentences as a writer’s utterances and generates the imagined reader’s questions or comments between them.

Applied to Wikipedia and web passages, the method produces WikiDialog and WebDialog, totaling 19 million information-seeking conversations. The authors describe this as 1,000 times the size of the largest existing conversational question-answering dataset. Human raters judge WikiDialog’s answer adequacy and conversationality to be as good as or better than those of existing manually collected datasets.

The approach also generates high-quality data without in-domain conversational question-answering examples, demonstrating strong zero-shot capability. Pretraining retrieval systems with the generated conversations improves results across QReCC, OR-QuAC, and TREC CAsT, with relative gains reaching 40% on standard metrics. The findings connect the generated data’s conversational quality to measurable benefits for retrieving information during a conversation.
summary.tldr: Dialog inpainting turns documents into synthetic conversations that improve conversational retrieval when used for pretraining.

title: Dialog Inpainting: Turning Documents into Dialogs

abstract: Supervised learning can improve the design of state-of-the-art solvers for combinatorial problems, but labelling large numbers of combinatorial instances is often impractical due to exponential worst-case complexity. Inspired by the recent success of contrastive pre-training for images, we conduct a scientific study of the effect of augmentation design on contrastive pre-training for the Boolean satisfiability problem. While typical graph contrastive pre-training uses label-agnostic augmentations, our key insight is that many combinatorial problems have well-studied invariances, which allow for the design of label-preserving augmentations. We find that label-preserving augmentations are critical for the success of contrastive pre-training. We show that our representations are able to achieve comparable test accuracy to fully-supervised learning while using only 1% of the labels. We also demonstrate that our representations are more transferable to larger problems from unseen domains. Our code is available at https://github.com/h4duan/contrastive-sat.

paragraphs: Learning can improve combinatorial solvers, but obtaining training labels may itself require solving expensive problems. This paper investigates whether contrastive pre-training can reduce that burden for Boolean satisfiability. The underlying challenge is to learn useful representations from transformed versions of problem instances before relying heavily on labeled examples.

The authors focus on how those transformations are chosen. Common graph augmentations do not account for labels, whereas combinatorial problems often have known invariances: changes that preserve the answer. The study uses such invariances to construct label-preserving augmentations. This matters because treating two transformed instances as related is useful only when the transformation respects the information the eventual task needs.

The experiments find that preserving labels is critical to successful contrastive pre-training in this setting. The resulting representations reach test accuracy comparable to fully supervised learning while using only 1% of the labels. They also transfer better to larger problems from previously unseen domains. The findings identify augmentation design as a substantive part of learning combinatorial structure.
summary.tldr: Label-preserving augmentations make contrastive learning effective for satisfiability problems, achieving comparable supervised accuracy with only 1% of the labels.

title: Augment with Care: Contrastive Learning for Combinatorial Problems

abstract: We propose Neuro-Symbolic Hierarchical Rule Induction, an efficient interpretable neuro-symbolic model, to solve Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) problems. In this model, which is built from a pre-defined set of meta-rules organized in a hierarchical structure, first-order rules are invented by learning embeddings to match facts and body predicates of a meta-rule. To instantiate, we specifically design an expressive set of generic meta-rules, and demonstrate they generate a consequent fragment of Horn clauses. As a differentiable model, HRI can be trained both via supervised learning and reinforcement learning. To converge to interpretable rules, we inject a controlled noise to avoid local optima and employ an interpretability-regularization term. We empirically validate our model on various tasks (ILP, visual genome, reinforcement learning) against relevant state-of-the-art methods, including traditional ILP methods and neuro-symbolic models.

paragraphs: Inductive logic programming seeks rules that explain facts. This paper introduces Hierarchical Rule Induction, a neuro-symbolic model that combines learning with an explicit structure for constructing interpretable rules. Its starting point is a predefined hierarchy of meta-rules, which serve as templates from which more specific first-order rules can be formed.

The model learns embeddings that match facts and the predicates appearing in the bodies of these templates. The authors design a generic collection of meta-rules and show that it generates a fragment of Horn clauses. Because the model is differentiable, it can be trained through either supervised learning or reinforcement learning.

To encourage interpretable results, training includes controlled noise intended to avoid local optima and a regularization term aimed at interpretability. The authors evaluate the model on logic programming, Visual Genome, and reinforcement learning tasks against relevant traditional and neuro-symbolic methods. The work brings rule construction, gradient-based learning, and an explicit push toward readable rules into one framework.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Rule Induction learns interpretable logical rules through differentiable matching within a hierarchy of rule templates.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hierarchical Rule Induction

abstract: This paper shows how to adapt several simple and classical sampling-based algorithms for the k-means problem to the setting with outliers. Recently, Bhaskara et al. (NeurIPS 2019) showed how to adapt the classical k-means++ algorithm to the setting with outliers. However, their algorithm needs to output O(log(k)$\cdot$z) outliers, where z is the number of true outliers, to match the O(log k)-approximation guarantee of k-means++. In this paper, we build on their ideas and show how to adapt several sequential and distributed k-means algorithms to the setting with outliers, but with substantially stronger theoretical guarantees: our algorithms output (1 + $\epsilon$)z outliers while achieving an O(1/$\epsilon$)-approximation to the objective function. In the sequential world, we achieve this by adapting a recent algorithm of Lattanzi and Sohler (ICML 2019). In the distributed setting, we adapt a simple algorithm of Guha et al. (IEEE Trans. Know. and Data Engineering 2003) and the popular k-means\|{of} Bahmani et al. (PVLDB2012). A theoretical application of our techniques is an algorithm with running time O(nk^2/z) that achieves an O(1)-approximation to the objective function while outputting O(z) outliers, assuming k << z << n. This is complemented with a matching lower bound of $\Omega$(nk^2/z) for this problem in the oracle model.

paragraphs: Clustering with outliers requires balancing two goals: finding good clusters and limiting how many observations are discarded. This paper adapts familiar sampling-based k-means algorithms to that setting. It improves theoretical guarantees for both sequential algorithms and distributed algorithms, where the computation is spread across multiple participants.

The central guarantee permits (1 + epsilon)z outliers, where z is the true outlier count, while achieving an O(1/epsilon) approximation to the clustering objective. This exposes an explicit tradeoff: demanding an outlier count closer to z weakens the approximation bound. The earlier k-means++ adaptation discussed in the paper instead allowed O(log(k)z) outliers to retain an O(log k) approximation.

A further result gives an O(nk²/z)-time algorithm with constant-factor objective approximation and O(z) outliers, assuming k is much smaller than z and z is much smaller than n. A matching lower bound holds in the oracle model. Under that setting, the runtime result is supported by a corresponding theoretical barrier.
summary.tldr: Adaptations of classical k-means algorithms offer stronger tradeoffs between clustering quality and the number of discarded outliers.

title: Adapting k-means Algorithms for Outliers

abstract: We study goal misgeneralization , a type of out-of-distribution robustness failure in reinforcement learning (RL). Goal misgeneralization occurs when an RL agent retains its capabilities out-of-distribution yet pursues the wrong goal. For instance, an agent might continue to competently avoid obstacles, but navigate to the wrong place. In contrast, previous works have typically focused on capability generalization failures, where an agent fails to do anything sensible at test time.We provide the first explicit empirical demonstrations of goal misgeneralization and present a partial characterization of its causes.

Goal misgeneralization occurs when an RL agent retains its capabilities out-of-distribution yet pursues the wrong goal. For instance, an agent might continue to competently avoid obstacles, but navigate to the wrong place. In contrast, previous works have typically focused on capability generalization failures, where an agent fails to do anything sensible at test time.We provide the first explicit empirical demonstrations of goal misgeneralization and present a partial characterization of its causes.

paragraphs: An agent can remain capable after its environment changes while using those capabilities to pursue the wrong objective. This paper calls that failure goal misgeneralization. For example, a navigation policy may still avoid obstacles competently but head toward an unintended destination, so its failure is not simply a loss of basic skill.

The authors provide explicit empirical demonstrations of this behavior in deep reinforcement learning and partially characterize its causes. The distinction separates failures of what the agent appears to optimize from failures of its ability to act effectively. That separation is useful when assessing whether training performance reflects learning the intended goal or a correlated alternative.

The paper’s contribution is to identify and demonstrate a particular form of out-of-distribution failure. Its abstract does not claim a complete explanation or a method that eliminates the problem. The implication is that evaluating capability alone can miss a consequential mismatch between competent behavior and the objective the system was meant to pursue.
summary.tldr: Deep RL agents can retain effective skills out of distribution while pursuing an unintended goal.

title: Goal Misgeneralization in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Mixup is a data augmentation method that generates new data points by mixing a pair of input data. While mixup generally improves the prediction performance, it sometimes degrades the performance. In this paper, we first identify the main causes of this phenomenon by theoretically and empirically analyzing the mixup algorithm. To resolve this, we propose GenLabel, a simple yet effective relabeling algorithm designed for mixup. In particular, GenLabel helps the mixup algorithm correctly label mixup samples by learning the class-conditional data distribution using generative models. Via theoretical and empirical analysis, we show that mixup, when used together with GenLabel, can effectively resolve the aforementioned phenomenon, improving the accuracy of mixup-trained model.

paragraphs: Mixup creates additional training examples by blending pairs of inputs. Although it generally improves prediction, it can sometimes reduce performance. This paper examines that failure through theoretical and empirical analysis, then develops a method intended to correct the labels assigned to the mixed examples.

The method, GenLabel, learns class-conditional data distributions using generative models. These distributions describe the data associated with each class and provide information for labeling mixup samples. The intervention therefore focuses on the supervision attached to an augmented example: generating a blended input and assigning it an appropriate class target are connected parts of the training procedure.

The authors use both theory and experiments to show that combining GenLabel with mixup can address the identified degradation and improve the accuracy of a mixup-trained model. The result supports using learned class distributions to improve augmentation labels. It is a qualified improvement claim: the paper shows that relabeling can resolve the problem, rather than establishing that every use of mixup or generative relabeling must improve performance.
summary.tldr: GenLabel uses generative models of class distributions to relabel mixup examples and can remedy mixup-related accuracy degradation.

title: GenLabel: Mixup Relabeling using Generative Models

abstract: Satisfying safety constraints almost surely (or with probability one) can be critical for the deployment of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in real-life applications. For example, plane landing and take-off should ideally occur with probability one. We address the problem by introducing Safety Augmented (Saute) Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), where the safety constraints are eliminated by augmenting them into the state-space and reshaping the objective. We show that Saute MDP satisfies the Bellman equation and moves us closer to solving Safe RL with constraints satisfied almost surely. We argue that Saute MDP allows viewing the Safe RL problem from a different perspective enabling new features. For instance, our approach has a plug-and-play nature, i.e., any RL algorithm can be "Sauteed”. Additionally, state augmentation allows for policy generalization across safety constraints. We finally show that Saute RL algorithms can outperform their state-of-the-art counterparts when constraint satisfaction is of high importance.
originalAbstract: Satisfying safety constraints almost surely (or with probability one) can be critical for the deployment of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in real-life applications. For example, plane landing and take-off should ideally occur with probability one. We address the problem by introducing Safety Augmented (Saute) Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), where the safety constraints are eliminated by augmenting them into the state-space and reshaping the objective. We show that Saute MDP satisfies the Bellman equation and moves us closer to solving Safe RL with constraints satisfied almost surely. We argue that Saute MDP allows viewing the Safe RL problem from a different perspective enabling new features. For instance, our approach has a plug-and-play nature, i.e., any RL algorithm can be "Sauteed”. Additionally, state augmentation allows for policy generalization across safety constraints. We finally show that Saute RL algorithms can outperform their state-of-the-art counterparts when constraint satisfaction is of high importance.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning applications require safety constraints to hold with probability one, also called almost surely. This is a demanding target for learning systems. Saute RL approaches it by reformulating the decision problem so that safety constraints become part of the state representation and the objective is reshaped.

The resulting Safety Augmented Markov Decision Process satisfies the Bellman equation. This matters because it connects the reformulated problem to a central structure used by reinforcement learning algorithms. The authors describe the approach as compatible with any RL algorithm through this augmentation, and they identify policy generalization across safety constraints as another capability enabled by the expanded state.

The paper presents the formulation as progress toward almost-sure constraint satisfaction, rather than claiming that every adapted learning algorithm automatically achieves it. Experiments show that Saute RL algorithms can outperform leading counterparts when satisfying constraints is especially important. The contribution is a reusable problem transformation that lets safety information shape decisions through the state and learning objective.
summary.tldr: Saute RL incorporates safety constraints into the state and objective, providing a reusable formulation aimed at almost-surely safe learning.

title: Saute RL: Almost Surely Safe Reinforcement Learning Using State Augmentation

abstract: Dimensionality reduction (DR) of high-dimensional data is of theoretical and practical interest in machine learning. However, there exist intriguing, non-intuitive discrepancies between the geometry of high- and low-dimensional space. We look into such discrepancies and propose a novel visualization method called Space-based Manifold Approximation and Projection (SpaceMAP). Our method establishes an analytical transformation on distance metrics between spaces to address the “crowding problem" in DR. With the proposed equivalent extended distance (EED), we are able to match the capacity of high- and low-dimensional space in a principled manner. To handle complex data with different manifold properties, we propose hierarchical manifold approximation to model the similarity function in a data-specific manner. We evaluated SpaceMAP on a range of synthetic and real datasets with varying manifold properties, and demonstrated its excellent performance in comparison with classical and state-of-the-art DR methods. In particular, the concept of space expansion provides a generic framework for understanding nonlinear DR methods including the popular t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection

paragraphs: Visualizing high-dimensional data in fewer dimensions requires reconciling spaces with different geometric properties. The crowding problem reflects a mismatch in how much room those spaces provide for representing relationships among points. SpaceMAP addresses this mismatch through an analytical transformation of distance metrics between the original and visualization spaces.

The method introduces an equivalent extended distance intended to match the capacities of high- and low-dimensional spaces in a principled way. It also uses hierarchical manifold approximation to construct a similarity function tailored to the data. This second component accommodates datasets whose underlying manifolds have different properties, rather than treating their geometry identically.

Evaluations on synthetic and real datasets with varied manifold properties report strong performance relative to classical and state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction methods. Beyond the particular algorithm, the authors present space expansion as a general framework for understanding nonlinear visualization methods, including t-SNE and UMAP. The contribution therefore combines a visualization procedure with an account of the geometric mismatch such procedures must manage.
summary.tldr: SpaceMAP transforms distances and adapts similarities to data geometry to address crowding in high-dimensional data visualization.

title: SpaceMAP: Visualizing High-Dimensional Data by Space Expansion

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms are often known for sample inefficiency and difficult generalization. Recently, Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) emerged as a new paradigm for zero-shot generalization by simultaneously learning a task distribution and agent policies on the generated tasks. This is a non-stationary process where the task distribution evolves along with agent policies; creating an instability over time. While past works demonstrated the potential of such approaches, sampling effectively from the task space remains an open challenge, bottlenecking these approaches. To this end, we introduce CLUTR: a novel unsupervised curriculum learning algorithm that decouples task representation and curriculum learning into a two-stage optimization. It first trains a recurrent variational autoencoder on randomly generated tasks to learn a latent task manifold. Next, a teacher agent creates a curriculum by maximizing a minimax REGRET-based objective on a set of latent tasks sampled from this manifold. Using the fixed-pretrained task manifold, we show that CLUTR successfully overcomes the non-stationarity problem and improves stability. Our experimental results show CLUTR outperforms PAIRED, a principled and popular UED method, in the challenging CarRacing and navigation environments: achieving 10.6X and 45% improvement in zero-shot generalization, respectively. CLUTR also performs comparably to the non-UED state-of-the-art for CarRacing, while requiring 500X fewer environment interactions. We open source our code at https://github.com/clutr/clutr.

paragraphs: Automatically generating training tasks can help reinforcement learning agents handle unfamiliar environments. However, learning the task distribution while also updating the agent creates a moving target: both sides change together. CLUTR addresses this instability by separating the learning of a task representation from the later construction of a training curriculum.

First, a recurrent variational autoencoder learns a latent task space from randomly generated tasks. That pretrained representation is then held fixed. A teacher samples tasks from this space and builds a curriculum using a minimax regret objective. Fixing the representation gives curriculum learning a stable task space, which the paper reports resolves the targeted non-stationarity problem and improves stability.

In CarRacing and navigation experiments, CLUTR improves zero-shot generalization over PAIRED by 10.6 times and 45%, respectively. It also reaches performance comparable to a non-UED state-of-the-art CarRacing method while using 500 times fewer environment interactions. These results connect the two-stage design to both adaptation to unseen tasks and more economical use of training experience.
summary.tldr: CLUTR stabilizes automatic curriculum learning by first learning a fixed task representation, improving generalization and interaction efficiency in its experiments.

title: CLUTR: Curriculum Learning via Unsupervised Task Representation Learning

abstract: Despite their importance for assessing reliability of predictions, uncertainty quantification (UQ) measures in machine learning models have only recently begun to be rigorously characterized. One prominent issue is the curse of dimensionality : it is commonly believed that the marginal likelihood should be reminiscent of cross-validation metrics and both should deteriorate with larger input dimensions. However, we prove that by tuning hyperparameters to maximize marginal likelihood (the empirical Bayes procedure), performance, as measured by the marginal likelihood, improves monotonically with the input dimension. On the other hand, cross-validation metrics exhibit qualitatively different behavior that is characteristic of double descent. Cold posteriors, which have recently attracted interest due to their improved performance in certain settings, appear to exacerbate these phenomena. We verify empirically that our results hold for real data, beyond our considered assumptions, and we explore consequences involving synthetic covariates.

paragraphs: Different measures of model quality need not respond to increasing input dimension in the same way. This paper studies that issue for uncertainty estimation with Gaussian processes, focusing on marginal likelihood and cross-validation. It challenges the expectation that both measures should behave similarly and deteriorate as more input dimensions are introduced.

Under the theoretical setting studied, tuning hyperparameters to maximize marginal likelihood makes performance measured by that same criterion improve monotonically with dimension. Cross-validation measures instead show behavior characteristic of double descent. The distinction matters because improvement in a model-selection criterion does not establish that a separate predictive evaluation measure follows the same trend.

Cold posteriors appear to intensify these effects, preserving the paper’s qualified claim about their role. Experiments also find the predicted behavior on real data beyond the assumptions used in the analysis, and the authors examine consequences involving synthetic covariates. Together, the results show why conclusions about dimensionality depend on which uncertainty-related performance measure is being examined and how hyperparameters are selected.
summary.tldr: For the analyzed Gaussian processes, optimized marginal likelihood improves with dimension while cross-validation exhibits double-descent behavior.

title: Monotonicity and Double Descent in Uncertainty Estimation with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Trustworthy policy learning has significant importance in making reliable and harmless treatment decisions for individuals. Previous policy learning approaches aim at the well-being of subgroups by maximizing the utility function (e.g., conditional average causal effects, post-view click-through&conversion rate in recommendations), however, individual-level counterfactual no-harm criterion has rarely been discussed. In this paper, we first formalize the counterfactual no-harm criterion for policy learning from a principal stratification perspective. Next, we propose a novel upper bound for the fraction negatively affected by the policy and show the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator. Based on the estimators for the policy utility and harm upper bounds, we further propose a policy learning approach that satisfies the counterfactual no-harm criterion, and prove its consistency to the optimal policy reward for parametric and non-parametric policy classes, respectively. Extensive experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the proposed policy learning approach for satisfying the counterfactual no-harm criterion.

paragraphs: A policy that improves average outcomes for a subgroup can still negatively affect some individuals. This paper focuses on that distinction by formalizing a counterfactual no-harm criterion for treatment policies. It uses a principal stratification perspective to express individual-level harm in terms of counterfactual outcomes.

The authors propose an upper bound on the fraction of people negatively affected by a policy. They establish consistency and asymptotic normality for its estimator, giving a statistical basis for assessing the bound. Policy learning then uses estimates of both utility and the harm upper bound, bringing the no-harm criterion into the optimization process.

For parametric and nonparametric policy classes, the paper proves consistency toward the optimal policy reward for the proposed approach. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in satisfying the counterfactual no-harm criterion. The contribution connects an individual-focused definition of harm to estimable population quantities and a policy-learning method, rather than treating good average utility as sufficient evidence of harmless decisions.
summary.tldr: The paper learns policies using utility estimates and an estimated upper bound on individual counterfactual harm.

title: Trustworthy Policy Learning under the Counterfactual No-Harm Criterion

abstract: Recent deep-learning-based super-resolution (SR) methods have been successful in recovering high-resolution (HR) images from their low-resolution (LR) counterparts, albeit on the synthetic and simple degradation setting: bicubic downscaling. On the other hand, super-resolution on real-world images demands the capability to handle complex downscaling mechanism which produces different artifacts (e.g., noise, blur, color distortion) upon downscaling factors. To account for complex downscaling mechanism in real-world LR images, there have been a few efforts in constructing datasets consisting of LR images with real-world downsampling degradation. However, making such datasets entails a tremendous amount of time and effort, thereby resorting to very few number of downscaling factors (e.g., $\times$2, $\times$3, $\times$4). To remedy the issue, we propose to generate realistic SR datasets for unseen degradation levels by exploring the latent space of real LR images and thereby producing more diverse yet realistic LR images with complex real-world artifacts. Our quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the generated LR images, and we show that the various conventional SR networks trained with our newly generated SR datasets can produce much better HR images.

paragraphs: Super-resolution models trained on simple synthetic downscaling may struggle with real low-resolution images. Real degradation can include noise, blur, and color distortion, and those effects change with the downscaling factor. Collecting realistic training pairs takes substantial effort, so available datasets often cover only a few factors.

This paper proposes generating additional realistic training data at previously unseen degradation levels. The approach explores the latent space of real low-resolution images to produce a wider variety of degraded images while preserving complex real-world artifacts. The intended benefit is broader coverage of realistic degradation without collecting a separate dataset for every level.

Quantitative and visual experiments support the accuracy of the generated low-resolution images. The authors also train several conventional super-resolution networks on the new datasets and report substantially better high-resolution outputs. This second result connects the quality of the generated data to its practical training value. The contribution therefore improves super-resolution through the examples used to train models, with the generated degradation diversity benefiting multiple existing network designs.
summary.tldr: Generating realistic low-resolution images at unseen degradation levels improves training data and the outputs of conventional super-resolution networks.

title: Learning Controllable Degradation for Real-World Super-Resolution via Constrained Flows

abstract: Federated Learning is highly susceptible to backdoor and targeted attacks as participants can manipulate their data and models locally without any oversight on whether they follow the correct process. There are a number of server-side defenses that mitigate the attacks by modifying or rejecting local updates submitted by clients. However, we find that bursty adversarial patterns with a high variance in the number of malicious clients can circumvent the existing defenses. We propose a client-self defense, LeadFL, that is combined with existing server-side defenses to thwart backdoor and targeted attacks. The core idea of LeadFL is a novel regularization term in local model training such that the Hessian matrix of local gradients is nullified. We provide the convergence analysis of LeadFL and its robustness guarantee in terms of certified radius. Our empirical evaluation shows that LeadFL is able to mitigate bursty adversarial patterns for both iid and non-iid data distributions. It frequently reduces the backdoor accuracy from more than 75% for state-of-the-art defenses to less than 10% while its impact on the main task accuracy is always less than for other client-side defenses.
