paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants train locally, which also gives malicious participants opportunities to manipulate data or model updates. Server-side defenses can modify or reject suspicious updates. This paper finds that attacks with bursts in the number of malicious clients can circumvent existing defenses, motivating protection within the clients’ own training process.

LeadFL adds client self-defense alongside existing server defenses. Its core is a regularization term in local training designed to nullify the Hessian matrix of local gradients. The paper provides convergence analysis and a robustness guarantee expressed through a certified radius, connecting the proposed training change to formal properties of the method.

Empirical evaluations show mitigation of bursty attacks with both identically distributed and non-identically distributed client data. LeadFL frequently lowers backdoor accuracy from above 75% under state-of-the-art defenses to below 10%. Across the reported evaluations, its effect on main-task accuracy is smaller than that of the other client-side defenses. These results support combining protections at the server and client levels.
summary.tldr: LeadFL adds local-training regularization to server defenses to mitigate bursty backdoor and targeted attacks in federated learning.

title: LeadFL: Client Self-Defense against Model Poisoning in Federated Learning

abstract: Diffusion models have established new state of the art in a multitude of computer vision tasks, including image restoration. Diffusion-based inverse problem solvers generate reconstructions of exceptional visual quality from heavily corrupted measurements. However, in what is widely known as the perception-distortion trade-off, the price of perceptually appealing reconstructions is often paid in declined distortion metrics, such as PSNR. Distortion metrics measure faithfulness to the observation, a crucial requirement in inverse problems. In this work, we propose a novel framework for inverse problem solving, namely we assume that the observation comes from a stochastic degradation process that gradually degrades and noises the original clean image. We learn to reverse the degradation process in order to recover the clean image. Our technique maintains consistency with the original measurement throughout the reverse process, and allows for great flexibility in trading off perceptual quality for improved distortion metrics and sampling speedup via early-stopping. We demonstrate the efficiency of our method on different high-resolution datasets and inverse problems, achieving great improvements over other state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods with respect to both perceptual and distortion metrics.

paragraphs: A reconstructed image can look convincing while matching the measurements less faithfully. This tension is especially relevant for diffusion-based restoration, where attractive outputs may come with worse distortion scores. DiracDiffusion addresses both perceptual quality and measurement consistency within the reconstruction process itself.

The framework assumes that the observation results from a stochastic process that progressively degrades the clean image and adds noise. It learns to reverse that process, recovering the image incrementally while maintaining consistency with the original measurement throughout. The assumed degradation process therefore defines both how corruption occurs and how reconstruction should proceed.

The reverse trajectory also offers a way to choose among perceptual quality, distortion performance, and computational cost. Early stopping can improve distortion metrics and reduce sampling time while adjusting the perceptual trade-off. Experiments across high-resolution datasets and inverse problems report improvements over other leading diffusion methods on both perceptual and distortion measures. The contribution is a reconstruction framework that keeps faithfulness to observations central while retaining flexibility over output quality and speed.
summary.tldr: DiracDiffusion reverses a gradual degradation process while preserving measurement consistency and allowing quality–speed trade-offs through early stopping.

title: DiracDiffusion: Denoising and Incremental Reconstruction with Assured Data-Consistency

abstract: Learning an effective policy to control high-dimensional, overactuated systems is a significant challenge for deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Such control scenarios are often observed in the neural control of vertebrate musculoskeletal systems. The study of these control mechanisms will provide insights into the control of high-dimensional, overactuated systems. The coordination of actuators, known as muscle synergies in neuromechanics, is considered a presumptive mechanism that simplifies the generation of motor commands. The dynamical structure of a system is the basis of its function, allowing us to derive a synergistic representation of actuators. Motivated by this theory, we propose the Dynamical Synergistic Representation (DynSyn) algorithm. DynSyn aims to generate synergistic representations from dynamical structures and perform task-specific, state-dependent adaptation to the representations to improve motor control. We demonstrate DynSyn’s efficiency across various tasks involving different musculoskeletal models, achieving state-of-the-art sample efficiency and robustness compared to baseline algorithms. DynSyn generates interpretable synergistic representations that capture the essential features of dynamical structures and demonstrates generalizability across diverse motor tasks.

paragraphs: Controlling a system with many actuators is difficult for reinforcement learning, especially when several actuators offer overlapping ways to produce movement. Musculoskeletal systems provide a motivating example. The paper draws on muscle synergies, a proposed biological mechanism in which coordinated actuator activity simplifies the generation of motor commands.

DynSyn derives coordinated actuator representations from a system's dynamical structure. It then adapts those representations to the task and the current state. This combines information about how the system moves with flexibility about what movement is needed now. The intended benefit is a more useful representation for learning control than treating the high-dimensional actuator space without this coordination.

Across tasks involving different musculoskeletal models, the authors report state-of-the-art sample efficiency and robustness relative to the tested baselines. They also find that the learned representations are interpretable, capture essential dynamical features, and generalize across diverse motor tasks. These results support using system dynamics to guide actuator coordination while allowing that coordination to change with the control situation.
summary.tldr: DynSyn uses system dynamics to learn adaptable actuator coordination, improving reported learning efficiency and robustness in musculoskeletal control tasks.

title: DynSyn: Dynamical Synergistic Representation for Efficient Learning and Control in Overactuated Embodied Systems

abstract: Nowadays Spiking Transformers have exhibited remarkable performance close to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), while enjoying the inherent energy-efficiency of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs). However, training Spiking Transformers on GPUs is considerably more time-consuming compared to the ANN counterparts, despite the energy-efficient inference through neuromorphic computation. In this paper, we investigate the token sparsification technique for efficient training of Spiking Transformer and find conventional methods suffer from noticeable performance degradation. We analyze the issue and propose our Sparsification with Timestep-wise Anchor Token and dual Alignments (STATA). Timestep-wise Anchor Token enables precise identification of important tokens across timesteps based on standardized criteria. Additionally, dual Alignments incorporate both Intra and Inter Alignment of the attention maps, fostering the learning of inferior attention. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of STATA thoroughly, which demonstrates up to $\sim$1.53$\times$ training speedup and $\sim$48% energy reduction with comparable performance on various datasets and architectures.

paragraphs: Spiking transformers combine strong task performance with the energy advantages of spiking computation, yet training them on GPUs can take substantially longer than training conventional neural-network counterparts. This paper investigates token sparsification as a way to reduce that burden. The authors find that conventional sparsification methods cause noticeable performance losses in this setting.

They propose STATA, which combines timestep-wise anchor tokens with two attention-alignment mechanisms. The anchor tokens provide standardized criteria for identifying important tokens across timesteps. The intra- and inter-alignment components operate on attention maps to improve weaker attention. Together, these mechanisms address both which tokens are retained and how attention is learned during sparsification.

Experiments across multiple datasets and architectures report training speedups of up to approximately 1.53 times and energy reductions of approximately 48%, with comparable task performance. These results show that token sparsification can deliver useful efficiency gains when adapted to the temporal structure of spiking transformers. The reported improvements support the framework as a way to reduce training costs while maintaining performance in the evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: STATA adapts token sparsification to spiking transformers, reporting up to roughly 1.53× faster training and roughly 48% lower energy use with comparable performance.

title: Towards Efficient Spiking Transformer: a Token Sparsification Framework for Training and Inference Acceleration

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have improved significantly in their capabilities, but their complex architecture makes their safety alignment challenging. In this paper, we reveal an uneven distribution of harmful information across the intermediate layers of the image encoder and show that skipping a certain set of layers and exiting early can increase the chance of the VLM generating harmful responses. We call it as “Image enCoder Early-exiT” based vulnerability (ICET). Our experiments across three VLMs: LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2 show that performing early exits from the image encoder significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful outputs. To tackle this, we propose a simple yet effective modification of the Clipped-Proximal Policy Optimization (Clip-PPO) algorithm for performing layer-wise multi-modal RLHF for VLMs. We term this as Layer-Wise PPO (L-PPO). We evaluate our L-PPO algorithm across three multi-modal datasets and show that it consistently reduces the harmfulness caused by early exits.

paragraphs: Vision-language models process images through multiple encoder layers before producing responses. This paper finds that harmful information is unevenly distributed across those intermediate layers. Skipping certain layers and leaving the image encoder early can increase the likelihood of harmful responses, revealing a vulnerability the authors call ICET.

Experiments on LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2 show significant increases in harmful output when early exits are used. The result makes the processing path through the image encoder relevant to safety: behavior observed after the usual sequence of layers does not fully characterize behavior when intermediate representations are used instead.

To address the vulnerability, the authors modify Clipped Proximal Policy Optimization to perform layer-wise multimodal reinforcement learning from human feedback. Their method, Layer-Wise PPO, consistently reduces early-exit harmfulness across three multimodal datasets. The finding supports training that addresses safety across encoder layers, with the reported benefit specifically concerning the harmfulness introduced by early exits.
summary.tldr: Early image-encoder exits increase harmful responses in three tested vision-language models, and layer-wise PPO reduces this vulnerability.

title: Layer-wise Alignment: Examining Safety Alignment Across Image Encoder Layers in Vision Language Models

abstract: Conformal prediction is a flexible framework for calibrating machine learning predictions, providing distribution-free statistical guarantees. In outlier detection, this calibration relies on a reference set of labeled inlier data to control the type-I error rate. However, obtaining a perfectly labeled inlier reference set is often unrealistic, and a more practical scenario involves access to a contaminated reference set containing a small fraction of outliers. This paper analyzes the impact of such contamination on the validity of conformal methods. We prove that under realistic, non-adversarial settings, calibration on contaminated data yields conservative type-I error control, shedding light on the inherent robustness of conformal methods. This conservativeness, however, typically results in a loss of power. To alleviate this limitation, we propose a novel, active data-cleaning framework that leverages a limited labeling budget and an outlier detection model to selectively annotate data points in the contaminated reference set that are suspected as outliers. By removing only the annotated outliers in this “suspicious” subset, we can effectively enhance power while mitigating the risk of inflating the type-I error rate, as supported by our theoretical analysis. Experiments on real datasets validate the conservative behavior of conformal methods under contamination and show that the proposed data-cleaning strategy improves power without sacrificing validity.

paragraphs: Conformal outlier detection uses a reference set of normal examples to calibrate false-alarm control. In practice, some supposed normal examples may actually be outliers. This paper studies what happens under that contamination, focusing on both type-I error, which concerns falsely flagging normal data, and power, the ability to detect outliers.

The authors prove that contamination yields conservative type-I error control under realistic, non-adversarial conditions. The method can therefore remain cautious about false alarms, but that conservativeness typically reduces detection power. This explains how contamination can make a detector less useful even when it does not invalidate false-alarm control.

Experiments on real datasets show the predicted conservative behavior and report improved power without loss of validity after cleaning.
summary.tldr: Under non-adversarial conditions, contaminated conformal reference data produce conservative detection, and targeted labeling can recover power while preserving validity.

title: Robust Conformal Outlier Detection under Contaminated Reference Data

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems face a fundamental challenge in aligning independently developed retrievers and large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically involve modifying either component or introducing simple intermediate modules, resulting in practical limitations and sub-optimal performance. Inspired by human search behavior—typically involving a back-and-forth process of proposing search queries and reviewing documents, we propose C-3PO, a proxy-centric framework that facilitates communication between retrievers and LLMs through a lightweight multi-agent system. Our framework implements three specialized agents that collaboratively optimize the entire RAG pipeline without altering the retriever and LLMs. These agents work together to assess the need for retrieval, generate effective queries, and select information suitable for the LLMs. To enable effective multi-agent coordination, we develop a tree-structured rollout approach for reward credit assignment in reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments in both in-domain and out-of-distribution scenarios demonstrate that C-3PO significantly enhances RAG performance while maintaining plug-and-play flexibility and superior generalization capabilities.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation combines a retriever with a language model, but those components are often developed independently. Finding documents and generating a useful answer are related tasks, yet the two components may not communicate effectively. C-3PO addresses that coordination problem through a lightweight system positioned between them.

The framework uses three specialized agents to decide whether retrieval is needed, formulate useful queries, and select information suited to the language model. Its inspiration is the repeated query-and-review process people use when searching. Because these responsibilities sit in an intermediate system, the approach can optimize the retrieval pipeline without modifying either the retriever or the language model.

Training coordinated agents also requires deciding how their individual choices contributed to an outcome. The authors introduce tree-structured rollouts for assigning reward credit during reinforcement learning. Experiments within and outside the training distribution show significant improvements in RAG performance and strong generalization. These results support the value of improving communication between components while retaining plug-and-play flexibility.
summary.tldr: C-3PO coordinates retrieval decisions, queries, and information selection through three lightweight agents without changing the retriever or language model.

title: C-3PO: Compact Plug-and-Play Proxy Optimization to Achieve Human-like Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Benchmark datasets have proved pivotal to the success of graph learning, and good benchmark datasets are crucial to guide the development of the field. Recent research has highlighted problems with graph-learning datasets and benchmarking practices—revealing, for example, that methods which ignore the graph structure can outperform graph-based approaches. Such findings raise two questions: (1) What makes a good graph-learning dataset, and (2) how can we evaluate dataset quality in graph learning? Our work addresses these questions. As the classic evaluation setup uses datasets to evaluate models, it does not apply to dataset evaluation. Hence, we start from first principles. Observing that graph-learning datasets uniquely combine two modes—graph structure and node features—, we introduce RINGS, a flexible and extensible mode-perturbation framework to assess the quality of graph-learning datasets based on dataset ablations—i.e., quantifying differences between the original dataset and its perturbed representations. Within this framework, we propose two measures—performance separability and mode complementarity—as evaluation tools, each assessing the capacity of a graph dataset to benchmark the power and efficacy of graph-learning methods from a distinct angle. We demonstrate the utility of our framework for dataset evaluation via extensive experiments on graph-level tasks and derive actionable recommendations for improving the evaluation of graph-learning methods. Our work opens new research directions in data-centric graph learning, and it constitutes a step toward the systematic evaluation of evaluations.

These dataset ablations provide a way to investigate the role of each information source rather than relying only on model scores from the unchanged dataset.

Each assesses a different aspect of a dataset’s ability to benchmark graph-learning methods. Experiments on graph-level tasks demonstrate the framework’s usefulness and lead to recommendations for evaluation practice. The contribution is a flexible method for scrutinizing benchmarks themselves, recognizing that dataset quality has more than one relevant dimension.
summary.tldr: RINGS evaluates graph-learning datasets by perturbing graph structure and node features and measuring distinct aspects of benchmark quality.

title: No Metric to Rule Them All: Toward Principled Evaluations of Graph-Learning Datasets

abstract: We study the problem of distributed distinct element estimation, where $\alpha$ servers each receive a subset of a universe $[n]$ and aim to compute a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation to the number of distinct elements using minimal communication. While prior work establishes a worst-case bound of $\Theta\left(\alpha\log n+\frac{\alpha}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ bits, these results rely on assumptions that may not hold in practice. We introduce a new parameterization based on the number $C = \frac{\beta}{\varepsilon^2}$ of pairwise collisions, i.e., instances where the same element appears on multiple servers, and design a protocol that uses only $O\left(\alpha\log n\log\log n+\frac{\sqrt{\beta}}{\varepsilon^2} \log n\right)$ bits, breaking previous lower bounds when $C$ is small. We further improve our algorithm under assumptions on the number of distinct elements or collisions and provide matching lower bounds in all regimes, establishing $C$ as a tight complexity measure for the problem. Finally, we consider streaming algorithms for distinct element estimation parameterized by the number of items with frequency larger than $1$. Overall, our results offer insight into why statistical problems with known hardness results can be efficiently solved in practice.

paragraphs: When several servers each hold a set of items, estimating the total number of distinct items requires accounting for overlap. The goal is an estimate within a multiplicative factor of one plus epsilon while exchanging as few bits as possible. This paper asks how communication changes when overlap is limited.

The authors parameterize difficulty by pairwise collisions: occurrences of the same element across servers. Their protocol has a communication term that depends on the square root of a rescaled collision count, alongside a term reflecting the number of servers and universe size. This yields improved communication when collisions are few, identifying easier instances within a problem with established worst-case bounds.

Further improvements use assumptions about the number of distinct items or collisions, and matching lower bounds establish collision count as a tight complexity measure across the studied regimes. The paper also examines streaming estimation using the number of items appearing more than once. The results explain how instance structure can make a counting task substantially easier than its worst-case communication requirements suggest.
summary.tldr: Collision-sensitive algorithms and matching lower bounds explain when distributed distinct counting needs less communication than worst-case bounds suggest.

title: On Fine-Grained Distinct Element Estimation

abstract: Neural operators have emerged as a promising approach for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs). However, existing neural operators often have difficulty in dealing with constrained PDEs, where the solution must satisfy additional equality or inequality constraints beyond the governing equations. To close this gap, we propose a novel neural operator, Hyper Extended Adaptive PDHG (HEAP) for constrained high-dim PDEs, where the learned operator evolves in the parameter space of PDEs. We first show that the evolution operator learning can be formulated as a quadratic programming (QP) problem, then unroll the adaptive primal-dual hybrid gradient (APDHG) algorithm as the QP-solver into the neural operator architecture. This allows us to improve efficiency while retaining theoretical guarantees of the constrained optimization. Empirical results on a variety of high-dim PDEs show that HEAP outperforms the state-of-the-art neural operator model.

paragraphs: Neural operators offer a way to solve high-dimensional partial differential equations, but some problems require more than satisfying the governing equation. Their solutions must also obey equality or inequality constraints. HEAP addresses this constrained setting, where an effective learned solver must account for these additional requirements as part of its computation.

The authors formulate learning the evolution operator as a quadratic programming problem. They then incorporate the steps of an adaptive primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm into the neural operator architecture. This process, called unrolling, makes the optimization procedure part of the network's structure. The learned operator evolves in the parameter space of the differential equations.

This design links neural computation to a constrained optimization method, with the stated benefit of improved efficiency while retaining theoretical guarantees from that optimization. Experiments on a variety of high-dimensional equations show HEAP outperforming a state-of-the-art neural operator model. The contribution is therefore an architectural route for incorporating constraints, supported by both an optimization formulation and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: HEAP embeds an adaptive constrained-optimization algorithm into a neural operator for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations.

title: HEAP: Hyper Extended A-PDHG Operator for Constrained High-dim PDEs

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) collaborative decoding techniques improve output quality by combining the outputs of multiple models at each generation step, but they incur high computational costs. In this paper, we introduce Collaborative decoding via Speculation (CoS), a novel framework that accelerates collaborative decoding without compromising performance. Inspired by Speculative Decoding—where a small proposal model generates tokens sequentially, and a larger target model verifies them in parallel, our approach builds on two key insights: (1) the verification distribution can be the combined distribution of both the proposal and target models, and (2) alternating each model as the proposer and verifier can further enhance efficiency. We generalize this method to collaboration among n models and theoretically prove that CoS is never slower than standard collaborative decoding, typically achieving faster speed. Extensive experiments demonstrate CoS is 1.11x–2.23x faster than standard collaborative decoding without compromising generation quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kamichanw/CoS/.

paragraphs: Combining several language models during generation can improve output quality, but consulting them at every step is computationally expensive. Collaborative decoding via Speculation, or CoS, adapts speculative decoding to this setting. The aim is to retain the benefits of combined model predictions while reducing the time needed to produce text.

In speculative decoding, one model proposes tokens sequentially and another checks them in parallel. CoS changes the verification rule so that it can use the combined probability distribution of the proposing and checking models. It also allows the models to alternate between these roles. This turns speculation into a mechanism for collaboration rather than assigning each model a permanently fixed responsibility.

The authors extend the method to collaboration among an arbitrary number of models and prove that CoS is never slower than standard collaborative decoding in their theoretical analysis. Experiments show speedups from 1.11 to 2.23 times without reduced generation quality. The results connect a theoretical efficiency guarantee with measured acceleration of collaborative generation.
summary.tldr: CoS accelerates collaborative language-model decoding through combined-distribution verification and alternating proposer roles, with reported speedups of 1.11–2.23 times.

title: Fast Large Language Model Collaborative Decoding via Speculation

abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) provides a resource-efficient solution for on-device monitoring of tinyML models deployed remotely without access to true labels. However, existing UQ methods impose significant memory and compute demands, making them impractical for ultra-low-power, KB-sized tinyML devices. Prior work has attempted to reduce overhead by using early-exit ensembles to quantify uncertainty in a single forward pass, but these approaches still carry prohibitive costs. To address this, we propose QUTE, a novel resource-efficient early-exit-assisted ensemble architecture optimized for tinyML models. QUTE introduces additional output blocks at the final exit of the base network, distilling early-exit knowledge into these blocks to form a diverse yet lightweight ensemble. We show that QUTE delivers superior uncertainty quality on tiny models, achieving comparable performance on larger models with 59% smaller model sizes than the closest prior work. When deployed on a microcontroller, QUTE demonstrates a 31% reduction in latency on average. In addition, we show that QUTE excels at detecting accuracy-drop events, outperforming all prior works.

Uncertainty estimates can help, but conventional methods often demand too much memory or computation for devices with only kilobytes of resources. Even ensembles built from early exits in a network can remain too expensive.

QUTE introduces additional output blocks at the final exit of the base network. It distills knowledge from early exits into those blocks, creating a lightweight ensemble whose members retain useful diversity. The architecture is designed to obtain uncertainty information while reducing the resource burden associated with earlier early-exit ensemble approaches.

summary.tldr: QUTE distills early-exit knowledge into a lightweight ensemble to improve uncertainty monitoring within tinyML memory and compute budgets.

title: QUTE: Quantifying Uncertainty in TinyML models with Early-exit-assisted ensembles for model-monitoring

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) exhibit significant potential due to their low energy consumption. Converting Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to SNNs is an efficient way to achieve high-performance SNNs. However, many conversion methods are based on rate coding, which requires numerous spikes and longer time-steps compared to directly trained SNNs, leading to increased energy consumption and latency. This article introduces differential coding for ANN-to-SNN conversion, a novel coding scheme that reduces spike counts and energy consumption by transmitting changes in rate information rather than rates directly, and explores its application across various layers. Additionally, the threshold iteration method is proposed to optimize thresholds based on activation distribution when converting Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) to spiking neurons. Experimental results on various Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers demonstrate that the proposed differential coding significantly improves accuracy while reducing energy consumption, particularly when combined with the threshold iteration method, achieving state-of-the-art performance. The source codes of the proposed method are available at https://github.com/h-z-h-cell/ANN-to-SNN-DCGS.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer the possibility of low-energy computation, and converting an existing artificial neural network provides a route to obtaining one. However, many conversion methods represent activation values through spike rates. Communicating those rates can require many spikes and long sequences of time steps, increasing both energy use and latency.

This paper proposes differential coding, which communicates changes in rate information rather than repeatedly transmitting the rates themselves. The authors investigate how this coding scheme applies across different layers. They also introduce threshold iteration, a method that uses activation distributions to adjust firing thresholds when converting rectified linear units into spiking neurons.

Experiments cover both convolutional networks and Transformers. The reported results show improved accuracy alongside reduced energy consumption, with particularly strong performance when differential coding is combined with threshold iteration. The paper reports state-of-the-art results for this combination. Its contribution is a training-free conversion approach that addresses how activations are encoded and how neuron thresholds are chosen, making converted spiking networks more efficient in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Differential coding improves training-free conversion to spiking networks by transmitting rate changes and tuning firing thresholds from activation distributions.

title: Differential Coding for Training-Free ANN-to-SNN Conversion

abstract: Existing works on the expressive power of neural networks typically assume real-valued parameters and exact mathematical operations during the evaluation of networks. However, neural networks run on actual computers can take parameters only from a small subset of the reals and perform inexact mathematical operations with round-off errors and overflows. In this work, we study the expressive power of floating-point neural networks, i.e., networks with floating-point parameters and operations. We first observe that for floating-point neural networks to represent all functions from floating-point vectors to floating-point vectors, it is necessary to distinguish different inputs: the first layer of a network should be able to generate different outputs for different inputs. We also prove that such distinguishability is sufficient, along with mild conditions on activation functions. Our result shows that with practical activation functions, floating-point neural networks can represent floating-point functions from a wide domain to all finite or infinite floats. For example, the domain is all finite floats for Sigmoid and tanh, and it is all finite floats of magnitude less than 1/8 times the largest float for ReLU, ELU, SeLU, GELU, Swish, Mish, and sin.

paragraphs: Neural-network expressiveness is often studied as though computers could store arbitrary real numbers and perform exact arithmetic. Actual networks use floating-point numbers, so rounding and overflow can change what they compute. This paper asks which functions networks can represent when those computational realities are included in the mathematical model.

The key property is whether the first layer can distinguish its inputs. If two different inputs become the same representation there, later layers cannot assign them different outputs when needed. The authors establish this distinguishability as necessary for representing every function on the input domain. Under mild conditions on the activation function, they also prove that it is sufficient.

The resulting guarantees cover broad, activation-dependent domains and outputs that may be finite or infinite floating-point values. Sigmoid and tanh support all finite floating-point inputs. For ReLU and several other listed activations, the guarantee covers finite inputs whose magnitudes are less than one eighth of the largest float. The result establishes representational capacity under actual floating-point operations.
summary.tldr: Floating-point networks can represent every floating-point function on broad domains when their first layer distinguishes inputs and their activations satisfy mild conditions.

title: Floating-Point Neural Networks Can Represent Almost All Floating-Point Functions

abstract: Consistency models imitate the multi-step sampling of score-based diffusion in a single forward pass of a neural network. They can be learned in two ways: consistency distillation and consistency training. The former relies on the true velocity field of the corresponding differential equation, approximated by a pre-trained neural network. In contrast, the latter uses a single-sample Monte Carlo estimate of this velocity field. The related estimation error induces a discrepancy between consistency distillation and training that, we show, still holds in the continuous-time limit. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel flow that transports noisy data towards their corresponding outputs derived from a consistency model. We prove that this flow reduces the previously identified discrepancy and the noise-data transport cost. Consequently, our method not only accelerates consistency training convergence but also enhances its overall performance. The code is available at https://github.com/thibautissenhuth/consistency_GC.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to produce in one neural-network pass what score-based diffusion models generate through multiple sampling steps. This paper examines a difference between two ways of learning these models and proposes a new flow to improve consistency training.

Consistency distillation uses a pretrained network to approximate the velocity field of a differential equation: the directions that guide samples along their paths. Consistency training instead estimates that field using a single Monte Carlo sample. The authors show that the resulting estimation error creates a discrepancy between the two learning approaches. That discrepancy persists even in the continuous-time limit, so moving to that limit does not eliminate it.

The proposed flow moves noisy data toward their corresponding outputs from a consistency model. This lets the model’s outputs help define the transport process used to address the estimation problem. The authors prove that the flow reduces both the identified discrepancy and the cost of transporting noise toward data.

The paper reports faster convergence and improved overall performance for consistency training. Its contribution connects an explanation of why the two learning approaches differ with a change to the transport flow that reduces that difference.
summary.tldr: A flow guided by consistency-model outputs reduces a discrepancy between consistency training and distillation, accelerating training convergence and improving performance.

title: Improving Consistency Models with Generator-Augmented Flows

abstract: The trade-off between accuracy and interpretability has long been a challenge in machine learning (ML). This tension is particularly significant for emerging interpretable-by-design methods, which aim to redesign ML algorithms for trustworthy interpretability but often sacrifice accuracy in the process. In this paper, we address this gap by investigating the impact of deviations in concept representations—an essential component of interpretable models—on prediction performance and propose a novel framework to mitigate these effects. The framework builds on the principle of optimizing concept embeddings under constraints that preserve interpretability. Using a generative model as a test-bed, we rigorously prove that our algorithm achieves zero loss while progressively enhancing the interpretability of the resulting model. Additionally, we evaluate the practical performance of our proposed framework in generating explainable predictions for image classification tasks across various benchmarks. Compared to existing explainable methods, our approach not only improves prediction accuracy while preserving model interpretability across various large-scale benchmarks but also achieves this with significantly lower computational cost.
originalAbstract: The trade-off between accuracy and interpretability has long been a challenge in machine learning (ML). This tension is particularly significant for emerging interpretable-by-design methods, which aim to redesign ML algorithms for trustworthy interpretability but often sacrifice accuracy in the process. In this paper, we address this gap by investigating the impact of deviations in concept representations—an essential component of interpretable models—on prediction performance and propose a novel framework to mitigate these effects. The framework builds on the principle of optimizing concept embeddings under constraints that preserve interpretability. Using a generative model as a test-bed, we rigorously prove that our algorithm achieves zero loss while progressively enhancing the interpretability of the resulting model. Additionally, we evaluate the practical performance of our proposed framework in generating explainable predictions for image classification tasks across various benchmarks. Compared to existing explainable methods, our approach not only improves prediction accuracy while preserving model interpretability across various large-scale benchmarks but also achieves this with significantly lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Models designed to be interpretable can lose predictive accuracy when their concept representations deviate from what the prediction task needs. This paper studies that source of error and proposes refining the concept embeddings themselves. The aim is to improve prediction while retaining the constraints that make the concepts interpretable.

The framework optimizes concept representations under explicit interpretability-preserving constraints. This gives the model room to correct representation problems without abandoning its explanatory structure. Using a generative model as a theoretical test-bed, the authors prove that their algorithm reaches zero loss while progressively improving interpretability. That proof is tied to the stated test-bed.

Practical evaluation focuses on explainable image classification across several benchmarks. Compared with existing explainable methods, the framework improves predictive accuracy while preserving interpretability and using significantly less computation. These findings identify concept refinement as a way to address the accuracy–interpretability tension within interpretable models, with theoretical evidence in a generative setting and empirical evidence in image classification.
summary.tldr: Constrained concept refinement improves explainable models’ accuracy while preserving interpretability and reducing computation in reported image-classification evaluations.

title: Enhancing Performance of Explainable AI Models with Constrained Concept Refinement

abstract: Scaling laws have emerged as important components of large language model (LLM) training as they can predict performance gains through scale, and provide guidance on important hyper-parameter choices that would otherwise be expensive. LLMs also rely on large, high-quality training datasets, like those sourced from (sometimes sensitive) user data. Training models on this sensitive user data requires careful privacy protections like differential privacy (DP). However, the dynamics of DP training are significantly different, and consequently their scaling laws are not yet fully understood. In this work, we establish scaling laws that accurately model the intricacies of DP LLM training, providing a complete picture of the compute-privacy-utility and the optimal training configurations in many settings.

paragraphs: Scaling laws help predict how language-model performance changes as training grows and guide configuration choices that would otherwise require expensive experimentation. This paper addresses those questions when training must protect sensitive data through differential privacy, a setting whose training dynamics differ substantially from ordinary language-model training.

The authors establish scaling laws designed to capture the specific behavior of differentially private language models. Their formulation describes the relationship between computation, privacy, and utility. Treating these quantities together matters because a useful training configuration must account for the privacy requirement alongside the available computational resources and desired model performance.

The resulting laws accurately model the intricacies of private training and identify optimal configurations in many settings. Their practical role is to support training decisions with predictions that reflect privacy-preserving training itself. The contribution extends the planning value of scaling laws to a setting where relying on the dynamics of ordinary training would leave an essential part of the compute and performance relationship unaccounted for.
summary.tldr: The paper develops scaling laws for differentially private language models that characterize compute, privacy, and utility trade-offs and guide training configurations.

title: Scaling Laws for Differentially Private Language Models

abstract: Randomized smoothing (RS) is popular for providing certified robustness guarantees against adversarial attacks. The average certified radius (ACR) has emerged as a widely used metric for tracking progress in RS. However, in this work, for the first time we show that ACR is a poor metric for evaluating robustness guarantees provided by RS. We theoretically prove not only that a trivial classifier can have arbitrarily large ACR, but also that ACR is extremely sensitive to improvements on easy samples. In addition, the comparison using ACR has a strong dependence on the certification budget. Empirically, we confirm that existing training strategies, though improving ACR, reduce the model’s robustness on hard samples consistently. To strengthen our findings, we propose strategies, including explicitly discarding hard samples, reweighing the dataset with approximate certified radius, and extreme optimization for easy samples, to replicate the progress in RS training and even achieve the state-of-the-art ACR on CIFAR-10, without training for robustness on the full data distribution. Overall, our results suggest that ACR has introduced a strong undesired bias to the field, and its application should be discontinued in RS. Finally, we suggest using the empirical distribution of $p_A$, the accuracy of the base model on noisy data, as an alternative metric for RS.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing provides certified guarantees against adversarial perturbations, and average certified radius is commonly used to compare its progress. This paper argues that the average can give a misleading picture of robustness. A model can improve the metric by concentrating on easy examples while becoming less robust on difficult ones.

The authors prove that even a trivial classifier can have an arbitrarily large average certified radius. They also show that the metric is highly sensitive to gains on easy samples and that comparisons depend strongly on the certification budget. Empirical results find that existing training strategies can raise the average while consistently reducing robustness on hard samples.

To demonstrate the problem directly, the paper explores discarding hard examples, reweighting data, and aggressively optimizing easy examples. These strategies can reproduce reported progress and reach state-of-the-art average certified radius on CIFAR-10 without training for robustness across the full distribution. The authors recommend abandoning this metric and propose examining the empirical distribution of the base model’s accuracy on noisy inputs instead.
summary.tldr: Average certified radius can reward gains on easy examples while concealing weaker robustness on hard examples.

title: Average Certified Radius is a Poor Metric for Randomized Smoothing

abstract: Image steganography ensures secure information transmission and storage by concealing secret messages within images. Recently, the diffusion model has been incorporated into the generative image steganography task, with text prompts being employed to guide the entire process. However, existing methods are plagued by three problems: (1) the restricted control exerted by text prompts causes generated stego images resemble the secret images and seem unnatural, raising the severe detection risk; (2) inconsistent intermediate states between Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models and its inversion, coupled with limited control of text prompts degrade the revealed secret images; (3) the descriptive text of images(i.e. text prompts) are also deployed as the keys, but this incurs significant security risks for both the keys and the secret images.To tackle these drawbacks, we systematically propose the SSHR, which joints the Reference Images with the adaptive keys to govern the entire process, enhancing the naturalness and imperceptibility of stego images. Additionally, we methodically construct an Exact Reveal Process to improve the quality of the revealed secret images. Furthermore, adaptive Reference-Secret Image Related Symmetric Keys are generated to enhance the security of both the keys and the concealed secret images. Various experiments indicate that our model outperforms existing methods in terms of recovery quality and secret image security.

paragraphs: Generative image steganography conceals a secret image inside another generated image. Existing diffusion-based approaches can leave the visible image looking unnatural or too similar to the secret, increasing detection risk. The paper also identifies degraded secret-image recovery and security problems when descriptive text prompts serve as the keys used in the process.

SSHR combines reference images with adaptive keys to guide generation and recovery. Reference-based guidance aims to make the visible images more natural and the hidden content less perceptible. The framework also introduces an Exact Reveal Process to improve reconstruction, addressing problems associated with inconsistent intermediate states between diffusion sampling and inversion.

Its symmetric keys depend on both the reference and secret images, providing an alternative to using descriptive prompts as keys. Experiments report better recovery quality and secret-image security than existing methods. The contribution brings together control of the visible image, improved recovery of the hidden image, and a revised key mechanism. The reported security advantage is comparative experimental evidence, rather than a claim that concealment is impossible to detect.
summary.tldr: SSHR combines reference-image guidance, adaptive symmetric keys, and an improved reveal process to strengthen image concealment and recovery.

title: SSHR: More Secure Generative Steganography with High-Quality Revealed Secret Images

abstract: We introduce a novel kernel learning framework toward efficiently solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). In contrast to the state-of-the-art kernel solver that embeds differential operators within kernels, posing challenges with a large number of collocation points, our approach eliminates these operators from the kernel. We model the solution using a standard kernel interpolation form and differentiate the interpolant to compute the derivatives. Our framework obviates the need for complex Gram matrix construction between solutions and their derivatives, allowing for a straightforward implementation and scalable computation. As an instance, we allocate the collocation points on a grid and adopt a product kernel, which yields a Kronecker product structure in the interpolation. This structure enables us to avoid computing the full Gram matrix, reducing costs and scaling efficiently to a large number of collocation points. We provide a proof of the convergence and rate analysis of our method under appropriate regularity assumptions. In numerical experiments, we demonstrate the advantages of our method in solving several benchmark PDEs.

paragraphs: This paper develops a kernel-based approach to solving nonlinear partial differential equations with lower computational overhead. The authors identify a scaling problem in solvers that embed differential operators inside kernels: constructing relationships among solutions and their derivatives becomes complicated as the number of collocation points grows.

The proposed method represents the solution with standard kernel interpolation and computes derivatives by differentiating that interpolant. This avoids the complex Gram matrix construction used by the compared approach. In a particular implementation, grid-based collocation points and a product kernel produce a Kronecker product structure, allowing computation without constructing the full Gram matrix.

The authors prove convergence and analyze its rate under appropriate regularity assumptions. Numerical experiments on several benchmark PDEs demonstrate advantages of the approach. Its significance lies in separating the solution representation from derivative evaluation and then exploiting structured interpolation. The convergence claim depends on the stated regularity conditions, while the described computational shortcut uses the grid and product-kernel structure.
summary.tldr: A kernel PDE solver differentiates a standard interpolant and exploits product structure to reduce computation, with convergence under regularity assumptions.

title: Toward Efficient Kernel-Based Solvers for Nonlinear PDEs

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is widely applied in multiple fields due to its advantages in efficiency and risk control. However, a major problem it faces is the distribution shift between offline datasets and online environments. This mismatch leads to out-of-distribution (OOD) state-action pairs that fall outside the scope of the training data. Therefore, existing conservative training policies may not provide reliable decisions when the test environment deviates greatly from the offline dataset. In this paper, we propose Test-time Adapted Reinforcement Learning (TARL) to address this problem. TARL constructs unsupervised test-time optimization objectives for discrete and continuous control tasks, using test data without depending on environmental rewards. In discrete control tasks, it minimizes the entropy of predicted action probabilities to decrease uncertainty and avoid OOD state-action pairs. For continuous control tasks, it represents and minimizes action uncertainty based on the normal distribution of policy network outputs. Moreover, to prevent model bias caused by overfitting and error accumulation during the test-time update process, TARL enforces a KL divergence constraint between the fine-tuned policy and the original policy. For efficiency, TARL only updates the layer normalization layer parameters during testing. Extensive experiments on popular Atari game benchmarks and the D4RL dataset demonstrate the superiority of our method. Our method achieved a significant improvement over CQL, with a 13.6% episode return relative increase on the hopper-expert-v2 task.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can struggle when deployment environments differ from its training data. The resulting unfamiliar state-action pairs can make even conservatively trained policies unreliable. TARL addresses this mismatch by adapting the policy during testing using unsupervised objectives, without requiring environmental rewards.

For discrete actions, TARL minimizes the entropy of predicted action probabilities to reduce uncertainty and avoid out-of-distribution state-action pairs. For continuous actions, it measures and minimizes uncertainty through the normal distribution represented by policy outputs. A KL divergence constraint keeps the adapted policy close to the original policy, addressing overfitting and error accumulation during repeated test-time updates.

To limit adaptation costs, TARL updates only layer normalization parameters. Experiments on Atari benchmarks and D4RL report improvements, including a 13.6% relative increase in episode return over CQL on hopper-expert-v2. The findings support a focused form of reward-free test-time adaptation that combines uncertainty reduction with a constraint on how far policy behavior can change.
summary.tldr: TARL adapts offline reinforcement learning policies at test time by reducing action uncertainty while constraining changes to the original policy.

title: Test-time Adapted Reinforcement Learning with Action Entropy Regularization

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are emerging as a brain-inspired alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), prized for their potential energy efficiency on neuromorphic hardware. Despite this, SNNs often suffer from accuracy degradation compared to ANNs and face deployment challenges due to fixed inference timesteps, which require retraining for adjustments, limiting operational flexibility. To address these issues, our work considers the spatio-temporal property inherent in SNNs, and proposes a novel distillation framework for deep SNNs that optimizes performance across full-range timesteps without specific retraining, enhancing both efficacy and deployment adaptability. We provide both theoretical analysis and empirical validations to illustrate that training guarantees the convergence of all implicit models across full-range timesteps. Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among distillation-based SNNs training methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Intelli-Chip-Lab/snn_temporal_decoupling_distillation.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy savings on neuromorphic hardware, but their accuracy and deployment flexibility remain challenges. In particular, a network trained for a fixed number of inference timesteps may need retraining when that number changes. This paper develops a distillation framework intended to make deep spiking networks effective across the full range of timesteps.

The approach accounts for the networks' spatial and temporal properties and uses logit-based knowledge distillation. Its central objective is to train the implicit models associated with different timestep choices together, enabling deployment adjustments without separate retraining. The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence supporting convergence of these implicit models across the timestep range.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet report state-of-the-art performance among distillation-based training methods for spiking networks. The practical significance is the combination of accuracy and flexibility: one training framework supports different inference durations. This addresses the deployment constraint directly, alongside the broader effort to make spiking networks more competitive with conventional neural networks.
summary.tldr: A distillation framework trains deep spiking networks for flexible inference across timestep choices without separate retraining.

title: Efficient Logit-based Knowledge Distillation of Deep Spiking Neural Networks for Full-Range Timestep Deployment

abstract: Recently, incorporating knowledge from pretrained language models (PLMs) into decision transformers (DTs) has generated significant attention in offline reinforcement learning (RL). These PLMs perform well in RL tasks, raising an intriguing question: what kind of knowledge from PLMs has been transferred to RL to achieve such good results? This work first dives into this problem by analyzing each head quantitatively and points out Markov head, a crucial component that exists in the attention heads of PLMs. It leads to extreme attention on the last-input token and performs well only in short-term environments. Furthermore, we prove that this extreme attention cannot be changed by re-training embedding layer or fine-tuning. Inspired by our analysis, we propose a general method GPT-DTMA, which equips a pretrained DT with Mixture of Attention (MoA), to enable adaptive learning and accommodate diverse attention requirements during fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GPT-DTMA: it achieves superior performance in short-term environments compared to baselines, significantly reduces the performance gap of PLMs in long-term scenarios, and the experimental results also validate our theorems.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can improve decision transformers used in offline reinforcement learning, but the source of that transferred benefit is not obvious. This paper analyzes individual attention heads and identifies Markov heads that concentrate strongly on the most recent input token. The authors link these heads to good performance in short-term environments and difficulties beyond them.

The paper also proves that retraining the embedding layer or fine-tuning cannot change the extreme attention behavior it analyzes. This finding motivates changing the attention mechanism itself. The proposed GPT-DTMA equips a pretrained decision transformer with a Mixture of Attention, allowing adaptive learning to accommodate different attention requirements during fine-tuning.

Experiments show better performance than baselines in short-term environments and a substantial reduction in the performance gap affecting pretrained language models in long-term scenarios. The results also support the theoretical findings. The contribution connects an internal attention pattern to the circumstances in which transfer helps, then introduces an architectural response intended to make the transferred model useful across a broader range of temporal demands.
summary.tldr: GPT-DTMA adds adaptive mixtures of attention to address pretrained heads that overemphasize the latest token in offline reinforcement learning.

title: Unveiling Markov heads in Pretrained Language Models for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail in systematic, model-specific ways under meaning-preserving question rewrites (paraphrases, format changes, benign distractors). In this work, we address this instability by identifying where the model’s reasoning process diverges across semantically-equivalent inputs. For each target LLM, we sample multiple solution traces under rewrites and aggregate them into a graph of recurring intermediate steps, which pinpoints where incorrect traces diverge from correct ones. We then generate a small set of semantics-preserving examples that mirror the rewrite patterns most responsible for these divergences, and use them to steer the model (targeted alternation training), either via fine-tuning or via in-context learning. Across MMLU-Pro, Big-MATH, and DROP, this yields consistent gains and cross-dataset generalization. On Humanity’s Last Exam, using 200 in-context examples, it improves GPT-5.2 (xhigh) from 35.4% to 38.1%, demonstrating that targeted alternation training can materially improve a frontier, API-accessible closed model under realistic access constraints.

paragraphs: A language model can answer a question correctly and fail when the same meaning appears in a different format or paraphrase. This paper targets such model-specific instability by examining where reasoning changes across equivalent inputs. Its starting point is the model’s intermediate solution process, which can reveal recurring patterns behind rewrite-induced errors.

For each target model, the method samples multiple solution traces under question rewrites and combines recurring intermediate steps into a graph. The graph helps locate where incorrect traces separate from correct ones. The authors then generate a small collection of meaning-preserving examples reflecting the rewrite patterns most responsible for those divergences, using them through fine-tuning or in-context learning.

The approach produces consistent gains across MMLU-Pro, Big-MATH, and DROP, including generalization across datasets. On Humanity’s Last Exam, two hundred in-context examples raise GPT-5.2 with xhigh reasoning from 35.4% to 38.1%. This demonstrates that examples targeted to observed reasoning failures can improve an API-accessible closed model without requiring access to its weights.
summary.tldr: Targeted examples drawn from rewrite-induced reasoning failures improve robustness through either fine-tuning or in-context learning.

title: Learning Rewrite-Invariant Reasoning with Targeted Alternation Training

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) based agents have demonstrated proficiency in multi-step interactions with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). While most research focuses on improving single-task performance, practical scenarios often involve repetitive GUI tasks for which invoking LLM reasoning repeatedly, i.e., the ReAct paradigm, is inefficient. Prior to LLMs, traditional Robotic Process Automation (RPA) offers runtime efficiency but demands significant manual effort to develop and maintain. To bridge this gap, we propose AutoRPA, a framework that automatically distills the decision logic of ReAct-style agents into robust RPA functions. AutoRPA introduces two core innovations: (1) A translator-builder pipeline where a translator agent converts hard-coded ReAct actions into soft-coded procedures, and a builder agent synthesizes robust RPA functions via retrieval-augmented generation over multiple trajectories; (2) A hybrid repair strategy during code verification, combining RPA execution with ReAct-based fallback for iterative refinement. Experiments across multiple GUI environments demonstrate that RPA functions generated by AutoRPA successfully solve similar tasks while reducing token usage by 82% 96%, significantly improving runtime efficiency and reusability.

paragraphs: AutoRPA addresses the cost of repeatedly asking a language model to reason through similar graphical interface tasks. Agents can handle multistep interactions, but repeating their reasoning consumes tokens and time. Traditional robotic process automation offers efficient execution, while requiring substantial manual work to create and maintain its scripts.

The framework converts interaction histories into reusable automation functions through a translator and builder pipeline. The translator turns actions tied to a particular interaction into more general procedures. The builder then uses retrieval over multiple trajectories to synthesize functions that capture reusable decision logic. This makes past agent behavior a source of automation code.

AutoRPA also verifies and repairs that code through a hybrid process: it executes the automation and uses a reasoning agent as a fallback during refinement. Across multiple GUI environments, the generated functions solve similar tasks with reported token reductions of 82–96%. These findings support reusing distilled procedures for repetitive work while retaining agent assistance during repair.
summary.tldr: AutoRPA turns GUI-agent interaction histories into reusable automation functions, reducing reported token use by 82–96% on similar tasks.

title: AutoRPA: Efficient GUI Automation through LLM-Driven Code Synthesis from Interactions

abstract: Recent work increasingly synthesizes agentic tasks for post-training tool-using LLMs, yet robust generalization under shifts in tasks and toolsets remains an open challenge. We trace this brittleness to insufficient diversity in synthesized training tasks. Scaling diversity is difficult because training requires tasks to remain executable and verifiable, while generalization demands diverse tool types, toolset combinations, and heterogeneous tool-use patterns. We propose DIVE, an evidence-driven recipe that inverts synthesis order, executing diverse real-world tools first and reverse-deriving tasks strictly entailed by the resulting traces, providing grounding by construction. DIVE scales structural diversity along two controllable axes, tool-pool coverage and per-task toolset variety, synthesizing 48k trajectories over 374 tools across five domains that cover 46,398 unique toolsets and 39,810 unique tool-call graphs. Training Qwen3-8B on DIVE data (48k SFT + 3.2k RL) improves by +22 average points across 9 OOD benchmarks and outperforms the strongest 8B baseline by +68%. Under a fixed budget, controlled scaling shows diversity scaling consistently outperforms quantity scaling, even with 4$\times$ less data.

Its challenge is to increase that diversity while keeping generated tasks executable and verifiable, so that variety does not come at the expense of grounded supervision.

DIVE reverses the synthesis process: it first executes diverse real-world tools, then derives tasks strictly supported by the resulting execution traces. It controls diversity through tool-pool coverage and the variety of tools used within each task. The resulting collection contains 48,000 trajectories across 374 tools and five domains, with 46,398 distinct toolsets and 39,810 distinct tool-call graphs.

Training Qwen3-8B with 48,000 supervised examples and 3,200 reinforcement learning examples improves performance by 22 average points across nine out-of-distribution benchmarks. It also exceeds the strongest 8B baseline by a reported 68%. Controlled experiments under a fixed budget find that increasing diversity consistently beats increasing quantity, even with four times less data.
summary.tldr: DIVE derives training tasks from real tool executions and finds that structural diversity improves generalization more than data quantity.

title: DIVE: Scaling Diversity in Agentic Task Synthesis for Generalizable Tool Use

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving the timeliness of knowledge updates and the factual accuracy of large language models. However, incorporating a large volume of retrieved documents significantly increases input length, leading to prohibitive computational costs. Existing compression approaches often compromise task performance, primarily due to their reliance on predefined heuristics. These heuristics fail to ensure that the compressed context is conducive to the generation tasks. To address these limitations, we propose CORE-RAG, a novel framework for context compression in RAG systems. CORE eliminates reliance on proxy heuristics through a performance-driven learning framework, which directy utilizes task performance as a feedback signal to iteratively refine the compressor policy. Prior to this optimization process, we incorporate a knowledge distillation phase to initialize the compressor with a robust policy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach. At a high compression ratio of 3%, CORE not only avoids performance degradation but also improves the average Exact Match (EM) score by 3.3 points compared to using full documents. Our code is available at https://github.com/ziqiangcui/CORE-RAG-ICML26.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation gives a language model external documents to help answer questions accurately and use current information. Large amounts of retrieved text also make the input expensive to process. Compressing that text can help, but a rule for deciding what looks important may discard information that the generation task actually needs.

CORE-RAG trains its compressor using task performance as feedback. It first uses knowledge distillation to initialize a useful compression policy, then iteratively refines that policy according to how well the resulting context supports the task. This directly connects compression decisions to the quality of generated answers, addressing the mismatch between predefined compression heuristics and downstream performance.

At the reported 3% compression ratio, CORE improves average Exact Match by 3.3 points compared with providing full documents. The experiments therefore show that substantial compression can coexist with better answer accuracy in the evaluated settings. The result makes context compression a learned part of task optimization, with efficiency and predictive quality assessed together rather than treating shorter input as the sole objective.
summary.tldr: CORE-RAG learns context compression from task feedback, achieving higher reported answer accuracy than full documents at a 3% compression ratio.

title: Less Is More: Elevating RAG via Performance-Driven Context Compression

abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) systems are often evaluated using binary correctness or peer agreement, yet such evaluations obscure how individual agents revise their answers during social interaction. We study the microscopic dynamics of answer revision in large language models (LLMs) using ConceptARC, a 2D grid-reasoning benchmark that admits quantitative distance measures between candidate solutions. By exposing a target model to controlled configurations of peer answers, we analyze how the likelihood and direction of revision depend on both social context and the distance between answers and the ground truth. We find that agents are more likely to revise when their answers are farther from the correct solution, and that revisions of incorrect answers exhibit a systematic contraction toward the ground truth, even when the final answer remains incorrect. Conversely, correct answers can be overturned by social pressure, particularly when wrong peers are near-correct. Together, these results show that multi-agent interaction induces structured, distance-aware movements in solution space that are invisible under binary correctness, clarifying when social reasoning leads to improvement, stability, or gradual regression in solution quality.

Evaluations based only on correctness or agreement miss whether that change moved the answer closer to the solution. This paper studies those intermediate movements using ConceptARC, a grid-reasoning benchmark where candidate answers can be compared through quantitative distances.

The researchers expose a target model to controlled combinations of peer answers. They examine both whether the model revises its answer and which direction the revision takes, accounting for the social context and distance from the correct solution. This design makes answer revision itself the object of study, rather than only the final success rate.

The experiments find that answers farther from the solution are more likely to change, and incorrect answers tend to move toward it even when they remain incorrect. However, social pressure can also overturn correct answers, especially when wrong peers are nearly correct. Distance-based evaluation therefore reveals both partial improvements and regressions that binary scoring conceals.
summary.tldr: Distance-based analysis reveals how model debates can improve still-incorrect answers while also pulling correct answers toward plausible mistakes.

title: Beyond Correctness: Distance-Based Social Dynamics of Multi-Agent Debate

abstract: We introduce a recursive AlphaZero style Monte–Carlo tree search algorithm, "RMCTS". It first generates the search tree using prior policies, and then recursively re-estimates action values by using the regularized optimal posterior policies from “Monte–Carlo tree search as regularized policy optimization” (Grill et al., 2020) at each node of the search tree, starting from the leaves and working back up to the root. We find that RMCTS matches or exceeds the quality of AlphaZero’s MCTS-UCB in a tiny fraction of the time.

paragraphs: Recursive Monte-Carlo Tree Search revisits how an AlphaZero-style search assigns values to possible actions. Its procedure separates construction of the search tree from a recursive re-estimation of action values. Prior policies guide the initial tree generation, giving the algorithm the structure on which its subsequent value computation operates.

The re-estimation then works from the leaves toward the root. At each node, RMCTS uses a regularized optimal posterior policy from an existing formulation of tree search as regularized policy optimization. Values are therefore reconsidered using these policies throughout the tree, with results from deeper nodes feeding into the calculations closer to the root.

The authors find that RMCTS matches or exceeds the quality of AlphaZero’s MCTS-UCB while taking a tiny fraction of the time. The reported contribution is a more efficient search procedure built around recursive policy-based value re-estimation. This finding concerns the evaluated search quality and runtime, with the bottom-up recursion providing the algorithm’s distinguishing mechanism.
summary.tldr: RMCTS recursively re-estimates tree-search values using regularized posterior policies, matching or exceeding AlphaZero’s MCTS-UCB quality much faster.

title: Recursive Monte-Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Recent advancements in agentic test-time scaling allow models to gather environmental feedback before committing to final actions. A key limitation of existing methods is that they typically employ undifferentiated exploration strategies, lacking the ability to adaptively distinguish when exploration is truly required. In this paper, we propose an exploration-aware reinforcement learning framework that enables LLM agents to adaptively explore only when uncertainty is high. Our method introduces a fine-grained reward function via variational inference that explicitly evaluates exploratory actions by estimating their potential to improve future decision-making, together with an exploration-aware grouping mechanism that separates exploratory actions from task-completion actions during optimization. By targeting informational gaps, this design allows agents to explore selectively and transition to execution as soon as the task context is clear. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach achieves consistent improvements across a range of challenging text-based and GUI-based agent benchmarks.
