paragraphs: An agent can gather feedback from its environment before deciding what to do. That extra interaction is useful when information is missing, but a uniform exploration strategy does not distinguish uncertain situations from ones that are already clear. This paper trains language-model agents to make exploration more selective.

The proposed reinforcement learning framework introduces a fine-grained reward derived through variational inference. It estimates how much an exploratory action could improve future decisions, giving information gathering an explicit role in training. A separate grouping mechanism distinguishes exploratory actions from task-completion actions during optimization, so the two kinds of behavior are not treated as interchangeable.

The intended result is an agent that targets information gaps and moves into execution once it has enough context. Experiments report consistent improvements across challenging text-based and graphical-interface agent benchmarks. The findings support teaching agents when further investigation is valuable, alongside teaching them how to finish tasks. The central contribution is this coupling of selective exploration with a training signal tied to its potential decision-making benefit.
summary.tldr: The framework rewards exploration for its potential to improve future decisions, helping agents investigate uncertainty selectively before executing tasks.

title: Learning to Explore: Scaling Agentic Reasoning via Exploration-Aware Policy Optimization

abstract: Large language models excel at short-horizon reasoning tasks, but performance drops as reasoning horizon lengths increase. In this work, we introduce a scalable method to bootstrap long-horizon reasoning capabilities using only existing, abundant short-horizon data. Our approach synthetically composes simple problems into complex, multi-step dependency chains of arbitrary length. We train models on this data using outcome-only rewards under a curriculum that automatically increases in complexity, allowing RL training to be scaled much further without saturating. Empirically, our method generalizes remarkably well: curriculum training on composed 6th-grade level math problems improves accuracy on longer, competition-level benchmarks. It also transfers significantly to diverse out-of-distribution ReasoningGym domains and long-context benchmarks, indicating broader generalization. Importantly, our long-horizon improvements are significantly higher than baselines even at high pass@k, showing that models can learn new reasoning paths under RL. Theoretically, we show that curriculum RL with outcome rewards could achieve an exponential improvement in sample complexity over full-horizon training, providing training signal comparable to dense supervision. h1 therefore introduces an efficient path towards scaling RL for long-horizon problems using only existing data.

paragraphs: Reasoning performance often declines as a problem requires a longer chain of dependent steps. h1 builds training material for these longer horizons by composing existing simple problems into dependency chains of arbitrary length. This uses abundant short-horizon data to supply increasingly complex tasks without requiring a separate collection of long-horizon examples.

Models learn through reinforcement learning with rewards based only on the final outcome. An automatic curriculum increases task complexity, allowing training to continue further before saturating. The theoretical analysis shows that this curriculum approach could improve sample complexity exponentially over training directly on full-horizon tasks, with a learning signal comparable to dense supervision.

Empirically, training on composed sixth-grade mathematics problems improves accuracy on longer competition-level tasks. Improvements also transfer to other ReasoningGym domains and long-context benchmarks. Gains remain substantially above the evaluated baselines even when many answer attempts are allowed, supporting the authors’ interpretation that reinforcement learning can produce new reasoning paths. Together, the results connect progressively harder task composition with broader long-horizon reasoning gains.
summary.tldr: h1 composes simple problems into an adaptive reinforcement-learning curriculum that improves longer-horizon reasoning using final-outcome rewards.

title: h1: Bootstrapping LLMs to Reason over Longer Horizons via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Causal inference typically assumes centralized access to individual-level data. Yet, in practice, data are often decentralized across multiple sites, making centralization infeasible due to privacy, logistical, or legal constraints. We address this problem by estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) from decentralized observational data via a Federated Learning (FL) approach, allowing inference through the exchange of aggregate statistics rather than individual-level data. We propose a novel method to estimate propensity scores via a federated weighted average of local scores using Membership Weights (MW), defined as probabilities of site membership conditional on covariates. MW can be flexibly estimated with parametric or non-parametric classification models using standard FL algorithms. The resulting propensity scores are used to construct Federated Inverse Propensity Weighting (Fed-IPW) and Augmented IPW (Fed-AIPW) estimators. In contrast to meta-analysis methods, which fail when any site violates positivity, our approach exploits heterogeneity in treatment assignment across sites to improve overlap. We show that Fed-IPW and Fed-AIPW perform well under site-level heterogeneity in sample sizes, treatment mechanisms, and covariate distributions. Theoretical analysis and experiments on simulated and real-world data demonstrate clear advantages over meta-analysis and related approaches.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects across institutions is difficult when individual records cannot be pooled. This paper develops a federated approach to estimating the average treatment effect from observational data, exchanging aggregate statistics while keeping individual-level data at their original sites.

The method combines local propensity scores, which describe treatment-assignment probabilities, using membership weights. These weights estimate how likely someone with given covariates is to belong to each site. They can be learned with parametric or non-parametric classifiers through standard federated learning methods. The combined scores then support two treatment-effect estimators, Fed-IPW and Fed-AIPW.

The key opportunity is that different sites may assign treatments differently. Combining that information can improve overlap between treated and untreated populations, even when a site's own treatment coverage causes problems for meta-analysis. Theoretical analysis and experiments on simulated and real-world data report advantages over meta-analysis and related methods. The estimators also perform well with differing site sizes, treatment mechanisms, and covariate distributions, showing how site heterogeneity can contribute useful information rather than only complicating analysis.
summary.tldr: Federated propensity-score aggregation uses differences across sites to improve treatment-effect estimation without pooling individual records.

title: Federated Causal Inference on Multi-Site Observational Data via Propensity Score Aggregation

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve superior problem-solving through extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation, but the resulting key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and creates severe memory bottlenecks—often exceeding GPU capacity for long reasoning traces. Existing KV cache compression methods rely on recent queries to estimate future token importance, implicitly assuming these serve as reliable proxies for future attention patterns. We demonstrate that this assumption fails in long-horizon reasoning: certain decoding steps generate Thought Revisiting Tokens (TRT) that re-attend to distant previous context, such as task-solving plans formulated early in the trace. Through systematic analysis, we discover that queries corresponding to the TRT cluster into a small number of similarity groups in the embedding space. Based on this insight, we propose BeaconKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that maintains beacon queries—compact representatives for each global query cluster—to anticipate which KV pairs will be revisited without storing the entire query history. Across four open-source LRMs and diverse reasoning benchmarks, BeaconKV generally outperforms existing compression methods, achieving up to $5.8\times$ memory reduction while nearly preserving full cache accuracy and improving throughput by over $4.3\times$.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces make language models retain increasingly large key-value caches, creating a memory bottleneck. Compression methods often use recent attention queries to predict which earlier information will matter next. This paper finds that the assumption can fail during extended reasoning, when particular tokens revisit distant context such as an early problem-solving plan.

The authors observe that queries associated with these revisiting tokens fall into a small number of similarity groups. BeaconKV keeps compact representatives of global query groups, called beacon queries, and uses them to anticipate which cached entries may be needed again. The central implication is that compression benefits from anticipating returns to earlier reasoning, rather than estimating relevance solely from the most recent steps.
summary.tldr: BeaconKV compresses reasoning-model caches using representative attention queries that anticipate revisits to earlier context.

title: BeaconKV: Key-Value Cache Compression Guided by Beacon Queries for Efficient Large Reasoning Model Inference

abstract: Prefill-Decode (PD) disaggregation has become the standard architecture for modern LLM inference engines, which alleviates the interference of two distinctive workloads. With the growing demand for multi-turn interactions in chatbots and agentic systems, we re-examined PD in this case and found two fundamental inefficiencies: (1) every turn requires prefilling the new prompt and response from the last turn, and (2) repeated KV transfers between prefill and decode nodes saturate the bandwidth, leading to high latency and even service degradation. Our key insight is that not all prefill operations are equally disruptive: append-prefill—processing only the new input tokens while reusing cached KV states—incurs substantially less decoding slowdown than full prefill. This motivates routing append-prefill to decode nodes locally. However, through comprehensive analysis, we show that no single fixed routing strategy satisfies all Service Level Objectives (SLOs) simultaneously. Based on this insight, we propose Prefill Prefill-capable Decode (PPD) disaggregation, a dynamic routing system that decides when to process Turn 2+ requests locally on decode nodes using cached KV states. PPD adapts to varying SLOs via configurable weights and seamlessly integrates with traditional PD deployments. With extensive evaluations, we show that PPD reduces Turn 2+ time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 68% while maintaining competitive time-per-output-token (TPOT), effectively alleviating KV transfer congestion under high load. We believe PPD represents a flexible and efficient paradigm for multi-turn LLM serving.

paragraphs: Language-model serving often separates prompt processing, called prefill, from token-by-token decoding. In multi-turn conversations, repeated processing and transfers of cached key-value states can cause high latency and congest the network. This paper observes that append-prefill, which processes new input while reusing cached states, disrupts decoding substantially less than full prefill.

That distinction creates an opportunity to handle later turns directly on decode nodes. However, the authors find that no single fixed routing strategy meets all service-level objectives simultaneously. Their Prefill Prefill-capable Decode architecture, or PPD, dynamically decides when to process Turn 2 and later requests locally. Configurable weights adapt routing to different service objectives, and the system integrates with existing prefill-decode deployments.

Evaluations show a 68% reduction in time to first token for later turns while maintaining competitive time per output token. PPD also alleviates cache-transfer congestion under high load. The results support treating cached continuation processing as a distinct workload whose placement should respond to service requirements.
summary.tldr: PPD dynamically routes later conversation turns to cache-holding decode nodes, reducing response latency and cache-transfer congestion.

title: Not All Prefills Are Equal: PPD Disaggregation for Multi-turn LLM Serving

abstract: Extending traditional graph anomaly detection (GAD) from one-for-one to one-for-all paradigms, generalist GAD aims to learn a universal detector for identifying anomalies on unseen graphs without graph-specific retraining. Nevertheless, existing approaches primarily focus on aligning heterogeneous features across different data domains via PCA-based projection, which harmonizes feature dimensions but neglects semantic alignment. As a result, GAD models fail to acquire semantically transferable knowledge from source-domain pre-training, and even exhibit negative transfer on unseen graphs. To address this issue, we propose a Relational Fingerprint-based generalist GAD approach (REFI-GAD for short), aligning heterogeneous raw features with a universal and semantics-aware relational fingerprint (REFI) that encodes anomaly-indicative cues from both contextual and structural perspectives. Building on REFI, we design a fingerprint-grounded generalist GAD model, which combines a transformer-based encoder to capture domain-invariant knowledge with an SNR-guided refinement module for domain-specific adaptation. Extensive experiments on 14 datasets demonstrate that REFI-GAD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Generalist graph anomaly detection aims to identify unusual patterns in previously unseen graphs without retraining a detector for each graph. A central obstacle is that features from different domains can have different meanings. Making feature vectors the same size through projection does not necessarily align those meanings.

REFI-GAD addresses this issue with a shared relational fingerprint. It encodes anomaly-related information from both context and graph structure, giving the detector a common representation grounded in relationships. The intended benefit is semantic transfer: pretraining should teach cues that remain meaningful on new graphs, avoiding the negative transfer associated with inadequate alignment.

The model combines a transformer encoder for learning domain-invariant information with an SNR-guided refinement module for domain-specific adaptation. This separates the pursuit of shared knowledge from the need to respond to differences in a target graph. Across 14 datasets, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support relational fingerprints as a more useful foundation for transfer than alignment that only harmonizes feature dimensions.
summary.tldr: REFI-GAD uses context-and-structure fingerprints to transfer anomaly-detection knowledge across graphs with heterogeneous features.

title: Rethinking Feature Alignment in Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection: A Relational Fingerprint-based Approach

abstract: Modern large language models are increasingly deployed under compute and memory constraints, making flexible control of model capacity a central challenge. While sparse and low-rank structures naturally trade off capacity and performance, existing approaches often rely on heuristic designs that ignore layer and matrix heterogeneity or require model-specific architectural modifications. We propose SALAAD, a plug-and-play framework applicable to different model architectures that induces sparse and low-rank structures during training. By formulating structured weight learning under an augmented Lagrangian framework and introducing an adaptive controller that dynamically balances the training loss and structural constraints, SALAAD preserves the stability of standard training dynamics while enabling explicit control over the evolution of effective model capacity during training. Experiments across model scales show that SALAAD substantially reduces memory consumption during deployment while achieving performance comparable to ad-hoc methods. Moreover, a single training run yields a continuous spectrum of model capacities, enabling smooth and elastic deployment across diverse memory budgets without the need for retraining.

paragraphs: Deploying language models under different memory budgets requires control over how much model capacity is retained. Sparse and low-rank weight structures offer this flexibility, but existing designs can ignore differences between layers and matrices or require architecture-specific changes. SALAAD introduces a framework that learns these structures during training across different model architectures.

The method formulates structured weight learning through an augmented Lagrangian approach. An adaptive controller dynamically balances the ordinary training loss against structural constraints. This is intended to preserve stable training behavior while explicitly controlling how effective model capacity evolves. The structural requirements therefore participate in optimization instead of being handled only through fixed heuristic choices.

Across model scales, experiments show substantially lower deployment memory use with performance comparable to ad-hoc methods. A single training run produces a continuous spectrum of capacities, allowing deployment to adapt smoothly to different memory budgets without retraining. The practical significance is the ability to obtain multiple usable capacity levels from one training process while keeping the framework applicable across architectures.
summary.tldr: SALAAD learns sparse and low-rank structures during training, enabling flexible deployment across memory budgets from a single training run.

title: SALAAD: Sparse And Low-Rank Adaptation via ADMM for Large Language Model Inference

abstract: In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have achieved remarkable progress, with Spiking Transformers emerging as a promising architecture for energy-efficient sequence modeling. However, existing Spiking Transformers still lack a principled mechanism for effective temporal fusion, limiting their ability to fully exploit spatiotemporal dependencies. Inspired by feedforward–feedback modulation in the human visual pathway, we propose TEFormer, the first Spiking Transformer framework that achieves bidirectional temporal fusion by decoupling temporal modeling across its core components. Specifically, TEFormer employs a lightweight and hyperparameter-free forward temporal fusion mechanism in the attention module, enabling fully parallel computation, while incorporating a backward gated recurrent structure in the MLP to aggregate temporal information in reverse order and reinforce temporal consistency. Extensive experiments across a wide range of benchmarks demonstrate that TEFormer consistently and significantly outperforms strong SNN and Spiking Transformer baselines under diverse datasets. Moreover, through the first systematic evaluation of Spiking Transformers under different neural encoding schemes, we show that the performance gains of TEFormer remain stable across encoding choices, indicating that the improved temporal modeling directly translates into reliable accuracy improvements across varied spiking representations. abstract: We compare the efficacy and distributional effects of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for PlasmidGPT, a foundation model for whole-plasmid generation, using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for the RL model. Using a biologically motivated reward function encoding functional annotations, length constraints, and repeat penalties, the RL model achieves a 71.6% quality-control pass rate across 8 prompts on 4,000 sequences, compared to 4.3% for the pretrained baseline and 11.0% for SFT. A five-model reward ablation identifies the cassette arrangement bonus, which rewards correct promoter$\rightarrow$CDS$\rightarrow$terminator ordering, as the critical reward component. Rejectionsampling baselines indicate that the gain is not recovered by sampling more heavily from the base model. Beyond directly optimized features, RLgenerated sequences converge toward real plasmid distributions in 3-mer composition and minimum free energy density, neither of which is directly optimized by the reward function. Minimum free energy density independently converges to the real-plasmid regime under both SFT and RL despite these being parallel post-training paths. On a small curated hold-out set, RL improves continuation log-likelihood over the pretrained baseline on all 29 held-out sequences (mean $\Delta$ = +0.83 nats).

summary.tldr: Structural reward shaping substantially improves plasmid-generation quality control and shifts some unrewarded properties toward real-plasmid distributions.

title: Effects of Structural Reward Shaping on Biophysical Properties in RL-Trained Plasmid Generators

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) can achieve competitive performance by converting already existing well-trained Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), avoiding further costly training. This property is particularly attractive in Reinforcement Learning (RL), where training through environment interaction is expensive and potentially unsafe. However, existing conversion methods perform poorly in continuous control, where suitable baselines are largely absent. We identify error amplification as the key cause: small action approximation errors become temporally correlated across decision steps, inducing cumulative state distribution shift and severe performance degradation. To address this issue, we propose Cross-Step Residual Potential Initialization (CRPI), a lightweight gradient-free mechanism that carries over residual membrane potentials across decision steps to suppress temporally correlated errors. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks with both vector and visual observations demonstrate that CRPI can be integrated into existing conversion pipelines and substantially recovers lost performance. Our results highlight continuous control as a critical and challenging benchmark for ANN-to-SNN conversion, where small errors can be strongly amplified and impact performance. Code is available at https://github.com/xuzijie32/ANN2SNN-CRPI.

paragraphs: Converting a trained artificial neural network into a spiking neural network can avoid another expensive training process. That possibility is attractive for reinforcement learning, where gathering experience can be costly or unsafe. However, the paper finds that existing conversion methods struggle when the resulting network must produce continuous control actions.

The identified problem is error amplification across decisions. Small errors in approximating actions become correlated over time, changing the states the controller encounters and progressively damaging performance. CRPI addresses this by carrying residual membrane potentials across decision steps. This lightweight, gradient-free mechanism is designed to suppress the temporal correlations that allow small conversion errors to accumulate.

Experiments with both vector and visual observations show that CRPI can fit into existing conversion pipelines and substantially recover lost performance. The findings make continuous control an informative test of conversion quality: preserving individual outputs approximately can still leave harmful errors across a sequence of interacting decisions. CRPI targets that sequential failure directly.
summary.tldr: CRPI carries residual membrane potentials across control steps to reduce error amplification when converting trained networks into spiking networks.

title: Error Amplification Limits ANN-to-SNN Conversion in Continuous Control

abstract: A reliable reward model is essential for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, standard reward models are susceptible to spurious features that are not causally related to human labels. This can lead to reward hacking, where high predicted reward does not translate into better behavior. In this work, we address this problem from a causal perspective by proposing a factored representation learning framework that decomposes the model’s contextual embedding into (1) causal factors that are sufficient for reward prediction and (2) non-causal factors that capture reward-irrelevant attributes such as length or sycophantic bias. The reward head is then constrained to depend only on the causal component. In addition, we introduce an adversarial head trained to predict reward from the non-causal factors, while applying gradient reversal to discourage them from encoding reward-relevant information. Experiments on both mathematical and dialogue tasks demonstrate that our method learns more robust reward models and consistently improves downstream RLHF performance over state-of-the-art baselines. Analyses on length and sycophantic bias further validate the effectiveness of our method in mitigating reward hacking behaviors.

paragraphs: A reward model can assign high scores for superficial attributes that do not reflect the behavior people actually prefer. Optimizing against such a model can produce reward hacking: the score improves without a corresponding improvement in behavior. This paper addresses that problem by separating the contextual representation used to predict rewards into two components.

One component is intended to contain causal factors sufficient for reward prediction. The other captures reward-irrelevant attributes, including length or sycophantic bias. The reward prediction head can access only the causal component. An additional adversarial head tries to predict reward from the non-causal component, while gradient reversal discourages that component from retaining reward-relevant information.

Experiments on mathematical and dialogue tasks report more robust reward models and consistent improvements in downstream RLHF over state-of-the-art baselines. Analyses focused on length and sycophancy also support reduced reward hacking. These findings support controlling which parts of a learned representation can influence reward predictions as a way to improve the behavior produced by subsequent optimization.
summary.tldr: Separating reward-relevant and irrelevant representations improves reward robustness and reduces observed reward hacking in RLHF.

title: Factored Causal Representation Learning for Robust Reward Modeling in RLHF

abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models in language modeling, offering the advantages of parallel decoding and bidirectional context processing within a simple yet effective framework. Specifically, their explicit distinction between masked tokens and data underlies their simple framework and effective conditional generation. However, MDMs typically require many sampling iterations due to factorization errors stemming from simultaneous token updates. We observe that a theoretical lower bound of the factorization error exists, which standard MDMs cannot reduce due to their use of a deterministic single-state mask. In this paper, we propose the Infinite Mask Diffusion Model (IMDM), which introduces a stochastic infinite-state mask to mitigate the theoretical bound while directly inheriting the benefits of MDMs, including the compatibility with pre-trained weights. We empirically demonstrate that MDM fails to perform few-step generation even in a simple synthetic task due to the factorization error bound, whereas IMDM can find an efficient solution for the same task. Finally, when equipped with appropriate distillation methods, IMDM surpasses existing few-step distillation methods at small step counts on LM1B and OpenWebText.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models generate text through repeated updates to masked tokens, allowing parallel decoding and access to context in both directions. However, updating several tokens simultaneously introduces factorization errors. These errors make it difficult to produce good outputs in very few sampling steps, even though parallel generation is a central attraction of the approach.

The paper identifies a theoretical lower bound on this error that standard masked diffusion models cannot reduce because they use one deterministic mask state. Infinite Mask Diffusion replaces that state with a stochastic mask having infinitely many possible states. The proposed model retains the advantages of distinguishing masked positions from data and remains compatible with pretrained weights.

On a simple synthetic task, standard masked diffusion fails at few-step generation because of the identified error bound, while the new model finds an efficient solution. With appropriate distillation methods, it also outperforms existing few-step distillation approaches at small step counts on LM1B and OpenWebText. The result ties faster generation to changing the mask representation itself.
summary.tldr: Infinite Mask Diffusion replaces a single deterministic mask state with stochastic mask states to improve few-step text generation.

title: Infinite Mask Diffusion for Few-Step Distillation

abstract: The long-standing dominance of gradient-boosted decision trees for tabular data has recently been challenged by in-context learning tabular foundation models. In-context learning methods fit and predict in one forward pass without parameter updates by leveraging the training data as context for predicting on query test points. While recent tabular foundation models achieve state-of-the-art performance, their transformer architecture based on the attention mechanism has quadratic complexity regarding dataset size, which in turn increases the overhead on training and inference time, and limits the capacity of the models to handle large-scale datasets. In this work, we propose TACO, an end-to-end tabular compression model that compresses the training dataset in a latent space. We test our method on the TabArena benchmark, where our proposed method is up to 94x faster in inference time, while consuming up to 97% less memory compared to the state-of-the-art tabular Transformer architecture, all while retaining performance without significant degradation. Lastly, our method not only scales better with increased dataset sizes, but it also achieves better performance compared to other baselines.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models can make predictions by taking training examples as context, without updating their parameters for each new dataset. This makes their use different from fitting a separate model through repeated parameter updates. However, transformer attention has quadratic complexity in dataset size, creating substantial time and memory costs as the context grows.

TACO addresses that bottleneck by learning to compress the training dataset into a latent representation. The compression is trained end to end, making it part of the overall modeling approach. The central idea is to reduce the amount of contextual information the tabular model must process while retaining the information needed for useful predictions.

On TabArena, the method reports inference up to 94 times faster and memory consumption up to 97% lower than the compared state-of-the-art tabular Transformer, without significant performance degradation. The abstract also reports better scaling with dataset size and stronger performance than other baselines. These are reported maximum efficiency gains, supporting learned dataset compression as a practical route to larger tabular workloads.
summary.tldr: TACO compresses tabular training data into latent representations, reporting much faster inference and lower memory use while largely retaining predictive performance.

title: End-to-End Compression for Tabular Foundation Models

abstract: The scaling hypothesis assumes that increasing model parameters yields emergent reasoning capabilities. This position paper argues that applying this probabilistic paradigm to generic quantum circuit synthesis is a directional error. Unlike natural languages, quantum circuits require strict adherence to mathematical constraints that manifest a significant syntax-semantics gap. Training on unverified quantum programs means that models learn syntax but fail to capture the physical semantics of the Hilbert space. Since the valid subset of circuit designs decays exponentially with the number of qubits, post-hoc filtering is mathematically intractable. We propose a pivot from human-centric copilots to verifier-centric agents. We integrate hierarchical constraints, topological masks, and symbolic proxies directly into generation. Our analysis suggests that scale alone cannot bridge the validity gap. Verification-aware architectures offer a viable path for modular quantum program generation. These considerations point toward generation methods that encode task-specific rules of quantum information, rather than relying on imitation alone.

paragraphs: The paper argues that generating valid quantum programs requires mathematical constraints to shape generation itself. A circuit can resemble valid examples at the level of syntax while failing to capture the physical meaning required in Hilbert space. The authors contend that training on unverified programs encourages this gap, making generic quantum circuit synthesis a poor fit for relying on model scaling alone.

Their argument emphasizes the shrinking fraction of valid circuit designs as qubit counts increase, which they describe as exponential. On that basis, they argue that filtering generated candidates afterward becomes mathematically intractable. Their analysis suggests that greater scale alone cannot close the gap between plausible program form and valid quantum behavior.

The proposed alternative centers generation on verification. Hierarchical constraints, topological masks, and symbolic proxies are integrated into the process so task-specific quantum rules influence what can be produced. The authors present verification-aware architectures as a viable direction for modular program generation, shifting the design objective toward circuits whose validity is supported during construction.
summary.tldr: The paper argues for incorporating quantum validity constraints into program generation rather than relying on scaling and post-generation filtering.

abstract: A new algorithm for training Restricted Boltzmann Machines is introduced. The algorithm, named Persistent Contrastive Divergence, is different from the standard Contrastive Divergence algorithms in that it aims to draw samples from almost exactly the model distribution. It is compared to some standard Contrastive Divergence algorithms on the tasks of modeling handwritten digits and classifying digit images by learning a model of the joint distribution of images and labels. The Persistent Contrastive Divergence algorithm outperforms other Contrastive Divergence algorithms, and is equally fast and simple.

It is compared to some standard Contrastive Divergence algorithms on the tasks of modeling handwritten digits and classifying digit images by learning a model of the joint distribution of images and labels. The Persistent Contrastive Divergence algorithm outperforms other Contrastive Divergence algorithms, and is equally fast and simple.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Persistent Contrastive Divergence, a training algorithm for Restricted Boltzmann Machines. Its key distinction from standard Contrastive Divergence is the sampling objective: it aims to obtain samples from almost exactly the model's distribution. This places the quality of the samples used during learning at the center of the proposed change.

The authors compare the algorithm with standard Contrastive Divergence methods on two digit-related tasks. One is modeling handwritten digits. The other is classifying digit images by learning a joint distribution over images and labels. These tasks examine the training method in both a data-modeling role and a classification setting built around a learned joint model.

Persistent Contrastive Divergence outperforms the comparison algorithms in the reported study while remaining equally fast and simple. The finding matters because the observed improvement does not come with a reported increase in those practical costs. The sampling description remains an aim of the algorithm, while the stronger performance claim is grounded in the digit experiments presented.
summary.tldr: Persistent Contrastive Divergence improves reported RBM digit-modeling and classification results while remaining as fast and simple as the compared methods.

title: Training restricted Boltzmann machines using approximations to the likelihood gradient

abstract: In this paper, we present a novel method to speed up the learning of embeddings for large-scale learning tasks involving very sparse data, as is typically the case for Natural Language Processing tasks. Our speed-up method has been developed in the context of Denoising Auto-encoders, which are trained in a purely unsupervised way to capture the input distribution, and learn embeddings for words and text similar to earlier neural language models. The main contribution is a new method to approximate reconstruction error by a sampling procedure. We show how this approximation can be made to obtain an unbiased estimator of the training criterion, and we show how it can be leveraged to make learning much more computationally efficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on the Amazon and RCV1 NLP datasets. Instead of reducing vocabulary size to make learning practical, our method allows us to train using very large vocabularies. In particular, reconstruction sampling requires 22x less training time on the full Amazon dataset.

paragraphs: Learning embeddings from very sparse data can become computationally expensive when the input vocabulary is large. This paper addresses that problem in denoising auto-encoders, which learn representations without labeled supervision by capturing the input distribution. The target applications include word and text representations for natural-language processing.

The main contribution is reconstruction sampling: a procedure that approximates reconstruction error through sampling. The authors show how to construct an unbiased estimator of the training criterion, meaning that the sampled estimate agrees with that criterion on average. This connects the computational shortcut to the original learning objective while making training substantially more efficient.

Experiments on Amazon and RCV1 data demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Instead of shrinking the vocabulary to make training feasible, the approach permits learning with very large vocabularies. On the full Amazon dataset, the reported training-time reduction is a factor of 22. That result is specific to the reported setting, while the broader contribution is a sampling-based way to reduce reconstruction cost when learning from large, sparse inputs.
summary.tldr: Reconstruction sampling provides an unbiased training-criterion estimate and reduces full-Amazon training time by a reported factor of 22.

title: Large-Scale Learning of Embeddings with Reconstruction Sampling
